Sales routes for a Philadelphia homeowner

Most Philadelphia owners pick from three paths: an agent, a sale by owner, or a cash buyer. Each ends at the Department of Records with a recorded deed and the city's transfer tax. The difference lies in timing, repairs and what you walk away with.

The city is also its own county. Philadelphia and Philadelphia County have shared one government since 1854, so the assessment office, the tax collector and the deed recorder are all city departments, and no outside courthouse comes into a typical sale.

  • A listing works for a rowhouse in good shape that can sit through weeks of showings while a buyer's loan is approved.
  • Going it alone saves the commission, though you handle the contract and settlement details yourself.
  • Cash fits deferred repairs, a clouded title, a tenant in the house or an estate being closed out.

Transfer tax and recording costs

The largest single cost the city sets is the realty transfer tax. Since July 1, 2025 the combined rate has been 4.578%, made up of 3.578% for the city and 1% for the Commonwealth. The rate had last changed in 2018, and the increase is earmarked for affordable housing programs.

Your sales agreement assigns the cost, so check that clause first. The tax is due when the deed is recorded. The city allows up to 30 days after the purchase, yet the Department of Revenue advises settling it at closing, and the Philadelphia Tax Center takes online payment.

Philadelphia transfer tax and recording charges, rates in effect from July 1, 2025
ChargeAmount
City realty transfer tax3.578% of price or assessed value
Commonwealth realty transfer tax1%
Combined transfer tax4.578%
Recording a deed$277.75
Recording a mortgage$247.75
Recording a mortgage satisfaction$230.75

When there is no sale price, such as a transfer between relatives, the tax is figured on the value the Office of Property Assessment has set for the property.

Exempt transfers

Deeds to a spouse, child or grandchild escape the tax, as do transfers under a will. Each family exemption must be backed by papers filed with the deed. Collect them before settlement rather than counting on the settlement agent to do it.

Estates trip up many families. The house passes tax-free to the heirs under the will, but a later sale by those heirs to a buyer is taxed. If you inherited a Philadelphia house and plan to sell, budget for the full rate at that second step.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Philadelphia house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Rowhouses and the housing market

The city had an estimated 1,574,281 residents in July 2025, down about 1.8% from April 2020. Most of the housing stock dates to the 18th, 19th and early 20th centuries. Federal-style blocks stand in Old City and Society Hill, Victorian homes fill North Philadelphia, and twin houses are common in West Philadelphia. A buyer or investor looking at an older rowhouse will price in the roof, the party walls and the plumbing, which is why condition drives offers more here than in newer suburbs.

  • The middle home value for owners is $243,100 in the 2020 to 2024 figures, with 51.8% of households owning.
  • Rent runs a median $1,397 a month across 679,428 households of 2.26 people on average.
  • Commutes average 31.7 minutes.

Property taxes and the Homestead Exemption

The Office of Property Assessment sets values, and the Department of Revenue bills them. Bills go out each December 1, new assessments take effect January 1, and payment is due March 31. Ask the Office of Property Assessment how to dispute a value, since the review deadlines fall in early fall each year.

The Homestead Exemption takes $100,000 off the taxable portion of an owner-occupied home's assessed value, and most owners save $1,399 a year. A mortgage or delinquent taxes leave eligibility intact, while a 10-year abatement rules it out. An accepted application keeps working until the deed changes, so a buyer who will live in the house files their own application. The final date to apply is December 1 each year, and applying by October 1 puts the credit on the first bill.

  • An heir without their name on the deed can ask for a conditional Homestead Exemption, granted for up to three years, using a paper application marked Tangled Title.
  • Seniors and income-qualified owners can pay in eleven monthly installments if they apply by March 31.
  • The owner-occupied payment agreement can set a monthly payment as low as zero for past-due tax.

For a house with back taxes, ask the Department of Revenue for a payoff figure before you accept an offer, because delinquent tax is paid from the proceeds.

Seller disclosure

Chapter 73 of Title 68, the Real Estate Seller Disclosure Law, calls for a signed statement about known defects, handed over before any agreement of transfer is signed. Seventeen subjects appear on the form, among them the roof, basement, wiring, drainage and title questions. Nothing forces you to hire testers, yet you cannot assert what you know is untrue.

Act 74 adds section 7305.2, a flood insurance notice that goes to the buyer once the Insurance Department publishes its flood information page. Suits over a violation must start within two years of final settlement, and an executor selling for an estate stands outside the chapter.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Philadelphia houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Where to begin

Two records decide how fast a closing moves: the deed and the tax account. The city's property search shows the assessed value, any homestead credit and the balance owed, while the deed tells you who has to sign.

  • Collect the deed, your latest bill and a lender payoff letter if you have a mortgage.
  • Keep papers proving family relationships if the transfer could be exempt.
  • Compare each repair with what it would add to your price.
  • Agree on the transfer tax split in writing, whoever the buyer is.

Any buyer worth talking to will explain the tax, the recording charge and the payoff up front and let you say no.

What happens on closing day

The signing is brief. You execute the deed, the transfer tax and recording charge are paid, and the title company deducts your mortgage payoff and any past-due tax before wiring the rest. Without a lender in the deal, timing hinges on how fast the title search and payoff figures arrive. When the buyer needs a loan, the lender controls part of the calendar.

Inherited houses need the will paperwork in hand. With a tenant in place, set the move-out date in writing so closing isn't left to chance.

Frequently asked questions

What is the transfer tax rate for a Philadelphia house sale?

The rate is 4.578%, made of 3.578% for the city and 1% for the Commonwealth, and it has applied since July 1, 2025. It is figured on the price, or on the assessed value if no price exists. The contract says who pays.

Can heirs sell an inherited house in Philadelphia?

Yes. The passing of the house under a will is exempt from transfer tax, but when the heirs sell to an outside buyer that sale is taxed. An heir whose name is missing from the deed may request a conditional Homestead Exemption lasting up to three years.

Does the Homestead Exemption pass to a buyer?

No, a buyer who will live in the home applies separately, since an accepted application lasts only until the deed changes. December 1 is the yearly cutoff, and October 1 is the date that gets the credit onto the first bill.

When is the Philadelphia real estate tax due?

March 31. Bills are mailed from December 1 of the prior year. Seniors and income-qualified owners may spread payment over eleven monthly installments by applying before March 31.

What if a Philadelphia seller omits a known defect?

The seller can owe the buyer actual damages. A buyer may sue a seller who willfully or negligently breaks the disclosure duties, with the case filed inside two years of final settlement.

Selling in Pittsburgh?

Your choices for selling a Pittsburgh house

Pittsburgh sellers usually weigh three paths: an agent listing, a sale by owner, or a purchase for cash. A listing reaches the most shoppers but leans on showings and a buyer's financing. A cash buyer takes the property in whatever condition it is in and can often close on a date you pick, which helps when the roof leaks, the stairs are failing or an estate wants out quickly.

Three local facts shape every path. The city doesn't demand a Certificate of Occupancy at sale, Allegheny County gathers the transfer tax at recording, and school tax on the city bill has its own collection rules. Sorting them out early keeps the closing date from slipping, and it tells you what the sale will really put in your pocket.

  • Find out who holds title and whether a mortgage or lien must be cleared from the proceeds.
  • Look up the Certificate of Occupancy record on the city's online search.
  • Have the settlement agent total the transfer tax before you agree to a price.

Transfer tax on a Pittsburgh sale

A sale inside the city carries a 5% realty transfer tax in most cases: 1% to the Commonwealth, 3% to the city and 1% to the Pittsburgh School District. Allegheny County collects it for all three when the deed goes on record, and it is paid by a separate check from the recording fees. Residential deeds recorded from February 1, 2020 onward carry the city's full 5%.

Part of the city lies in the Baldwin-Whitehall School District, where the school share is one half of one percent instead of 1%, so addresses there total 4.5%. The county's rate table lists each school district, so match your parcel to the right line before you estimate your proceeds.

Transfer tax split for a house in the city of Pittsburgh
Taxing bodyRate
Commonwealth of Pennsylvania1%
City of Pittsburgh3%
Pittsburgh School District1%
Total5%

The sales agreement states who pays. Transfers between close family members may need only a statement on the deed describing the relationship, while other exemptions need the state's Statement of Value form.

Certificate of Occupancy

Pittsburgh doesn't require a Certificate of Occupancy to sell or buy a property, unlike many municipalities around it. That doesn't mean a property meets every zoning and building code, and many older single-family homes have no certificate on file because past rules didn't call for one.

A buyer may have to apply for an Occupancy Permit if the use of the building differs from the use on the latest certificate. The city tells parties to complete a Zoning Certificate request so the transaction meets Pennsylvania law. The most recent certificate is the current legal use, and two certificates can together cover a building approved in stages.

  • Search the Permits, Licenses, and Inspections online occupancy tool by address, parcel number, permit number or ward.
  • If a certificate should exist but doesn't appear, email the records office and expect a reply within five business days.
  • If you hold a certificate that is missing from the city's files, send a copy so it is added to the library.

Owning and selling in Pittsburgh

Pittsburgh had 302,971 residents in 2020 and an estimate of 307,632 for July 2025, a gain of 1.5%. The city is divided into 90 neighborhoods, and the terrain is hilly: many streets are steep two-lane roads, and the city keeps about 800 sets of public stairways. Buyers pay attention to slope, drainage and retaining walls.

  • The middle home value among owners is $205,800 in the 2020 to 2024 figures.
  • Only 47.7% of households own, so more rent than own.
  • Median rent is $1,261 across 138,188 households.

Property taxes a seller must settle

The city, the parks fund, the Carnegie Library and the Pittsburgh School District all bill on the value set by the Allegheny County Office of Property Assessments. County values follow a base year of 2012, so the assessed figure is not a current market price. Bills go out in January, the full amount is due at the end of February, and a 2% discount applies for early payment. Installments fall at the end of February, April and July.

If you owe tax from earlier years, the city keeps past-due city, library and parks tax, while past-due school tax sits with Jordan Tax Service, Inc. An unpaid balance can lead to a Treasurer's Sale. Ask the Department of Finance and the collector for payoff figures before closing, since both come out of the proceeds.

The homestead program reduces the taxable value of an owner-occupied home. The city's reduction is $15,000, worth $120.90 a year in city tax, and a county homestead application also activates the city, school and library exemptions. A buyer who will live in the house should apply through the county.

Assessment appeals follow an annual window that opens July 1 and closes in early September. Check the county's real estate portal for the exact dates.

Seller disclosure

Under Title 68, Chapter 73 of the state code, you hand the buyer a signed, dated statement of known defects before anyone signs the agreement of transfer. Its subjects include additions and remodeling, water and sewer service, and land features such as sinkholes, drainage and flood risk indicators. Because of the city's slopes, take extra care with the land and drainage lines.

No special investigation is required, but a false statement is not allowed. A change in the facts before settlement must be passed to the buyer, a condominium seller covers only the unit, and a fiduciary selling for an estate is exempt from the chapter.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Pittsburgh houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Work out your net before agreeing to a price

Take the offer, then subtract the 5% or 4.5% transfer tax if you pay it, recording fees, any mortgage payoff, unpaid tax and the repairs a buyer will ask for. The result is the number to compare across a listing, a sale by owner and a cash bid.

  • Is the parcel in the city, or in a nearby borough with a lower rate?
  • Does the certificate on file match how the house is used?
  • Are the city, library, parks and school installments current?
  • Whose name is on the deed, and does probate or a payoff come first?

A cash sale skips the buyer's loan approval and appraisal. At closing the deed is signed, the county records it with the transfer tax, and the title company pays off tax balances and your mortgage before sending you the rest.

Frequently asked questions

Is a Certificate of Occupancy needed for a Pittsburgh sale?

No. The city doesn't require one at sale. A buyer may still need an Occupancy Permit when the intended use differs from the last certificate, and the city points parties to a Zoning Certificate request.

How big is the transfer tax inside Pittsburgh?

Five percent for most addresses: 1% state, 3% city, 1% Pittsburgh School District. Part of the city sits in the Baldwin-Whitehall district, whose half-percent share brings the total to 4.5%. The county takes payment when the deed is filed.

When do Pittsburgh property tax payments fall due?

The full bill is due at the end of February, with installments at the end of February, April and July. Early payment earns a 2% discount.

When can I contest my Allegheny County assessment?

During the annual window that opens July 1 and closes in early September. The county portal announces the exact dates if you believe the value is wrong.

Does my homestead exemption go with the house?

No. It ends with your ownership and the new owner applies. The city reduction is $15,000, and an application to the county also switches on the city, school district and library exemptions for a resident owner.

Pre-sale inspection

Allentown requires a safety and maintenance inspection before a residential or commercial property is sold. The city's pre-sale inspection page describes a visit that checks the property against the Allentown Property Maintenance Code and the zoning rules.

How the pre-sale inspection runs
StageWhat happens
ApplicationFollow the Pre-Sale Inspection Procedure, then apply online for a Pre-Sale permit
InspectionAn inspector schedules the visit
Passing resultThe property receives a Certificate of Compliance before the sale
Violations foundThe seller fixes them, or the buyer agrees to take the repairs on using the city's Acceptance Form
After settlementThe seller or agent submits a Buyer's Information Report within three days

There is no exception for cash or as-is sales, so plan on the inspection whichever way you sell. Call Building Standards and Safety to learn today's fee and how soon an appointment is available, and only then pick a closing date.

If the inspector finds violations

Two paths follow a failed visit. Make the repairs and request a second inspection, or find a buyer who will take the work over. That buyer signs the Acceptance Form, so the agreement sits with the city and not only in the sales contract.

Be candid with buyers about problems you cannot fund before closing. Investors and cash buyers frequently agree to the repairs, and raising it before the inspection date goes better than raising it after a failed visit. Keep the Certificate of Compliance with your settlement papers once you have it.

Preparing for the inspector's visit

The code is the Allentown Property Maintenance Code plus the zoning rules, so the visit covers more than the living space. Walk the house and yard first and write down anything that looks unsafe or neglected. Loose stair rails, missing detectors, damaged porches, peeling exterior paint and debris in the yard are the sort of items an inspector can note.

Whoever is at the property should be able to let the inspector in and answer questions. If tenants live there, tell them the date in advance. Zoning matters for houses that were split into units years ago. If your building has more units than zoning permits, learn that now, because it changes who can buy it.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Allentown house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Allentown housing at a glance

Allentown, the Lehigh County seat, is the Lehigh Valley's biggest city. The July 1, 2025 estimate is 126,044 residents, almost the same as the 125,845 counted in 2020. Only 43.2 percent of occupied homes are owner-occupied, which means two-family and multi-unit buildings turn up in many sales next to single houses.

The median value of an owner-occupied home is $206,600, median gross rent is $1,317 and median household income is $55,494. Those medians describe the entire city, and an individual house can sell well above or below them. The Allentown School District covers most addresses, though a small area near Trexler Park falls in the Parkland School District, so check yours.

Neighborhoods and house types

The age and style of houses shift as you cross town.

  • Center City: Victorian and terraced rowhouses, plus loft apartments in converted mills. Old Allentown and the Old Fairgrounds are historic districts.
  • West Park: mostly Victorian and American Craftsman houses, in a historic district with its own home tour.
  • West End: starts roughly at 15th Street, with tree-lined blocks built mostly in the 1920s through the 1940s.
  • East Side and South Side: single and twin homes from the 1940s to the 1960s, with some older Victorians.
  • The Wards: residential blocks east of Center City from the late 19th and early 20th century boom.

Buyers and inspectors judge a house by its age, so know which era yours belongs to and what usually fails first in it.

Selling a rental or multi-unit building

With owners in under half of occupied homes, Allentown has plenty of two-family and multi-unit buildings, and sales of them draw investors. Those buyers will ask for the leases, the rent history and the pre-sale paperwork, and some will want to see each unit.

Give tenants written notice before showings and keep to the lease terms on access. If you are a landlord selling to an investor, mention the county's contact-information rule for non-owner-occupied property. The new owner has 30 days after purchase to comply.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Allentown houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What to bring to the settlement table

Show up with photo ID, every key, garage openers and appliance manuals. Add the Certificate of Compliance, a signed Acceptance Form if one exists, recent tax bills and a mortgage payoff letter when a loan is open. The title company drafts the deed and the settlement sheet. Go through each line of that sheet before signing and question any charge you cannot explain.

After the deed is signed, the report is due three days later, filed by you or your agent. Mark that date before you leave.

Lehigh County assessments and appeals

Lehigh County assesses every Allentown parcel. The county's base year is 2013, the date of its last countywide reassessment, with values set at 100 percent of fair market value at that time. New construction and demolition change a parcel's assessment in between. The Assessment Office is in Room 517 of the Government Center at 17 South Seventh Street, Allentown, phone 610-782-3038.

  • Appeal deadline: the Board of Assessment Appeals needs an original signed appeal, with the filing fee, in hand by August 1 each year. Postmarks and faxes do not count as timely.
  • Interim appeals: these run from the date printed on a Change of Assessment Notice.
  • Act 29 of 2026: an owner of non-owner-occupied property must send the county contact information within 30 days of buying. Owner-occupants are exempt, so this falls mostly on landlords and investors buying from you.

Ways to sell quickly

You can hire an agent, sell it yourself or accept a cash offer. Working with an agent brings in the most buyers, along with showings and an inspection ordered by the buyer. A cash offer drops the mortgage approval stage, the piece of a closing that usually waits on a lender.

All three still require the city's pre-sale permit, so request it early. If you cannot afford the repairs an inspector lists, ask buyers in writing to accept them through the Acceptance Form.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

A sensible order of steps

  1. Apply online for the Pre-Sale permit and get the inspection on the calendar.
  2. Fix what you can before the inspector arrives, such as railings, smoke detectors and exterior upkeep.
  3. Collect your deed, your tax bills and any permit records.
  4. Compare offers by what you take home, and ask each buyer how violations will be handled.
  5. Close, then file the Buyer's Information Report within three days.

A cash buyer has no lender appraisal to wait on, so the inspection and the title search decide your closing date.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need an inspection before selling my Allentown house?

Yes. The city requires a pre-sale safety and maintenance inspection for residential and commercial property. A house that passes receives a Certificate of Compliance before the sale.

Can the buyer take over repairs the inspector finds?

Yes. The seller can repair the violations, or the buyer can agree to take them on. That agreement is recorded on the city's Acceptance Form.

What do I file after an Allentown closing?

A Buyer's Information Report goes to the city within three days of settlement. The seller or the real estate agent can submit it.

Which school district serves my Allentown home?

Most of the city is in the Allentown School District, but a small area near Trexler Park is in the Parkland School District. Check your exact address with the district.

What is the deadline to appeal a Lehigh County assessment?

August 1 each year. The Board of Assessment Appeals needs the original signed appeal and the filing fee by then, and postmarks and faxes are not accepted.

What makes selling in Reading different

Reading is a dense, rowhouse-heavy city where a sale needs a city Certificate of Transfer, carries a transfer tax of 5%, and often involves a house that has not been updated in decades. Those three facts shape price, timing and who is likely to buy.

Housing costs are far below the Philadelphia suburbs, and most households rent. The buyer pool leans toward investors, rehab buyers and first-time owners. Sellers here usually weigh a repair-and-list route against a quick sale to an investor, and the sections below show what each route requires at the city and county level.

With only about four in ten homes owner-occupied, a large share of Reading's houses are rentals. Owners of those properties also deal with the city's housing registration and rental inspection cycle, which matters if tenants are in place at the time of sale.

Certificate of Transfer

The seller must obtain this city document before a sale closes, and it applies to every property sold in Reading regardless of use. The seller applies before the sale and hands the buyer a property packet with summary sheets.

A Health and Safety Inspection that checks code compliance is part of the process. Either the buyer or the seller may arrange it, and the city allows limited exemptions. The forms are a Certificate of Transfer and Property Sale Inspection Application, and a Property Sale Inspection Acknowledgement.

  • Download the sale application from the city's Housing Welcome Packet page and complete it as early as the sales agreement is signed.
  • Ask the City of Reading Property Maintenance division, which works from 815 Washington Street, for the current fee and processing time.
  • Agree in the sales contract who schedules the inspection and who pays for any violations it finds.
  • For help or complaints, the Citizen's Service Center is at 1-877-727-3234.

A seller who sells as-is to an investor should still get the certificate lined up. It is a city requirement, so it does not disappear because the buyer is paying cash.

Transfer tax in the City of Reading

The transfer tax rate is 5% in the City of Reading, compared with 2% in every other Berks municipality. One percent of that goes to the state, and the Berks County Recorder of Deeds collects the whole amount when the deed is recorded.

Pennsylvania law makes both parties liable, so the sales agreement should say who pays and how it is split. Settle that before the contract is signed, since it is a real negotiating point on a lower-priced house.

  • Personal checks are not accepted for transfer tax at the Recorder's office, and cash is no longer accepted either.
  • The base recording fee for a deed is $88 for up to four pages, with $4 for each additional page.
  • A Statement of Value (REV-183) goes with any deed that leaves the full price off. The Common Level Ratio on that form is 3.12 for July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027.
  • The Recorder of Deeds is in the Berks County Services Center, 633 Court Street, third floor, phone 610-478-3380.

Certain family transfers and property passing by will or intestacy are exempt under state law, so an inherited house passing to an heir may owe nothing.

Property taxes and code tickets

Reading homeowners are assessed through Berks County and pay the county, the city and the Reading School District. Call Berks County for the current millage on your parcel, and ask the Berks County Assessment Office for the appeal deadline and form, since the rules for contesting a value are set at the county level.

Call the Berks County Tax Claim Bureau about any unpaid years. A title company will request a tax certification before closing, and unpaid taxes are paid from sale proceeds.

The city's code program adds its own tickets. Reading's Quality of Life program issues immediate tickets that increase with repeat violations at the same property in a year, and the city holds blight hearings for deteriorated properties. Clearing open violations before closing keeps them from becoming a buyer's negotiating point.

List, repair or sell to a cash buyer

The answer depends on condition and timing. A house in good repair near a historic district may do well on the open market, but a vacant rowhouse with deferred maintenance may be worth more to a rehab investor than to a retail buyer who needs financing.

  • Get a rough repair estimate before listing. Many Reading buyers use loans that require inspections and appraisals.
  • Work out your net after the 5% transfer tax, the sale inspection, commissions and unpaid taxes.
  • If you own rental units, ask the Property Maintenance office how registration and open inspection findings pass to a new owner.
  • If time matters more than price, a cash sale on an as-is basis avoids lender delays, though the Certificate of Transfer is still required.
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Reading houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Steps from signed contract to closing

Start the paperwork on day one. Pull together the deed, recent tax bills and any city notices, then work down this list.

  1. Download and complete the Certificate of Transfer and Property Sale Inspection Application as soon as the sales agreement is signed.
  2. Decide in writing whether you or the buyer books the Health and Safety Inspection, and who pays for violations it turns up.
  3. Fix or disclose open code items. A violation the city has recorded does not go away at closing.
  4. Ask the closing agent to request the tax certification from the county and to confirm unpaid years with the Tax Claim Bureau.
  5. Agree on how the 5% transfer tax is split, and have the title company bring the deed to the Recorder with the tax paid by check.

Selling as-is for cash drops the mortgage appraisal and lender timeline. The city certificate and the inspection still apply, so your closing date hinges on how fast those two get done.

Selling with tenants or open violations

You can sell a Reading house with code violations, but the sale inspection will surface them, and the contract must say whether you repair them or the buyer does. A vacant or deteriorated property can also draw a blight hearing, so addressing it before you list protects your price.

For a rental, confirm the housing registration is current and read the lease before you accept an offer. An investor buyer will want to know the rent, the lease end date and whether inspection findings are open.

Frequently asked questions

Is a Certificate of Transfer required for every house sale in Reading?

Yes. The certificate is necessary for all properties sold in the city regardless of use, with limited exemptions only from the Health and Safety Inspection. The seller applies before the sale.

Who pays Reading's 5% transfer tax?

The law makes buyer and seller jointly liable, and the sales agreement decides who actually pays. The Berks County Recorder of Deeds collects it at recording, at 5% in the City of Reading versus 2% elsewhere in Berks.

Can I sell a Reading house with code violations?

Yes, but the sale inspection will surface them, and the contract must say whether you repair them or the buyer does. Open violations that the city has recorded do not go away at closing.

Does an inherited house in Reading owe transfer tax?

Property passed by will or intestate succession is exempt from realty transfer tax under state rules. A later sale by the heir to a third party is a normal taxable transfer at the Reading rate.

Where do I record the deed after a Reading sale?

At the Berks County Recorder of Deeds, third floor of the Services Center at 633 Court Street in Reading, or by e-recording through a title company. Your closing agent usually handles it and pays the transfer tax by check.

Selling in Erie?
We buy Erie houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Can you sell an Erie house fast?

Yes. Erie owners can go to market through a listing or a private sale, or they can take cash from a buyer who accepts every flaw. Pick by looking at the repairs, the occupants and your moving date.

Erie sits on the southern shore of Lake Erie and is the fifth largest city in Pennsylvania. The population was 91,838 in July 2025, down 3.3% from the 2020 base. A typical owner-occupied home was worth $115,200 for 2020 to 2024, typical gross rent was $870, and owners lived in 54.1% of homes. Median household income was $46,113.

Snow and the Erie inspection

Lake-effect snow is the weather that most often shows up in an Erie sale. The seasonal normal for 1991 to 2020 was 104.3 inches, and the Christmas 2017 storm dropped 53 inches in two days, a state record. That season finished at 198.5 inches. The city says much of its housing was built decades ago, so a buyer's inspector will look hard at:

  • Roof framing, shingles, flashing and ice dams along the eaves.
  • Gutters, downspouts and basement water after a thaw.
  • The age of the furnace and any history of frozen or burst pipes.
  • Porches, steps and driveways that take plows and salt.

Fixing these items, or pricing them in before you list, keeps surprises out of negotiations. A cash buyer will still discount for them, but usually with less drama and no inspection contingency.

Who handles what for an Erie seller

These are the offices a seller is most likely to deal with.

Erie offices and what they handle for sellers

Rental registrationCity of ErieRegistration and inspections now run by the city itself
Property maintenanceBureau of Building Standards and SafetyEnforces the 2021 International Property Maintenance Code
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Erie house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Rental and code rules

A rented house, or one with open violations, brings the city code office into the picture before any buyer shows up. The city counts 13,489 registered rental units. Code enforcement follows the 2021 International Property Maintenance Code, and the city is split into eight zones with a property maintenance inspector for each.

  • Violation notices: an inspector sends a Notice of Violation and gives the owner time to fix it. Cases left open can turn into a Quality of Life ticket and then a District Court case.
  • Rental ordinance: landlords typically get 30 days to correct problems after an initial inspection, and fines start at $1,000 per unit for each month a violation stays open.
  • Vacant houses: the city can place a lien for grass cutting, debris removal or securing a structure.
  • Who runs it: rental registration and inspection are now a city function, handled by a six-person team that includes three inspectors.

Paying a ticket does not cancel the duty to repair, so the buyer of a house with an open violation inherits the work. Ask the Citizen Response Center at City Hall whether your address has an open file.

Property tax breaks and bills

Erie offers a LERTA abatement, a homestead exclusion and a spring discount. The county handles appeals and recording. LERTA exempts 90% of the added value from improvements for five years, which is worth mentioning to a buyer if you renovated recently. Paying the city bill early in the spring earns a 2% discount.

If you think the assessment is too high, file with the county board. Appeals are accepted January 1 through August 1 on the county form. Hearings fall between July and October, and each parcel costs $50 to appeal. The state Property Tax/Rent Rebate, up to $1,000 by the city's count, is open to some seniors and people with disabilities.

At recording, the Recorder of Deeds collects the state and local transfer taxes. Transfers between spouses, between parent and child, and between siblings are exempt under 72 P.S. section 8101-C. Everyone else should call 814-451-6246 to learn the rate that applies at their price.

Selling with taxes owed

Unpaid taxes can end in a county tax sale. The Erie County Tax Claim Bureau holds an upset sale for parcels at least two years behind. An owner can pull a parcel out of the sale by paying the balance or by signing a stay-of-sale agreement with a down payment.

Even after bidding starts, you keep the property by paying the delinquency before the winning bidder pays in full. After the bidder pays, state law gives no redemption period. A parcel nobody buys can go to a judicial sale and then onto the repository list. The owner cannot bid on it at either step. Selling beforehand lets the sale price clear the taxes, and you keep what is left.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Erie houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What Pennsylvania requires of a seller

The Real Estate Seller Disclosure Law, 68 Pa.C.S. sections 7301 to 7315, covers sales of up to four dwelling units. You fill out the State Real Estate Commission's form and deliver it before the agreement of transfer is signed. Court-ordered sales, including probate-ordered transfers, are outside the law. A cash buyer does not change any of this.

How an Erie cash sale works

First you describe the house: its condition, any tenants, open code notices and tax status. The buyer makes an offer for the property as is, so you do not repair, stage or hold showings. Once you accept, title work begins, and any back taxes, liens or violation files show up. Closing follows on a date you and the buyer agree to.

Bring the deed, current tax bills, any lease and rental registration record, and payoff figures for loans. At closing, back taxes and liens come out of the price. Then the new deed is filed with the Recorder of Deeds, Room 121 of the Erie County Courthouse. Before you agree, put the cash figure next to the likely net from a listing after repairs, concessions and transfer tax. A fair number should survive that comparison.

With a rental, say up front which units have tenants and whether the city has inspected the building. If you inherited it, line up the estate paperwork first, because title questions are the most common cause of a slow closing. Get the closing date and each side's costs written down before you sign.

Frequently asked questions

How quickly does an Erie cash sale close?

With no bank involved, the closing date follows title work and the day you agree on. A clean title can close sooner than a listing held up by an appraisal.

Must open Erie code violations be repaired before a sale?

Open violations stay with the property until corrected, and the city can fine the owner. A buyer who takes the house as is takes over the repairs, so disclose every notice you hold.

Can the county tax sale take my Erie house while it is listed?

Only if the delinquency is at least two years old and the parcel is advertised for the upset sale. Paying up or signing a stay-of-sale agreement removes it, and sale proceeds can settle the taxes at closing.

Where is an Erie deed recorded?

The Recorder of Deeds, Room 121, Erie County Courthouse, 140 West Sixth Street, takes it. That office also takes the state and local realty transfer taxes.

Does a tenant block the sale of an Erie rental?

No. The rental should be registered and inspected under the city ordinance, so hand the buyer the lease and the registration record, and disclose any open violations.

Selling in Upper Darby?
We buy Upper Darby houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Selling a house in Upper Darby

Upper Darby is a dense, close-in Delaware County township just west of Philadelphia. It is a first-class township of more than 85,000 residents packed into 7.9 square miles, and the 2020 census counted 85,681 people. Most of the housing is older and built close together: row houses and twins along streets like Richfield Road, a legacy of the building boom that followed the 1907 extension of the Market-Frankford elevated line to 69th Street.

Neighborhood names matter when you price a home. Drexel Hill, Secane, Primos, Bywood, Beverly Hills, Aronimink, Highland Park and Stonehurst each draw a different kind of buyer. Transit is the strongest selling point most owners have: the 69th Street Transportation Center at Terminal Square is the end of the Market-Frankford Line and the start of the Norristown High Speed Line, with trolley routes 101 and 102 and many bus lines.

  • Time the walk to the El or a trolley stop before you write the listing.
  • Name the school zone in your description only after the school district confirms it.
  • Mention off-street parking if you have it. On rowhouse blocks it is scarce.

Use and occupancy certificate

Settlement cannot happen without a Use and Occupancy (U&O) certificate. The township applies it to every sale and transfer, and the seller is the one who has to obtain it.

The application has to reach the Licenses & Inspections office at least 14 business days before settlement, and the township suggests four weeks because of demand. An inspector then calls to set a visit. Inspectors look without opening walls, measuring the house against the property maintenance code and township ordinances. There are three possible results:

  • Final certificate: the house is compliant and can be occupied.
  • Temporary certificate: minor violations exist, and the buyer must correct them within one year of purchase.
  • Temporary access certificate: substantial violations exist. Current occupants may stay, but no new occupant may move in.

Substantial violations include missing or dead smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, absent fire extinguishers where required, structural or electrical hazards, and an unfiled sewer lateral certification. The sewer lateral certification has to come from an approved Upper Darby contractor. When the buyer agrees to handle repairs, a notarized Letter of Intent must be filed. If the buyer named on the application changes, a new application, new fees and a new inspection follow. Payment is by L&I online payment, check or money order. Cash is refused. Call 610-734-7613 to check the current fee schedule.

Taxes and fees that come out of a sale

Realty transfer tax is the big one. The state's 1 percent is collected along with a local tax by the Delaware County Recorder of Deeds. Most Delaware County municipalities charge 1 percent locally, but Upper Darby moved to 1.5 percent on January 1, 2022, for a combined 2.5 percent. The state holds buyer and seller jointly responsible, which makes the contract the place to assign the cost.

Property tax bills and unpaid balances

Three separate bills arrive, and the township collects only its own. The Upper Darby Tax Office bills real estate tax, a sewer charge and a trash fee. School tax goes to the Upper Darby School District Tax Office (610-789-7200, extension 3210), and county tax goes to the Delaware County Property Tax Office (610-891-4278).

On the township bill, real estate tax earns a 2 percent discount if paid before April 1, then carries face value through May 31 and a 10 percent penalty after that. Sewer and trash bills skip the discount: face value by May 31, then the same penalty. Anything unpaid after December 31 goes to an outside collection agency, and the township stops taking payment. A delinquent amount is a lien against the parcel, so expect the title company to find it and ask for payoff at settlement.

A tax certification tells a buyer's side exactly what is owed. Standard requests take five to seven business days and come back by mail or FedEx, so order one early if you are on a tight closing schedule.

Can I appeal my assessment before I sell?

Yes. The county, and not the township, hears assessment appeals. Forms are posted on the county's Board of Assessment page, with separate versions for residential, commercial and exemption appeals. Completed forms go to the Government Center Building in Media. Fax and electronic filings are refused, and each form must carry an original signature.

Because mail postmarks can slip, the county urges filers to walk the form in to the Media office. The other safe routes start at a post office counter: a manual postmark, a certificate of mailing, certified or registered delivery, or postage bought over the counter. If the Board rules against you, a court appeal has to start within 30 days of its findings, through the Office of Judicial Support.

The assessment office also handles homestead questions, and it can tell you the filing deadline for your tax year.

Should I list, repair or take a cash offer?

Condition and timing decide which route fits. A listing can bring the best price on a sound home in Drexel Hill or Secane, but it carries agent fees, showings and a U&O inspection. A cash buyer can often close without waiting on financing, though the sale still needs the U&O certificate and the sewer lateral paperwork.

  • A listing suits a house in good repair when you can wait out several weeks.
  • Fix the substantial violations first if you want a final certificate, because smoke and CO detectors are cheap to correct.
  • Sell as-is for cash if repairs, tenants or an inherited property make the timeline hard, and let the buyer take on the temporary certificate work.
  • If the home is a rental, the township requires a rental license application for non-owner-occupied properties.

Before signing anything, get the offer in writing, decide who covers the 2.5 percent transfer tax, and check that the U&O schedule fits the closing date.

Frequently asked questions

How long does the Upper Darby use and occupancy process take?

Plan on four weeks. The township requires the application at least 14 business days before settlement and recommends four weeks because inspections are in demand. If the buyer on the application changes, a new application and a fresh inspection are required.

Who pays the Upper Darby transfer tax?

Both sides are liable to the state, so the contract settles who actually pays. The total is 2.5 percent: 1 percent to the Commonwealth plus Upper Darby's 1.5 percent.

Can I sell a house in Upper Darby with code violations?

Yes, in many cases. Minor violations lead to a temporary certificate and the buyer has one year to fix them. Substantial violations lead to a temporary access certificate, which lets current occupants stay but bars new occupants until the work is done.

Does a landlord need a rental license before selling in Upper Darby?

Yes, a rental license application belongs in the U&O packet for any property that is not owner-occupied. Ask Licenses & Inspections whether your license is current before you list.

Where do I record the deed after an Upper Darby closing?

In Media, in Room 108 of the county Government Center, where transfer tax is collected with the deed. The recording desk takes documents from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., and whoever handles your settlement usually files for you.

Sell Your Bethlehem House for Cash

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Bethlehem?
We buy Bethlehem houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

How a Bethlehem sale works

A Bethlehem sale runs through an agreement of sale, a city housing inspection, settlement and a recorded deed. The city inspection is the step that surprises most sellers. Your parcel may sit in Northampton County or, on the West Side, in Lehigh County, and that decides which recorder of deeds and which assessment office you deal with. Confirm the county on your tax bill before you list.

The city is a separate jurisdiction from Bethlehem Township, which runs its own resale program. A house inside the city limits follows the city rules below.

Bethlehem market snapshot

Bethlehem is a Lehigh River city of roughly 79,600 people, with an estimate of 79,644 for July 2025, up 5.1 percent from 75,781 in April 2020. It has five areas: Center City, the West Side, the East Side, the South Side and the North Side. Only the West Side lies in Lehigh County.

Owners and renters are close to an even split, with 49.9 percent of homes owner-occupied for 2020 through 2024. The typical owned home is valued at $260,400, median gross rent is $1,382 a month, and median household income is $68,879. There are 31,052 households averaging 2.30 people. Because about half of households rent, many houses that change hands in the city have been rentals at some point, which makes the rental license rules below relevant to a lot of sellers.

The city inspection before title passes

Under Article 119 of the city's codified ordinances, every transferor of real property must have the city's Housing Inspections Bureau inspect it before title passes, and the rule covers residential and commercial property alike. The inspection checks the house against the International Property Maintenance Code and the uses the zoning ordinance allows.

Ordinance 2026-19 amended the requirement in July 2026. The table summarizes the current text of section 119.04.

RequirementWhat section 119.04 provides
When to callWithin 10 days of offering the property for sale
Lead timeBook the inspection a month or more ahead of the transfer
ReportLists uncorrected housing, building, safety or fire violations, plus zoning classification and legality of use
Who gets itGiven to the buyer and attached to the agreement of sale, with any notice of assessment for public improvements
Buyer's dutyBuyer must still obtain a certificate of occupancy
Penalty (section 119.99)Fine of $600 or up to 90 days in jail, or both

The bureau takes scheduling calls Monday through Friday at (610) 865-7091 or (610) 865-7097.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Bethlehem house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What happens after the inspector writes it up

The report lists whatever housing, building, safety or fire items are uncorrected. It goes to the buyer as an addendum to the agreement of sale. The buyer still has to obtain a certificate of occupancy, so sellers often repair the listed items first, or negotiate in the contract who will do it.

A cash buyer gets the same report. Paying cash does not skip the inspection, so call the bureau within 10 days of offering the house, whoever ends up buying it.

Choosing a sale route

Pick a route by weighing the repair list against your deadline. All three still require you to book the city inspection and give the buyer its report.

  • List with an agent: the widest buyer pool, with showings, repairs ahead of the inspection and a closing date set by the buyer's financing.
  • Sell it yourself: you keep the agent's fee, but you handle the agreement of sale, the city report and the disclosures on your own.
  • Take a cash offer: buyers who pay cash usually buy as is and close on a date you agree, which suits a house with open violations, tenants or deferred repairs.

Compare offers on the net you keep after repairs, taxes and any city-required fixes, not only on the headline price.

Selling a Bethlehem rental

Every residential rental unit in Bethlehem needs a rental license each year, and Article 1738 puts rental units on an inspection cycle of once every three years. A landlord who sells should find out where the license stands before listing, because a buyer who plans to keep tenants will ask for the license and the last inspection record.

Rooming houses need an annual inspection under Article 1735, and properties occupied by students or unrelated people fall under Article 1739. When a tenant lives in the house, plan the sale inspection around their access and notice rights, and ask the Housing Inspections Bureau whether your license is current before you list.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Bethlehem houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Transfer tax and fees

The state takes a 1 percent realty transfer tax on the value changing hands, and both seller and buyer are on the hook for it under state law. The recording office collects it together with any local transfer tax when the deed is filed.

Bethlehem's local tax comes from Article 335, which starts at 1 percent and halves the city's piece whenever another taxing body, such as the school district, levies on the same transfer. So the combined local rate on a Bethlehem deed turns on how those two split it. Whichever county recorder handles your parcel, Lehigh or Northampton, keeps a 2 percent commission and sends the rest to the city. Ask that office for the full figure on your deed before you set a price. Close relatives in certain cases, and property that passes by succession, are excluded.

Recording and assessment

The recorder of deeds for Northampton County or Lehigh County records the deed, depending on where the parcel sits. Section 119.04 also asks every buyer to give the City Engineer a description of the property within one month of acquiring title and to have the deed stamped as proof of registration. Mention it to your buyer early, so the step does not slip once the keys change hands.

Assessment appeals go to the county that assesses the parcel. Call the Northampton County Assessment Division or the Lehigh County assessment office for the current annual appeal filing date, since each office sets its own.

A simple Bethlehem timeline

  1. Confirm the county on your tax bill and whether the house sits in the city or the township.
  2. Within 10 days of offering the house for sale, call the Housing Inspections Bureau.
  3. Book the inspection a month or more before the transfer date.
  4. Fix the listed items or agree in writing who will.
  5. Attach the report to the agreement of sale for the buyer.
  6. Get the transfer tax total from the recorder of deeds, and close.
You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a city inspection if I sell to a cash buyer?

Yes. All properties must be inspected before title transfers, whatever the buyer's financing. Call the Housing Inspections Bureau within 10 days of offering the house, and plan for the report to go to the buyer.

How early should I schedule the Bethlehem sale inspection?

A month or more before the transfer date, and within 10 days of first offering the property for sale. Booking early leaves time to fix any housing, safety or fire items the inspector lists.

What happens if the inspection finds violations?

The report lists them and goes to the buyer as an addendum to the agreement of sale. The buyer must still obtain a certificate of occupancy, so many sellers repair the items first or negotiate who will.

Who bears the transfer tax on a Bethlehem sale?

Selling fast in Scranton

Three routes get a Scranton house sold: a cash offer, an agent listing, or doing it yourself. Cash has the fewest moving parts. Scranton sits in Lackawanna County, and the city has its own rules for permits, rental licenses and transfer tax that can slow a conventional sale.

A listing leans on a buyer's lender, an appraisal and a repair list. Cash skips nearly all of it, which suits the house is inherited, has tenants, needs work, or sits on a street where older homes take longer to move. The cost is price. Cash offers usually come in under a polished listing, so get both numbers first.

Homes sit on hills between roughly 650 and 1,400 feet above sea level, which puts lot slope, drainage and retaining walls on many inspection reports. Most older housing dates from the anthracite and railroad years: narrow lots, brick and frame doubles, steep driveways and basements that have seen decades of freeze and thaw. Green Ridge and the mountain neighborhoods read very differently to a buyer than the older streets near downtown, so a price from one area says little about another.

The 3.7 percent transfer tax

Sellers in Scranton face a combined realty transfer tax of 3.7 percent of the value, against 2 percent across most of Lackawanna County. No deed gets recorded until the tax is paid.

The state's piece is 1 percent, and the rest goes to local government and the school district. The county Recorder collects it all. Your sales agreement settles who pays, often a split, though the new owner is on the hook if the amount is ever questioned.

  • Transfers within a family, parent to child or between siblings, are exempt. Non-profit corporations get no such exemption.
  • A deed showing token consideration of $1 must carry a Statement of Value for state review.

Selling a house with tenants

City rules say each rental property needs a rental license. Renting an unlicensed unit is a violation. Renew by March 15 every year. A newly rented unit needs its license within 30 days of a tenant moving in.

The fee scales with unit count: $45 per unit at one to three units, rising to a $450 flat fee at fifty or more. A unit lived in by family still needs a license but costs nothing. The city inspects every three years, and the first re-inspection carries no charge.

Selling with tenants still in the unit? Bring the license up to date first. Lenders and investors both ask to see it, and a lapse can mean a refused license or fines. The rental licensing office can tell you where your property stands, so call before you choose a closing day.

Vacant, in default or heading to a tax sale

Registration with the city is required for any property, occupied or empty, in any of these situations: mortgage default, a lis pendens, a foreclosure action, a tax deed application, a pending tax lien sale, or a deed in lieu to the lender. There is no fee, and you register on the city's online portal.

The abandoned label stays until the house sells, the foreclosure is dismissed or the default is cured. A sale that closes before a judgment or tax sale ends the status, which is where a quick cash closing can help. Call the Lackawanna County Tax Claim Bureau for the exact upset sale dates that apply to your parcel.

Permits and repairs before you sell

A seller in Pennsylvania has no duty to renovate. If you do start work in Scranton, get a permit first, because every construction project needs one before work begins. The city exempts only painting and gutter installation.

Plans follow the 2021 International Code Council series, and existing buildings fall under the 2024 International Property Maintenance Code. Three more checks can catch a seller off guard:

  • A home in a historic district or landmark needs a Certificate of Appropriateness for exterior changes, building permit or not.
  • Work in a FEMA flood zone goes through the floodplain administrator. Improvements worth 50 percent or more of market value require elevation or flood-proofing.
  • Fences, sheds and pools can need zoning approval even without a building permit.

Code Enforcement's in-person counter is at 338 N Washington Avenue. Title companies often hold up a closing over open or expired permits. Request the permit history from the office before you list.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Scranton houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Mine subsidence

Underground anthracite workings lie beneath much of Scranton, and ordinary homeowner policies usually leave out damage from collapsed mines. The Department of Environmental Protection runs a Mine Subsidence Insurance program to cover that.

Policies range from $5,000 to $1,000,000, and $150,000 of residential coverage costs $41.25 a year. A risk map from DEP shows whether an address sits over mined ground, and a buyer's lender may ask. A policy does not transfer to the new owner, who has to apply for their own, and a seller who cancels at closing can get unused premium back when the notice arrives inside a month of the sale.

Cracks can also come from soil settlement or frost, so have an inspector look before you assume the worst.

Winter and the condition of the house

An average Scranton year brings 45.1 inches of snow and about 39 days when the high stays below freezing. That freeze-thaw cycle is hard on roofs, gutters, chimneys, retaining walls, concrete steps and old foundations, and buyers' inspectors look for exactly those items. A buyer who purchases as-is removes the need to schedule repairs around the weather.

Steps for a quick Scranton sale

  1. Pull the deed and any mortgage or lien payoff figures.
  2. If anyone rents the property, confirm the rental license is current before you list.
  3. Ask Code Enforcement for the permit history, and close out open or expired permits.
  4. If the house is in default or facing a tax sale, register it through the city's online portal and call the Tax Claim Bureau about upset sale dates.
  5. Decide in the sales agreement who pays the 3.7 percent transfer tax.
  6. Have the closing agent record the deed with the Recorder of Deeds, which will not take it until the tax is paid.

A cash sale can close in a few weeks because there is no lender underwriting or appraisal to wait on. Title work, lien payoffs and recording still take their normal time.

Frequently asked questions

How long does it take to sell a house in Scranton for cash?

A cash sale can close in a few weeks, since there is no lender underwriting or appraisal to wait on. The remaining steps are title work, payoff of any liens and recording the deed with the Lackawanna County Recorder of Deeds.

Who pays the transfer tax on a Scranton home sale?

The sales agreement decides, and in most deals the seller and buyer split it. The state and local governments only care that the 3.7 percent total is paid when the deed is recorded.

Can I sell a Scranton rental property without a rental license?

You can sell it, but an unlicensed rental is a violation, and the city can refuse a license or fine the owner. Apply for or renew the license first if tenants are in the unit, since renewals are due March 15.

Does Scranton require an inspection before I can sell?

Permit work is inspected, and rentals follow a three-year inspection cycle. Ask the Code Enforcement office whether anything is open on your address before you list.

Is mine subsidence insurance required when buying a Scranton home?

The state does not require it, but a lender may ask for it when the property sits over mined ground. DEP sells the coverage, and the new owner has to apply for a new policy because the seller's does not transfer.

Selling fast in Lower Merion Township

The quickest Lower Merion sale starts the township paperwork on day one, because the Resale Certification takes 30 to 60 days to come back. A cash buyer can agree to a closing date as soon as the contract is signed, but the certificate, the tax certification and the deed registration all have to be in hand before settlement.

Lower Merion is a first-class township in Montgomery County and the heart of the Main Line, with an estimated 64,691 residents. Around 74.7 percent of homes are owner-occupied, the typical owned home is valued at $810,400, and typical rent is $1,893. Sellers often need speed for everyday reasons: an estate with out-of-town heirs, a move, a divorce, a tenant situation, or an older house that needs more work than the owner wants to fund.

  • Order the Resale Certification application first, since it has the longest lead time.
  • Request the tax certification as soon as you have an accepted offer, because it takes two to three days.
  • Ask your buyer or title company to confirm who files the Real Estate Registration form and who pays the transfer taxes.

The Resale Certification

The township requires the owner to obtain a Resale Certification before selling. The property must meet a short list of conditions, and township staff also review the property file so the buyer hears about any open violations.

  • Sidewalks and curbs must be in good repair.
  • The street address must be posted where it can be seen from the street.
  • Smoke detectors must be installed in each bedroom and on every level.
  • The owner must certify how the building is used.

The township no longer requires the original deed to be registered with it before recording at the county, though the Real Estate Registration form is still required for any change in ownership or legal description. An abandoned underground fuel oil tank must be removed by a DEP-certified individual under a building permit, so deal with that before an inspector finds it. Building and Planning answers questions at 610-645-6200.

Tax certification

The township tax collector issues a four-year certification listing township tax, county tax, school tax, sewer and solid waste, including delinquent amounts. It is accurate only on the day it is issued, and free updates run for sixty days for whoever ordered it. Amounts due are not confirmed over the phone.

To order, email the tax collector's office for a credit card invoice, or mail a check payable to Tax Collector, Lower Merion, to 75 E Lancaster Ave, Ardmore. Lien taxes are checked at the Montgomery County Tax Claim Bureau. Most condominiums and apartments pay sewer and solid waste through their association, so those fees may not appear. The certification already carries sewer and solid waste data, so no separate final reading is taken.

Transfer tax and recording costs

The state tax is 1 percent of value, and the county Recorder of Deeds collects it along with the local tax. At recording, Montgomery County wants two separate checks: one for the recording fee and one for the realty transfer tax. The county's current fee chart lists a deed base fee of $87.75. Your title company can tell you the local rate that applies to your address.

For deeds that carry no market price, such as gifts, the state determines value using a common level ratio factor, which Montgomery County currently lists as 3.36.

How do assessment appeals and rentals work in Lower Merion?

Montgomery County takes annual assessment appeals until August 1, and the appeal must be postmarked or delivered by then. The form needs an original owner signature and three copies of supporting documents, and faxed or emailed appeals are not accepted. A single-family residential appeal carries a $50 processing fee, and the county hears all appeals by October 31. The Board of Assessment Appeals can be reached at 610-278-3761.

If you own a rental, the township requires a Rental Unit License from Building and Planning, an inspection against the housing code, a business registration and an annual business privilege tax return. A buyer of your tenant-occupied house will ask whether the license is current, and the township keeps a separate list of approved student homes.

Transit and neighborhoods to mention in your listing

Transportation is a selling point. The Schuylkill Expressway (I-76), the Blue Route (I-476), US 1, US 30, PA 320 and PA 23 all cross the township. SEPTA's Paoli/Thorndale Line stops in Merion, Wynnewood, Ardmore, Haverford, Bryn Mawr and Rosemont, the Cynwyd Line stops at Bala and Cynwyd, and the Norristown High Speed Line serves the western edge.

Communities include Ardmore, Bala Cynwyd, Bryn Mawr, Gladwyne, Merion Station, Penn Valley, Wynnewood, Rosemont and Villanova. Children attend the Lower Merion School District. Name your community and the nearest station in the listing or offer request, since buyers search that way.

Steps to a closing

Plan the sale in this order. Send in the Resale Certification application and fee first, then fix anything the inspection could flag: sidewalk or curb damage, a missing house number, smoke detectors that are absent or not working. Order the tax certification once an offer is accepted. While those clear, your title company prepares the settlement statement and the Real Estate Registration form, and the deed is recorded at the Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds after closing.

If you are working against a deadline, the certificate is the item to watch. It can take up to 60 days, and filing 20 or more days before settlement also saves $50 on the fee. A cash sale skips showings and lender timelines, but it does not skip the certificate, so the earlier you file, the sooner you can name a closing date. If the house has an old underground oil tank, add that to your list at the start, since removal needs a building permit.

If a buyer asks about rental history, hand over the Rental Unit License, the inspection result and the business privilege tax filings together. A complete packet shortens the due diligence period and keeps the buyer from asking for extra time.

Condominium and apartment owners have one less item to chase, since sewer and solid waste usually run through the association. Ask the association for its own resale paperwork when you file with the township, so both arrive before settlement and neither holds up the other.

Frequently asked questions

Is a resale certificate required to sell in Lower Merion Township?

Yes. The township requires a Resale Certification before a sale, and it takes 30 to 60 days. The fee is $100 if the application arrives 20 or more days before settlement and $150 if it arrives later.

What must be fixed to pass the Lower Merion resale inspection?

Sidewalks and curbs must be in good repair, the address must be visible from the street, and smoke detectors are needed in every bedroom and on every level. The owner also certifies the use of the building.

How much is a Lower Merion tax certification?

The regular certification is $50 with a two to three day turnaround, and the rush certification is $75 and comes back the same day. It covers township, county and school tax plus sewer and solid waste.

When must I file a Montgomery County assessment appeal?

The annual deadline is August 1. The appeal must be postmarked or hand delivered by that date, and faxed or emailed appeals are rejected.

Which school district serves Lower Merion Township?

The Lower Merion School District serves the township, and pupils attend its schools unless they go to a private school.

Bensalem at a glance

Bensalem is a township of about 62,800 people at the southern tip of Bucks County, up against the Northeast section of Philadelphia. Population is 62,783 for July 1, 2025, up slightly from 62,707 in the 2020 census, and it is the most populous municipality in the county. Despite the word township, it has had a mayor and a five-member council since voters chose that form in 1987. There are no boroughs inside its lines. Andalusia, Cornwells Heights, Eddington, Oakford and Trevose are communities within the one township, and each shows up in mailing addresses and listings, so a house with a Trevose address is still a Bensalem Township property for permits and taxes.

Homeownership runs at 62.3 percent for 2020 to 2024, and the median home value is $364,400. Treat that as a township-wide survey estimate, not a price for your address.

What a Bensalem seller must file before closing

Bensalem requires a Residential Resales Use and Occupancy permit whenever a dwelling changes hands. The Building and Planning Department's application form describes it as the permit to occupy a single or multi-family dwelling or condominium through new ownership or new use. The fee is $100.

  • File the application one month before the settlement date. The form is signed, and a signed copy is required before the permit issues.
  • Attach an electrical panel certificate from one of the approved electrical underwriters named on the form.
  • Attach a maintenance certificate from a registered contractor saying the heating system is in good working condition.
  • Attach a chimney, flue and vent inspection at NFPA 211 Level II, usually done with a camera.
  • Pay in cash, check or money order. The township does not accept credit cards or electronic payments.

The certifications may be obtained up to one year before settlement, so you can order them early and have them in hand when a buyer appears. Staff search the property's history for open permits, complaints and liens. Unresolved items delay the certificate, and clearing them falls to the seller.

Questions go to the Building and Planning Department at 2400 Byberry Road, phone 215-633-3644, open 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. on weekdays. The township posts its resale application on its website.

Timing the paperwork

The application asks for a settlement date and certificates from outside contractors, so the order of steps matters. Once you have a signed agreement of sale and a closing date, count back one month for the filing. Book the electrician, the heating contractor and the chimney inspector before that, because their certificates have to be attached.

If you are selling for cash on a short timeline, the same rule applies, since the permit follows the change in ownership no matter how the buyer pays. Ordering the three inspections the day you decide to sell is the simplest way to keep a closing date from slipping.

How Bucks County assesses a Bensalem house

The Bucks County Board of Assessment Appeals, at 55 East Court Street in Doylestown, keeps the assessment rolls for Bensalem. Its office number is 215-348-6219, and the board meets at 10 a.m. on the first and third Tuesday of each month.

Annual appeals are due each August, and a change from an annual appeal takes effect the following tax year. Call the board for the current year's date. Homestead and farmstead applications are due by March 1 for the tax year that starts July 1 of that year.

Act 29 also applies when you sell: a new owner must give the Board of Assessment contact information within 30 days of buying a property. Mention that to your buyer so it does not get missed after closing.

What happens if the township finds open items?

When staff search a property's history, they look for open permits, complaints and liens. If something turns up, the certificate waits until it is cleared. A permit left open by a previous owner, a deck built without sign-off or an old complaint can all stall a closing that is otherwise ready.

Walk through the house and the paperwork before you list. Pull any permits you remember pulling, note any work a past owner did, and call the Building and Planning Department if you are unsure. Sorting it out before a buyer is under contract gives you room to fix it on your own schedule instead of the buyer's.

A step by step timeline

  1. Decide how you will sell and set a rough closing date.
  2. Order the electrical panel certificate, the heating maintenance certificate and the chimney inspection. They can be dated up to one year before settlement.
  3. Sign an agreement of sale with a settlement date.
  4. File the signed application and the $100 fee at least one month before settlement.
  5. Clear anything the township flags in its search of permits, complaints and liens.
  6. Call the water, sewer and electric companies with the closing date.
  7. Close, and remind the buyer about the Act 29 contact notice owed to the county within 30 days.

Utilities and water at closing

Bensalem's sewer service comes from the Bucks County Water and Sewer Authority and its water from Aqua Pennsylvania, since the township sold both systems in 1999. Utility transfers at closing go through those companies. PECO supplies electricity and natural gas.

Call each provider with the settlement date so final readings and the buyer's start of service line up with the deed.

Drainage and basement checks

Houses near Poquessing Creek, Neshaminy Creek or the Delaware River are worth checking for drainage and basement moisture before you list. July is the wettest month, and thunderstorms peak then. A buyer can ask the township's engineering and building staff about the flood zone for a specific parcel, so know the answer for your own lot before the buyer's inspector raises it.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Ways to sell a house fast in Bensalem

A Bensalem owner can list the house, sell directly, or take a cash offer. A listing exposes the house to the most buyers, while a cash purchase removes the lender's appraisal and underwriting from the schedule.

All three routes depend on the same township paperwork. Order the electrical, heating and chimney inspections as soon as a buyer is lined up, and pick a closing date that leaves the one month filing window. Whoever buys, ask for proof of funds, the closing date and who pays for title work in writing.

Frequently asked questions

Does Bensalem require a certificate when a house is sold?

Yes. The township issues a Residential Resales Use and Occupancy permit for a change in ownership, based on electrical, heating and chimney certificates and a $100 application fee.

How far ahead should I apply for the Bensalem resale permit?

About one month before the settlement date. The township asks for the signed application and all three certifications at that point, and it accepts only cash, check or money order.

Who inspects the chimney for a Bensalem sale?

A chimney sweep company of your choice, with an NFPA 211 Level II inspection noted on the certification. The application form also names two companies whose certifications the township will not accept.

Where do I send a Bucks County assessment appeal?

To the Board of Assessment Appeals at 55 East Court Street, 6th floor, Doylestown. Call 215-348-6219 for the current annual filing date.

What do new owners of Bensalem property file with the county?

Under Act 29, a new owner submits contact information to the Board of Assessment within 30 days of the purchase.

Abington Township requires an affidavit at or before settlement on any single-family, two-family or multifamily dwelling. The seller swears that the house shows a clear street address, has smoke detectors and has at least one carbon monoxide detector. Under Resolution 92-008, a deed is not accepted for registration unless the certification comes with it.

Ordinance 1894 spells out the standards, and a buyer's agent will check them.

Ordinance 1894 requirements for the affidavit
RequirementWhat the ordinance requires
Address numeralsAt least three inches high on the street side, visible from the center of the street
Smoke detectorsOne on each level and in each bedroom or sleeping area
Carbon monoxide detectorNo more than 40 feet from every sleeping area
Detector approvalUL rated and approved

Breaking the ordinance is a summary offense. The penalty is a fine of $1,000 at most, up to 30 days in jail, or both, and each day of a continuing violation is charged separately. The affidavit form is in the township's document center. Alarms are cheap, and putting them in before you list removes a common closing delay.

No resale use and occupancy permit

Abington has no use and occupancy permit for residential properties. That review, with a Fire Marshal inspection, applies to commercial properties, new businesses and business transfers.

A typical house sale here carries less municipal paperwork than a town with a resale inspection, and the detector affidavit is the main township step. Work done without a permit is a separate matter. If you finished a basement, built a deck or added a bathroom, ask the Code Enforcement Division before you list.

What to prepare on the house itself

Look at the house as a buyer's agent would. From the curb, check that the numbers are readable from the middle of the street. Inside, count every sleeping area and find a detector for each one. Test each unit and swap out any that look worn or carry no UL mark.

If a previous owner finished the basement or attic, locate the permit papers now. Even a cash buyer will ask, and handing them over early keeps the deal moving.
