Real estate and transfer taxes

The 2026 tax sheet splits the real estate bill among the township, the Abington School District, a school referendum levy and Montgomery County with its community college. The school district rate is 39.8992 mills, by far the largest piece.

A township realty transfer tax of 1 percent is collected by Montgomery County, on top of the state's 1 percent. Ask your closing agent whether the school district adds a share on your deed. Pennsylvania exempts some transfers, such as property passing by will or intestate succession.

The township does not assess property. The Montgomery County Board of Assessments does, and the last countywide reassessment was in 1998. The township bill, which also covers sewer and refuse, is mailed in the first week of February for a January to December year. The school bill follows in the first week of July and runs July to June, so the closing agent will prorate each bill from its own start date.

Homestead exclusion and tax office

Owners of a primary residence can apply for a homestead exclusion through the Montgomery County Board of Assessments. Applications must arrive by March 1 to reduce the school tax bill.

For questions about the township tax sheet, call the Abington tax office at 267-536-1024 on weekdays between 8 am and 4 pm. Buyers often ask for the latest bill, so have both the township and school copies handy when you list.

Abington housing at a glance

Abington is a first-class township in Montgomery County, a first-ring suburb of Philadelphia, with a mid 2025 population estimate of 58,656. Owners live in 77.3 percent of occupied homes. A typical owned home is valued at $391,800, middle-of-the-market rent is $1,493, and middle household income is $103,645. Neighborhoods include Willow Grove, Roslyn, Crestmont, Glenside, Rydal, North Hills and Meadowbrook.

Seven SEPTA stations on three regional rail lines serve the township, with a ride to Center City under half an hour. Mention the train access when you market the house. Most of the township has public water from Aqua Pennsylvania and public sewer maintained by the township. The Abington School District is a separate body from the township government. About 92.5 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, so turnover is low, and a listing with defects or title questions takes more effort to place.

Which sale route fits an Abington house?

Three paths are open. Listing with an agent puts the house in front of the most buyers, at the price of staging, open houses and a wait while the buyer's bank and inspector do their work. Skipping the agent saves the commission, though you then handle every form yourself, from the detector affidavit to the deed.

Selling for cash to a direct buyer removes showings and repair work. People pick it for estate houses, rentals with tenants, homes with code problems or a hard move-out date. The offer is lower because the buyer takes on the repairs, so set it next to your likely net from a listing after commissions, fix-up costs and the months you would keep paying the mortgage and utilities.

Whichever path you take, the Abington requirements stay the same: detector affidavit, tax bills and a deed recorded with the Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds.

Steps from offer to closing

  1. Test or add detectors on each level and beside every bedroom, and check your house numerals from the street.
  2. Sign the affidavit and file it with your closing documents.
  3. Pull the newest township and school bills.
  4. Request a payoff statement if a loan is still open.
  5. Decide who has authority to sign when an owner has died or several people share title.
  6. At the settlement table you sign the deed, and it goes to the county to be recorded.

With cash there is no lender appraisal or underwriting step, so the timeline rests mainly on title work and when you can be out.

Inherited or tenant-occupied houses

If the owner has died, work out who may sign for the estate before anything else. A deed cannot be recorded until title is clean, and passing a house through an estate carries no state transfer tax, though the sale after it does.

If renters live there, the lease controls your timetable. Showings and move-out dates follow its terms and Pennsylvania landlord and tenant law. A buyer who wants to keep the renters will ask to see the lease and the rent history. The detector rules apply to rentals sold in the township as well.

Frequently asked questions

Does Abington require a smoke and carbon monoxide certification when I sell?

Yes. Ordinance 1894 requires smoke detectors on each level and in each bedroom, plus a carbon monoxide detector within 40 feet of every sleeping area, with a seller's affidavit at or before settlement.

Is there a residential use and occupancy permit in Abington?

No. That review applies to commercial buildings and business transfers, not to a house sale.

What is Abington's transfer tax?

The 2026 tax sheet shows a 1 percent real estate transfer tax, collected by Montgomery County. The state adds its own 1 percent. Ask the closing agent whether any other local share applies.

Who assesses property in Abington Township?

The Montgomery County Board of Assessments, not the township. The last countywide reassessment was in 1998, and interim bills reflect changes such as additions or demolitions.

When must I apply for the homestead exclusion?

Applications must reach the Board of Assessments by March 1 to cut the school tax bill. A move or a change of title means applying again.

How selling a house in Lancaster works

Whether you hire a broker, put up a sign yourself or take a cash offer, the same city and county paperwork applies. The city issues its own payoff figures, the recorder collects transfer tax, and the countywide reassessment is something buyers will ask about.

Lancaster is small and dense, with about 58,366 people on barely 7.2 square miles. Much of the housing is rowhomes on narrow lots, and the oldest are nineteenth century brick, so a sale often turns on the condition of one building. Less than half of occupied homes are lived in by their owners, which means many sales involve tenants. The middle home value is $219,500 and the middle rent is $1,240, a gap that explains why investors buy here. A seller with a rental can expect offers that price in the rent roll and the cost of the next inspection.

A cash sale can move faster, since no lender appraisal holds up the closing. It does not remove the city steps below. Someone still has to order the property certification, record the deed and pay the transfer tax.

City rules that can affect a sale

The ones that matter most are rental licensing, the vacant property registry and the lead safety rules for older rentals. The Bureau of Property Maintenance and Housing Inspections at 120 North Duke Street runs them.

  • Rental licenses and inspections. The city runs a residential rental program under its Chapter 238 and inspects every rental holding a city license at least once every six years, with at least three weeks of notice. For a tenant-occupied house, request the license status and open inspection items from the city before replying to any bid.
  • Lead safety. Rentals and child care facilities built before 1978 must meet lead safety requirements every two to four years under rules that took effect in January 2023. The city plans to cover roughly 12,000 older rentals over a four year cycle.
  • Vacant or abandoned houses. An owner must register a vacant building within 10 days. The semiannual fee is $200, with extra charges for buildings vacant two years or longer, and a house actively marketed for sale is outside the definition of vacant. If a registered property is sold, the new owner has 10 days to update the registration and inherits unpaid fees.
  • Short term rentals. The city allows them only in listed zoning districts, with a Certificate of Zoning Compliance, a rental license and an inspection first. A buyer planning an Airbnb use should confirm the district before paying for the house.

A house in mortgage default or under a pending sheriff sale counts as abandoned, and those properties face monthly inspections. If you are behind on the mortgage, factor that in before you list.

The 2027 Lancaster County reassessment

Every parcel in the county, including each house in Lancaster, received a new assessed value for the 2027 tax year. After the reassessment, annual appeals must be filed by August 1 of a given year to take effect for the following tax year.

The old values were based on market conditions from 2018. The new ones draw on arm's length sales from 2022 through 2024, adjusted by neighborhood. A buyer may notice a higher assessed value than the one on the old bill. The county points out that every taxing body must lower its millage so that the reassessment alone does not bring in more revenue.

  • County and municipal millage for 2027 gets set around the close of December 2026.
  • School district millage for the 2027 to 2028 school year is set in June 2027, and the reassessment does not change 2026 to 2027 school taxes.
  • The assessment office is at 150 North Queen Street, Suite 310, and property records can be searched free on the county reassessment site.

Have the new assessed value ready when you talk to a buyer. A parcel that jumped will raise questions about the tax bill, and the answer is that the rates reset before 2027 bills go out.

What paperwork does the city require before closing?

The settlement company must send the city a Request for Property Certification with payment, and for a house inside city limits a smoke detector certification has to be completed before the city will release information. The city asks for two full business days to return the figures once the request is complete.

The 2025 version of the city form listed an $18 tax certification, a $5 trash final, a $17 water final and a $40 combined final. It also asks for the meter reading, the new owner's details and the settlement date, and it tells the title agent to escrow estimates if the city does not answer in time. The form flags delinquent city taxes, property violations, police alarm charges, housing licenses and liens.

  1. Order the property certification early, since the smoke detector step comes first.
  2. Have the buyer open a water account using the city application.
  3. Check for delinquent county taxes with the Lancaster County Tax Claim office at 717-299-8232.
  4. Ask about Downtown Investment District (DID) charges if the house is downtown. The form has a line for them and a separate DID office number.

Transfer tax at the recorder's office

The state's cut is 1 percent of the property value. The county recorder gathers it at the same time as any local transfer tax. Buyer and seller are both liable for it. State exemptions cover certain family transfers and property passing by inheritance.

The title agent can quote the exact combined rate for a Lancaster deed, since the local portion depends on the taxing bodies involved. Who pays it is negotiated in the sales contract. With an as-is purchase, read the contract line by line to see who covers transfer tax and the city finals.

Which Lancaster houses suit a cash offer?

A cash sale makes sense when speed, condition or tenants matter more than the last dollar of price. A rowhouse with deferred repairs, a rental with an open inspection report, or a vacant inherited house are cases where a cash buyer can simplify the sale.

Compare any offer to a realistic list price less repairs, agent commission, transfer tax, city finals and months of carrying cost. To see what a direct buyer would pay for your Lancaster house, request a quote from Cash Home Buyers and weigh it against the net sheet.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a smoke detector certification to sell a house in Lancaster city?

Yes, for a house inside city limits. The city's property certification request requires a completed smoke detector certification before the city provides settlement information. Have it done before the title company orders the finals.

Can I still appeal my Lancaster County assessment?

Yes. Annual appeals can be filed each year by August 1 to take effect for the following tax year. An appeal can lower or raise the value.

What happens to a vacant house in Lancaster while I try to sell it?

A vacant house that is not actively marketed must be registered with the city within 10 days and carries a semiannual fee. Properties in mortgage default count as abandoned and face monthly inspections. Check the registry rules with the housing bureau at 717-291-4781 before the house sits empty.

Does a tenant have to leave before I sell a Lancaster rental?

No. Tenants do not have to move out for a rental to sell, because the buyer steps into the lease. The unit still needs a current city rental license, and any open inspection items should be cleared or priced into the sale.

Who collects the transfer tax when a Lancaster house sells?

The Lancaster County recorder takes payment when the deed is filed. The state's piece is 1 percent of the value, with local taxes added on top. The title company will show the exact figures on the settlement statement.

Lower Paxton is the most populous municipality in Dauphin County, with an estimated 55,564 residents, about 9 miles northeast of Harrisburg. Interstates 81 and 83 both run through it. Housing and neighborhoods

Owners live in about two thirds of the housing, 66.5 percent, so a third of homes are rentals or otherwise not owner-occupied. A typical owned home is valued at $284,700 and typical rent is $1,417. Those are modest numbers next to the Philadelphia suburbs, though transfer tax and closing costs still add up. A landlord selling a rental pays the same percentage, so settle the split before you sign.

Linglestown in the northeast, Paxtonia in the center and Colonial Park in the west and southwest are the main named communities, and children attend the Central Dauphin School District. Many neighborhoods date from the postwar suburban boom, so older systems are common. Use the community name in your listing.

Sewer and stormwater accounts at sale

Lower Paxton's sewer authority requires settlement agents to request balances on a specific form before a sale or refinance. The form can take up to five business days to be reviewed and returned, so start the day the contract is signed.

  • The completed Sewer and Stormwater Services Transfer Form goes to the authority's settlements email address or by fax.
  • A new sewer account carries a $15 processing fee collected at settlement.
  • The authority bills in arrears each January, April, July and October, so ask your settlement agent to prorate a mid-quarter sale. A flat residential sewer rate and a single family stormwater fee appear on the same quarterly bill.
  • Delinquent accounts can go to a collection law firm, and unpaid charges become a lien that follows the property.

If your account is on automatic withdrawal, call the Sewer and Utilities Department at 717-657-5617 so the draft stops after the sale. Bills stay in the owner's name, which matters when you own a rental and a tenant normally pays the household bills.

How do Lower Paxton property taxes work?

Real estate is taxed by the township, Dauphin County and the Central Dauphin School District, and the school district is by far the largest bill at 18.2934 mills for 2025 to 2026. Township assessments rest on a January 2002 base, adjusted for new construction and appeals, so the figure on your bill can differ a great deal from market value. Earned income tax is 2 percent, with 1.5 percent to the school district and 0.5 percent to the township, and the local services tax is $52 for people who work in the township.

Appealing a Dauphin County assessment

Dauphin County accepts annual appeals after June 1 and no later than 4:30 p.m. on August 1, and a late filing is rejected even if it was mailed on time. An appeal from a new or revised assessment must arrive within 40 days of the notice. The filing fee must come with the form and is not refunded, and all delinquent taxes on the parcel must be current before the Board will accept or hear it.

The Board of Assessment Appeals sits in the Administration Building at 2 South 2nd Street, Harrisburg, and takes filings by mail or in person on weekdays. The aggrieved party must appear at the hearing, and anyone representing an owner must be a Pennsylvania attorney who brings a power of attorney.

What closing costs should a Lower Paxton seller expect?

The state realty transfer tax is 1 percent, the township levies one half of one percent by ordinance, and the Central Dauphin School District levies one half of one percent. Together that is 2 percent of the sale price, collected at settlement by the Dauphin County Recorder of Deeds. Both parties are jointly liable under state law, so allocate it in the contract. Exempt transfers include certain moves between close family members and property that passes by will or intestacy.

Add prorated real estate tax, sewer and trash charges, any agent commissions, and payoff of any mortgage or lien. Ask the township codes office whether any sale-related inspection or certificate applies to your address.

Start by choosing the closing date you want, then ask your closing agent to send in the sewer transfer form on the day the contract is signed. Allow up to five business days for the authority to return balances. While you wait, find out whether your tax bills are current, since an unpaid balance can reach the Tax Claim Bureau after December 31 and a delinquent parcel cannot be appealed until it is current.

Next, line up payoffs for any mortgage or lien and gather your sewer and trash account details. If your sewer account is on automatic withdrawal, call the Sewer and Utilities Department so the draft stops after settlement. At the table, check that the transfer tax shares, the prorated taxes and the new account fee all match your contract. A cash sale tends to be quick here because no lender sits in the middle, though the sewer form still sets the pace, so file it first. How much is the transfer tax in Lower Paxton Township?

The total is 2 percent of the sale price: 1 percent to Pennsylvania, one half percent to the township and one half percent to the Central Dauphin School District. The county Recorder of Deeds collects it at settlement.

Does the Lower Paxton sewer authority need anything before closing?

Yes. The settlement agent must send the Sewer and Stormwater Services Transfer Form and allow up to five business days for balances. The authority charges a $15 new account fee at settlement.

What is the Dauphin County assessment appeal deadline?

August 1 at 4:30 p.m., with filing allowed after June 1. A new or revised assessment can be appealed within 40 days of its notice.

Who collects real estate tax in Lower Paxton Township?

An elected tax collector handles real estate tax payments for the township, county and school district. Unpaid taxes go to the Dauphin County Tax Claim Bureau after December 31.

How does the sewer bill work if I sell mid-quarter?

The authority bills in arrears each January, April, July and October. Ask your settlement agent to prorate the quarter so you pay only for the days you owned the house.

How a Bristol sale works

Bristol in Bucks County is most often Bristol Township, the large municipality of about 54,000 residents that includes Levittown neighborhoods, Croydon and Bath. A sale there runs through the agreement of sale, a township change of occupancy approval on resale, settlement and a deed recorded with the Bucks County Recorder of Deeds. Bristol Borough is a separate municipality with its own rules, so check which one your address falls in. Your tax bill names the municipality and school district, and the Bucks County Board of Assessment Appeals can tell you where the parcel sits.

The township's Building and Planning Department is at 2501 Bath Road and answers questions at 215-785-3680. Call before you list, so you know what the office will want to see for a resale in your part of the township.

Bristol Township housing snapshot

Buyers here are mostly owners. Owner-occupied homes make up 72.4 percent of housing units for 2020 to 2024. Commutes average 27.4 minutes, and the township sits at the junction of Interstate 95, the Pennsylvania Turnpike and Interstate 295.

The wettest day since 1981 delivered 6.42 inches of rain on August 27, 2011, so check basements and sump pumps before showings.

Resale fees and certifications

Transfer tax and property tax

The township's fee schedule lists a real estate transfer tax of 1 percent of the purchase price, split 0.5 percent to the township and 0.5 percent to the Bristol Township School District. Add the state's 1 percent and the total on a sale is 2 percent. Grantor and grantee are jointly liable under state law, so the agreement of sale should say who pays.

Assessment appeals and Act 29

A buyer must send contact information to the Bucks County Board of Assessment within 30 days of buying, under Act 29. Tell your buyer at closing, because the notice is theirs to send and it is easy to forget in the rush after settlement.

Annual appeals are due each August, with a $75 filing fee per parcel, and any change from an annual appeal takes effect the following tax year. Appeals are filed by the aggrieved party of record. Call the board for the current year's date.

How the township permit process runs

The township's permit page describes six steps from application to a Certificate of Approval, and a finished project closes the file for the next owner. Applications go through the township's online self-service portal or at the municipal building.

  • Submit the application, and staff check that forms and fees are complete.

  • Inspections happen in two phases, rough and final, and you call 48 hours ahead to schedule each one.
  • A Certificate of Approval issues when all work complies.

If an inspector finds unapproved work, the township demands compliance, and a stop work order follows when compliance is not found. Sellers with open permits should finish the final inspection before listing.

Open permits and unpermitted work

Unpermitted work is the common obstacle, because the township doubles permit fees when it finds work done without a permit and may add court fines. Permits are needed for additions, fences, renovations, decks, pools, demolitions and electrical, plumbing and HVAC equipment.

All contractors working in the township must be registered, and registrations are renewed annually from January through December. The township also asks everyone who lives or works there to complete a municipal and school income tax registration through Keystone Collection. Before you list, confirm that finals were signed off on past projects.

Order of steps for a Bristol Township sale

  1. Confirm the house is in the township, not the borough, using your tax bill.
  2. Order the four-year tax certification and the sewer certification early. A rush on the tax certification costs more.
  3. Call the Building and Planning Department about the $100 change of occupancy approval and book the inspection.
  4. Fix anything flagged. If a second inspection is needed it is $40.
  5. Clear any open permit with a final inspection, since the township asks for 48 hours of notice to schedule each one.
  6. Pay any lien or sewer balance, then settle and record the deed with the Bucks County Recorder of Deeds.

Doing the certifications first usually keeps the closing on the date you agreed.

Selling a tenant-occupied house

The fee schedule lists an annual rental fee of $100 for a single-family dwelling and an occupied rental fine of $320. A landlord selling a tenant-occupied house should check the rental status first and gather any records the buyer will want. Read the lease for notice terms before you schedule showings or the resale inspection.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Ways to sell fast in Bristol Township

You can list with an agent, sell on your own or accept a cash offer. A cash buyer skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting, but the change of occupancy approval and the tax and sewer certifications still apply. Ask for any offer in writing and compare them by the check you receive after fees, taxes and any repairs.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a use and occupancy inspection to sell a house in Bristol Township?

The township's 2026 fee schedule lists a $100 residential change of occupancy charge on resale and $40 for a second inspection if one is needed. Call 215-785-3680 to confirm the steps for your address.

Who pays the transfer tax on a Bristol Township sale?

The contract sets who pays, but state law makes seller and buyer jointly liable. The total is 2 percent: 1 percent to Pennsylvania, 0.5 percent to the township and 0.5 percent to the school district.

What certifications does the township issue at sale?

Tax and sewer certifications. A four-year tax certification costs $35, or $50 rushed, and a sewer certification costs $50. Order them before settlement is scheduled.

Is Bristol Township the same as Bristol Borough?

No. They are separate municipalities in Bucks County with separate rules and officials. The figures on this page describe the township.

Can I appeal my Bristol Township assessment after selling?

Appeals are filed by the aggrieved party of record. Annual appeals are due each August, and changes take effect the following tax year, so call the Bucks County board for the current date.

Millcreek housing snapshot

Millcreek Township wraps the lakefront and suburban ground west and south of the city of Erie. The 2020 count was 54,070, which makes it the biggest township in western Pennsylvania, and the July 2025 estimate is 52,680. Most land is given over to retail, services, light industry, schools and residential streets, so a house here is nearly always a suburban lot on public roads and utilities.

About two of every three homes are owner-occupied. Much of the housing went up in the postwar boom, when population climbed from 16,776 in 1950 to 36,946 in 1970, so the roof, furnace and wiring in a typical Millcreek house are decades old and buyers price that in. Because 23.1 percent of residents are 65 or older, long-owned homes and estates make up part of what reaches the market.

Millcreek township housing figures, 2020 to 2024

Code enforcement and open violations

Millcreek's Bureau of Code Enforcement applies the International Property Maintenance Code and the International Fire Code, so an unresolved violation on your parcel can hold up a closing. A neighbor's complaint or a phone call usually opens a case.

The office deals with problems such as these:

  • Weeds, debris and trash piling up on the lot
  • Sidewalks that are a tripping hazard, and unshoveled snow or ice on sidewalks
  • Electrical, building and fire violations
  • Pest infestations and abandoned vehicles on private property
  • Illegal burning, demolition permits and condemnations

A notice of violation gives you 20 days to appeal the inspector's decision. If you let it sit, the inspector comes back for a second look and can file a non-traffic summary citation with the local magistrate, who then schedules a hearing for the owner of record. Vacant houses follow the same path, and when compliance never arrives the township can move to clean and secure the building or raze it.

If your house is empty or run down, clear these items before you list, or write down what remains and share that list with the buyer before you sign a contract.

Short-term rentals

Millcreek calls Airbnb or VRBO style stays Limited Lodging: renting to the same guest for at least two and no more than 30 consecutive nights. A stay beyond 30 nights is a long-term rental and falls outside the rule. Limited Lodging is allowed only in certain zones, and only after the property registers with the Code Enforcement Office.

The allowed areas are the MU-1 Neighborhood Mixed Use, MU-2 Corridor Mixed Use and PI Presque Isle Gateway districts, plus two Limited Lodging Overlay areas near the lake. One overlay runs from the west line of the Hartt Estates Subdivision along Montpelier Avenue, south to West Lake Road and north to Lake Erie. The other starts at the east line of Calvary Cemetery and runs to West 11th Street, the Corridor Mixed Use 2 boundary and the Presque Isle district.

A buyer who wants a lakeside house for guest stays should phone the Zoning Office at 814-833-2935 and ask whether the parcel sits inside one of those areas. If you have been renting the house this way yourself, hand the registration paperwork to the buyer.

How to appeal your assessment

Erie County, not the township, sets your assessed value. The Board of Assessment Appeals takes the annual appeal form between January 1 and August 1 and holds hearings from July to October. Filing costs $50 for a parcel, with $10 more for each added parcel in the same property.

What the appeal form asks of you:

  • An owner may speak at the hearing, or a Pennsylvania attorney may; a company owner must use an attorney.
  • Name up to three comparables, either recent sales or active listings.
  • Send two copies of your evidence ten days ahead, and make sure any appraisal is effective within six months of the appeal.
  • An appeal reopens the valuation, so the figure can fall, hold or rise.

The county's assessment office also has forms for the homestead exclusion, owner changes, Clean and Green land and catastrophic loss, and it publishes a millage chart each year. Look up Millcreek Township and its school district on that chart to see the rates behind a bill.

Closing, transfer tax and disclosure

Deeds for Millcreek houses are recorded at the Erie County Recorder of Deeds in the courthouse on West Sixth Street. That office also collects the state and local transfer tax and the county's recording fees. Deeds between spouses, parents and children, or siblings can be exempt. The county's tax sale material quotes 2 percent as the standard transfer cost, so ask the Recorder how the local split works on an ordinary Millcreek sale.

Pennsylvania's seller disclosure law, Title 68 Chapter 73, has you fill out a statement and hand the buyer a signed copy before any agreement of transfer is signed. It covers the roof, basement, drainage and flood risk indicators. An executor or other fiduciary selling for an estate is excused from it, which applies to inherited Millcreek homes.

Act 74 of 2026 adds a written flood insurance warning to the seller package once the Insurance Department puts up its flood page. That matters most for parcels near the lake.

What if property taxes are behind?

The county's annual upset sale covers parcels with taxes two or more years behind, and it runs as an online auction. A winning bid does not end the owner's rights until the bidder pays in full, so you can still clear the debt first and keep the house. After full payment, nothing can be redeemed.

Parcels that do not sell go to a judicial sale and then a repository list, and the owner cannot bid on a parcel in either group. The buyer inherits liens and judgments and receives a quit claim deed. A sale before this point usually keeps more of your equity. Call the Tax Claim Bureau for a payoff figure and to learn where your parcel stands.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Millcreek houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What are the main ways to sell a house in Millcreek?

The right route depends on repairs, timing and any code problems at the property.

  • Agent listing: a fit when the house shows well and you can wait through showings, a buyer's inspection and loan approval.
  • Owner sale: skips the agent but puts pricing, the disclosure form and negotiation on you.
  • Cash sale as is: used for estate homes, houses with open Millcreek code notices, tenant-occupied properties and places needing work, generally at less than a repaired house would bring.

Whichever way you go, start with the same three chores. Pull the Erie County parcel record, confirm that no township notice is open, and complete the state disclosure statement. A cash sale skips the showings, the buyer's lender and the repair requests, so it can close faster, but compare the offer against what a repaired listing would net after repairs and fees.

Frequently asked questions

Is Millcreek a city or a township?

Millcreek is a township in Erie County. The city of Erie annexed pieces of it over the years, but the township keeps its own zoning, code enforcement and police.

Can a Millcreek house with open code violations still be sold?

Yes. A notice of violation leaves 20 days to appeal, and ignored notices can reach the local magistrate as a summary citation. Tell buyers about the notice and ask the Code Enforcement office what closes the file.

When can I appeal my Millcreek assessment?

Erie County takes the appeal form from January 1 through August 1, and hearings run July through October. Filing costs $50 a parcel, and an appeal can raise the value as well as lower it.

Must Millcreek sellers hand buyers a disclosure statement?

Usually yes. Pennsylvania requires a signed property disclosure statement before an agreement of transfer is signed, except for fiduciaries selling for an estate.

Can I run my Millcreek house as an Airbnb before selling?

Only inside the zones where the township allows Limited Lodging, meaning guest stays of 2 to 30 nights. Those are the MU-1, MU-2 and Presque Isle Gateway districts and two overlay areas, and registration with Code Enforcement is required.

Haverford Township housing at a glance

Haverford Township is an established inner suburb on Philadelphia's western edge, home to an estimated 50,997 people. About 87.4 percent of homes are owner-occupied, a typical home is valued at $466,400, and typical rent is $1,766. Most owners have been in their houses a long time, so sales here often follow a downsize, an inheritance or a house that has outlived its last update.

At these price levels, a roof, kitchen or electrical job adds up fast. Plenty of owners set the cost of getting a house market-ready against what an as-is sale would net, and that comparison is usually the starting point.

Name your neighborhood when you describe the house, because buyers search by it. Llanerch, Brookline, Beechwood, Oakmont, Manoa, Westgate Hills, Paddock Farms, Merwood, Bon Air and Chatham Park are all in common use, and many of the post-war tracts share the Havertown postal address. Transit helps listings too: the Norristown High Speed Line has seven stations inside the township.

Rental licensing and inspections

The Building and Codes Department licenses rentals every year and inspects them before a tenant moves in. The unit is inspected again each time occupancy changes, so a buyer taking over a rented Haverford house should plan for that step.

  • No more than three unrelated people may live in a rental house.

  • Student housing is allowed only as a special exception from the Zoning Hearing Board.
  • Renting counts as a business activity under the township's Business Privilege Tax, so a landlord also files a business tax return.

The license application needs a list of occupants and a copy of the signed lease. If you are selling a rental, give the buyer your current license and your inspection records, and tell them when the next inspection comes due.

Selling a house that has tenants

A rented house changes hands a little differently. The license runs on a March-to-February cycle and is due on or before March 1, so a sale that closes near that date is a good time to confirm the license is paid and the penalty has not been triggered. If your tenant is leaving, the township inspects the unit before the next occupant moves in, and the $50 inspection fee is yours or the buyer's depending on what the contract says.

Walk the rooms against the occupancy rules before you hand over records. Check the number of unrelated residents, any roomer or boarder arrangement, and whether any student housing was ever approved by the Zoning Hearing Board. A buyer who plans to keep renting will want the signed lease, the occupant list that went with the license application, and proof that your business tax return was filed.

If the buyer plans to move in, an owner-occupied unit follows simpler rules. Either way, put the license and inspection handover in writing so nothing slips between settlement and the next March 1.

Permits and township paperwork

Contractors working in the township must hold a township license. The department will not take a permit application without a signed contract, proof of insurance with workers compensation, and the cost estimate. Residential additions also need a plot plan showing building coverage and impervious surface.

Plumbing, generator, mechanical, electrical, roofing and siding, fences, sheds, rental housing licenses and contractor licenses can all be applied for online. If an earlier owner skipped a permit for a deck or addition, ask the department what its records show before you list, because a buyer's inspector may ask the same question.

Trees are regulated as well. A permit is required to plant, prune, remove or spray a public shade tree, and owners must keep private branches 12 feet above public walks and 14 feet above streets.

The department also has a contact for use and occupancy (U&O) inspections. Ask whether one applies to your sale, and what it costs, before you fix a closing date.

How are transfer tax and recording handled in Delaware County?

Your deed gets filed with the Delaware County Recorder of Deeds. Pennsylvania charges a 1 percent transfer tax on the property's value, and the recorder collects a local share that is divided among school districts and municipalities.

Property that passes to heirs by inheritance is exempt, which matters if you received the house and now plan to sell. For deeds accepted during the year that began July 1, 2026, the state's Delaware County valuation factor is 1.83. Your title company can give you the combined percentage and explain who pays which part under your contract.

From offer to closing

The order of events is much the same on every route. First you settle on a price and sign a sales agreement. A title company then searches the record and totals whatever is owed against the house. Next come the township items: a use and occupancy inspection if one applies, any open permits to close out, and the rental license records if the house has tenants. The deed is signed at settlement and filed with the recorder, who collects the transfer tax.

Gather these before you list or ask for an offer:

  • Your rental license, lease and inspection records, if the house is rented.
  • Permit paperwork for any deck, addition, roof or electrical work.
  • Your mortgage payoff details and any lien information.
  • If you inherited the house, the estate paperwork showing who has authority to sign.

A call to the Building and Codes Department early in the process costs nothing and prevents surprises late in the sale.

Choosing how to sell a Haverford Township house

Owners here tend to pick one of three routes.

  • An agent listing can fetch the strongest price for a well-kept house, with showings and repair requests along the way.
  • Selling yourself avoids a commission and puts pricing and paperwork on your desk.
  • A cash offer takes the house in its present state, which suits an estate or a property that needs major work.

A cash sale skips showings, buyer financing and repair negotiations, and you pick the closing date. The trade is that the price reflects the house as it stands. At Haverford price levels the gap between an as-is offer and a renovated sale can be wide, so work out what you would keep on each path before you decide. Frequently asked questions

Must a Haverford rental be inspected before sale?

The township inspects before a tenant moves in and again whenever occupancy changes, at $50 per unit. Keep your latest rental license and inspection record ready, and expect the buyer to plan for the next inspection.

Is an inherited Haverford house taxed on transfer?

State rules exempt property inherited with or without a will. Your later sale to a buyer is a new transfer and carries the state 1 percent plus any local share.

How many unrelated people can share a Haverford rental?

A rental house is capped at three unrelated residents. Student housing needs a special exception from the Zoning Hearing Board.

Do I need a permit to take down a tree before selling in Haverford?

A permit is required to plant, prune, remove or spray a public shade tree, meaning one on public property or a street. Trees on private land follow different rules, so call the Building and Codes Department if you are unsure.

Which school district serves Haverford Township addresses?

The School District of Haverford Township does. It runs five elementary schools, one middle school and one high school, so name the elementary zone when you describe the house.

Who sells houses in Harrisburg

Renters occupy most homes in this state capital, prices are modest, and a lot of sellers are landlords or heirs. The 2025 estimate is 50,522 people, and the 2020 to 2024 survey counts 22,137 households. Only 36.6 percent of occupied homes are lived in by their owners. A typical owned home is worth $124,200, rent runs $1,062 and the median household income is $48,099.

Buyers often are investors who value a house by the rent it earns, and lenders tend to hesitate over a property that needs work. A vacant or tenant-occupied house may suit someone who accepts it as it stands. The city's older rowhouses and brick twins often need updates, which is part of why cash buyers are active here.

Is your address inside the city?

Harrisburg sits on the east bank of the Susquehanna River and is the seat of Dauphin County and the capital of Pennsylvania. Be careful with addresses. Several nearby townships, including Lower Paxton and Middle Paxton, use Harrisburg as their mailing name even though they sit outside city limits and follow their own codes. Check whether your parcel is inside the city before you read any rule below. Your tax bill or the county parcel record shows which municipality bills you.

Inside the city, six municipal historic districts, several national historic districts and architectural conservation overlays guide new work in older blocks, so ask before you change an exterior.

Permits and codes for repairs

The city's Bureau of Codes handles building permits, trade licenses, rental registration and property complaints, and you can reach it at 717-255-6553. Harrisburg follows the Pennsylvania Uniform Construction Code, with the 2021 international code editions.

  • Permits are required for roofing, fences, sheds, decks, replacement windows and doors, any structural work, new furnaces and any work above $1,000.
  • Residential permit applications must be decided within 15 business days, or 5 days if a design professional stamps the plans. Historic Review Board review adds time.
  • A building permit expires after 6 months if work is not continuous.
  • Electricians and plumbers must hold a city license, and every contractor needs a city business privilege license.
  • The Bureau Health Officer enforces lead-based paint hazard rules for residential structures.

If you did work in the past without a permit, call the Bureau before you list. That way you know what is open on the property before a buyer asks.

Repairs buyers ask about

Older Harrisburg houses often carry deferred work: roofs, windows, furnaces and structural repairs are the items that trigger permits. If a past owner did that work without a permit, the buyer's inspector or lender can raise it. Lead-based paint is another topic, since the Bureau Health Officer enforces hazard rules for residential structures.

Decide early whether to repair or sell as-is. Repairs mean permits, electricians and plumbers with city licenses, and a good deal of time, and a failed inspection adds more. An as-is sale to a buyer who plans the work puts that burden on the buyer, at a price that reflects it. Either way, tell the buyer what you know.

Rentals and condemned houses

A buyer of a Harrisburg rental or condemned house takes on city deadlines from the day of recording. A non-condemned rental must be registered within 10 days of purchase, and a condemned property needs permits to lift the condemnation within 30 days of purchase.

The program under Ordinance 1-2017 also requires an inspection at least once every five years, taxes and utilities to be current before a unit can be rented, and a local managing agent when the owner lives more than 50 miles away. The annual landlord license is separate and runs through the Bureau of Licensing, Taxation and Central Support at 717-255-6513.

Transfer tax in Dauphin County

The Dauphin County Recorder of Deeds records your deed and collects transfer tax at the same time. The state's rate is 1 percent of value, and school districts and municipalities receive a local share. The Department of Revenue holds grantor and grantee jointly liable, so have your title company show the split on the closing statement.

Heirs who receive a house through a will, or with none, owe no transfer tax on that inheritance. Their own later sale is a fresh transfer. The current Dauphin County valuation factor from the revenue department is 2.61. A deed for token consideration between tax-exempt parties carries no transfer tax, and checks go to the Dauphin County Recorder of Deeds.

Steps before you list

  1. Confirm the parcel is inside the city by checking your tax bill or the county parcel record.
  2. Call the Bureau of Codes at 717-255-6553 and ask what is open on the property, including permits, complaints and any condemnation.
  3. If the house is a rental, gather the lease, deposit details and proof of registration and rental fees.
  4. Ask your title company to show the transfer tax split on the closing statement.
  5. Collect the deed and, for an inherited house, the papers that show who can sign.

Doing this work first gives a buyer clear answers, and clear answers shorten the time between an accepted offer and settlement. A cash buyer does not wait on a lender, so open code or permit items usually set the earliest closing date.

Which way to sell

Sellers here tend to choose one of three paths.

  • A listing suits a house in decent shape and an owner who can wait for a buyer with loan approval.
  • Going without an agent trims the listing fee, though showings, forms and bargaining fall to you.
  • A cash offer fits a vacant, damaged, inherited or rented property, with the closing date up to you.

On every path, subtract repairs, carrying costs and fees before you compare.

Selling a tenant-occupied or inherited house

With tenants in place, the buyer steps into the lease. Hand over the lease, deposit details and proof that rental fees are paid, and tell the buyer whether the unit is registered. A buyer who keeps renting must register it with the Bureau of Codes within 10 days.

If the house came to you from a relative, start by confirming who has authority to sign for the estate. The inheritance itself triggers no transfer tax, but your sale to a buyer does. Bring the paperwork to the title company early, along with the deed and any open permit records, so the settlement can stay on its date.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Can a Harrisburg house be sold with tenants in place?

Yes. The buyer steps into the lease, and one who keeps renting must register the unit with the Bureau of Codes within 10 days of purchase. Hand over your lease, deposit details and proof that rental fees are paid.

Can I sell a condemned Harrisburg house?

Yes. The new owner must secure permits to lift the condemnation within 30 days of purchase, so buyers who can handle repairs are the usual fit.

Is transfer tax due when I inherit a Harrisburg house?

No. Inheritance transfers, with or without a will, are exempt. Your later sale to a buyer carries the 1 percent state tax plus the local share.

Not always. Lower Paxton, Middle Paxton and other nearby townships carry a Harrisburg mailing name but are separate municipalities with their own codes. Your tax bill or the county parcel record shows which municipality bills you.

Selling in Middletown Township, Bucks County

Middletown Township requires a Level 2 chimney inspection on every home that is sold, and Levittown sections add a heater compartment wall inspection. That fire marshal rule is the main local step. After it comes the 2 percent transfer tax, which you pay when the deed is filed.

The township has about 46,040 residents spread across roughly 19 square miles. It surrounds the boroughs of Langhorne, Langhorne Manor, Penndel and Hulmeville, which is why many addresses read Langhorne even though they sit in the township. Other Pennsylvania townships share the Middletown name, so make sure you are looking at the Bucks County one.

Whether you list, sell on your own or take a cash purchase, the township rules below still apply.

Housing types you will find

The mix of housing shapes how buyers see a sale. Levittown sections in the south were built in the 1950s, with hundreds of similar homes per development. Parkland has houses from every decade of the 20th century and the 21st. Newer townhouses and condominiums cluster around the Oxford Valley Mall, alongside assisted living and 55-plus housing, and a few older farm properties remain.

Neshaminy School District serves the township, and buyers regularly want to know the elementary zone for a given street. Interstate 295 skirts the eastern side, and U.S. Route 1 cuts through the middle. Commuters can use Woodbourne station on SEPTA's West Trenton line, or Langhorne station just over the border. Basements and drainage are a fair question for any buyer inspection, so keep repair records handy.

Chimney inspection when a house sells

Every home sold in the township needs a Level 2 chimney inspection, and the Fire and Emergency Management office keeps a copy. The rule follows NFPA 211, which calls for the inspection any time a property is sold or transferred.

The inspection covers any appliance that vents combustion gases, including oil-fired and gas-fired heaters with a metal B-vent chimney, fireplaces, wood stoves and pellet stoves. A certified CSIA chimney sweep must do it, and the township website keeps a courtesy list of local sweeps. A home with only electric heating and cooling, or one whose fireplace is vent-less, is outside the rule, and plastic PVC exhaust pipe is also exempt from a Level 2 inspection.

Property taxes in Middletown Township

The 2026 combined millage is 252.2674 mills. Three taxing bodies make up that number: the county at 29.65 mills, the Neshaminy School District at 198.0124 mills and the township at 24.605 mills.

The township's own 24.605 mills break down into a general fund of 7.025, a debt service fund of 5.115, fire protection of 4.75, parks and recreation of 3.25 and fire apparatus of 2.5, plus smaller street light, ambulance, road machinery and hydrant levies. A mill works out to one dollar of tax per thousand dollars of assessed value. Assessed values come from the Bucks County Board of Assessment, and Neshaminy's share is the bulk of the total.

Transfer tax at sale

On a Middletown sale the recorder collects 2 percent: half goes to the state and half is shared by the municipality and school district. You pay at recording, and the taxable value is not always the sales price.

The law does not assign the cost, and buyers and sellers usually split it. If too little was paid, the new owner answers for the difference. Since January 2026 the recorder has refused personal checks, and accepts only cash at the office, a cashier's check, a money order or a credit card, so alert your title company.

  • Exemptions can cover transfers among spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, and siblings.
  • Former spouses may make one such transfer.
  • A deed for $1, or any transfer where no tax is paid, needs a statement of value so the state can check what the property is worth.

Exemption questions go to the recorder's office at 215-348-6209.

Appealing a Bucks County assessment

Early August is the yearly appeal deadline, and a successful appeal changes the bill starting the next tax year. Hearings are held at 55 East Court Street in Doylestown, at 10 a.m. on the first and third Tuesdays of every month, and the phone number is 215-348-6219. The county website posts forms and rules for residential and commercial properties.

Two more county items touch buyers and sellers. You apply for the homestead and farmstead exclusion by March 1 for the tax year that begins the next July 1. Under Act 29, someone who buys must send the Board of Assessment their contact information within 30 days.

Getting through the inspection and closing

Hire a CSIA chimney sweep the moment you decide to sell. Ask the sweep to check every vented appliance, including any fireplace or stove, and send the report to Fire and Emergency Management. If the report finds a problem, you will want time to repair it before settlement. In a Levittown section, call the fire marshal at 215-750-3812 and ask what the heater compartment wall inspection involves.

In the meantime, confirm with your title company how the transfer tax will be paid, because the recorder takes no personal checks. When the deed shows no price, the REV-183 statement of value goes in twice. At the table, compare the tax split and the school and township proration with your contract.

Is a listing or a cash sale the better fit in Middletown?

Deferred repairs point toward a cash sale, and a house a lender will finance as it stands points toward a listing. Either way, the chimney inspection comes first, and a failed inspection can change what you can ask.

  • Book a CSIA chimney sweep before you list and send the report to the fire marshal.
  • If the house is in Levittown, ask the fire office what the heater compartment wall inspection involves.
  • Compare offers after the 2 percent transfer tax, your mortgage payoff and the school and township tax proration.

A cash purchase skips showings, a buyer's loan approval and repair negotiations, which helps when the chimney or heater compartment needs work. The inspection still has to be done, though, so ask the buyer in writing who orders it and who pays for any repair it calls for. Cash Home Buyers CA can give you a figure to compare with a listing.

Yes. A Level 2 chimney inspection by a certified CSIA sweep is required for homes with combustion appliances, and a copy goes to Fire and Emergency Management. Levittown homes also need a heater compartment wall inspection.

What is the transfer tax in Middletown Township?

The Bucks County Recorder of Deeds lists 2 percent in total: 1 percent to the state and 1 percent to the municipality and school district. The tax is paid at the time of recording.

Which school district serves Middletown Township?

Neshaminy School District. Five elementary schools, two middle schools and Neshaminy High School serve the township.

What is the total property tax rate in Middletown Township?

The 2026 combined rate is 252.2674 mills: 29.65 for the county, 198.0124 for Neshaminy School District and 24.605 for the township.

When can I file a Bucks County assessment appeal?

Annual appeals are due in early August. Call the Board of Assessment at 215-348-6219 with questions about the process.

What should York, PA sellers know before listing?

York is a compact city of 5.3 square miles in York County, and its Bureau of Permits and Inspections decides several things a seller needs before closing, including tenant licenses and a possible certificate of compliance. The paperwork runs through an online permit system, and the office takes appointments only.

The Census Bureau estimates 45,342 residents for July 2025, up 1.2 percent from the 2020 base. Its 2020 to 2024 survey shows 43.7 percent of homes lived in by their owners, a middle value of $119,700 and typical rent of $1,014 a month across 17,893 households. Median household income is $48,420, and 21.1 percent of residents are in poverty.

York was founded in 1741, became a borough in 1787 and a city in 1887. The Continental Congress met in the courthouse from September 1777 to June 1778 and adopted the Articles of Confederation there. Colonial-era buildings and large Gothic churches still stand around town.

Permits have also moved to the 2021 Uniform Construction Code for applications filed from January 1, 2026.

Before any inspection, collect the deed, any prior certificates, receipts for permitted work and the names of every tenant. York City says permit applications must be filed before work begins, so have those records ready.

What does a tenant occupied license mean if I am selling a rental in York?

Owners of rental houses in York carry a license that depends on an inspection, and the city says no checklist exists. Inspectors apply the City of York Property Maintenance Code, which is posted on the city website, so landlords read the code itself to prepare.

  • Reinspections and the Consolidated Board of Appeals go through the tenant occupied administrative desk.
  • Typical complaints in the city include weeds over 10 inches, uncollected trash, pest problems, leaks, sewer backups and mold.
  • Neighborhood Improvement Ordinance tickets can be appealed, but the appeal form has to be mailed or hand-delivered, not emailed.
  • Property owners are responsible for the sidewalk and trees in front of the house.

A buyer who purchases rentals as is will usually want the current license and any open citations in hand before settlement. Clear those, or disclose them in writing, ahead of the contract.

How is a deed recorded and taxed in York County?

York County's Recorder of Deeds says the realty transfer tax is 2 percent in total, with 1 percent to the state and 1 percent to local governments. Documents go first to the county Assessment Office, which certifies the parcel number, and then to the Recorder for recording and fees.

  • You can record in person, by mail, or through Simplifile or Ingeo, with a stamped return envelope and payment for the fees.
  • One check may cover everything, or you can write three, and the county accepts either.
  • A Statement of Value is required when you claim an exemption or pay a different amount than the deed states. It adds $2 to the recording fee.
  • A deed from a father to a son and similar family transfers are tax exempt if the deed states the relationship.
  • Recorded documents come back after about four to eight weeks, depending on workload.

The state notes both buyer and seller are liable for the tax, and the sales contract decides who pays. Ask the Recorder for the share that applies to a York City address.

Which schools and neighborhoods influence York home values?

York sits inside the York City School District, one of 15 public districts across the York area, and charter options include Lincoln Charter School and Helen Thackston Charter School. York Catholic High School and Holy Trinity Catholic School are among the private options. York College of Pennsylvania, Penn State York and the Harrisburg Area Community College York campus add student renters and staff.

The Arch Street area holds WellSpan Park, home of the York Revolution since 2007, and the old Pennsylvania Railroad station now sits on the York County Heritage Rail Trail across from the stadium. The York County Judicial Center and new apartment lofts anchored later redevelopment downtown. Spring Garden and West Manchester townships border the city, and several of the area's large employers are based in them.

How do local employers and roads affect York sellers?

York has deep manufacturing roots. The area is home to a Harley-Davidson plant, Voith Hydro, BAE Systems, York International and a Starbucks roasting facility, and Dentsply Sirona and Glatfelter moved their headquarters out in 2019 and 2020. WellSpan York Hospital, a regional trauma center, and UPMC Memorial Hospital serve the city.

US 30 and Interstate 83 cross the area, Rabbit Transit runs bus routes in the city and suburbs, and a Greyhound and Trailways depot offers intercity service. The nearest commercial airports are BWI and Harrisburg International, with Lancaster's Amtrak service about 24 miles east. The Census gives a mean commute of 23.1 minutes for York workers, so sellers can market access to both Harrisburg and Baltimore.

Does York's weather or flood history matter when I sell?

The city has hot, humid summers and moderately cold winters. Rain and snow add up to about 41 inches a year, falling on roughly 127 days. Hurricane Agnes set the state's 24-hour precipitation record of 13.5 inches at the York weather station on June 22, 1972, so buyers do ask about basements.

Plan to show a dry basement and sound gutters, and keep records of sump pump work or waterproofing. An as-is purchaser prices roof and foundation questions differently from a buyer who needs a loan, so say plainly what you know.

Gather permit records for past work too. Electrical, plumbing, mechanical and demolition work in York City goes through the Bureau's online system, and sheds, decks and interior remodels need permits as well.

Do I need a certificate to sell my York house?

Possibly. York City says a structure changing ownership or tenancy without a change in use needs a Certificate of Compliance, though an FAQ on the same site ties it to commercial buildings. Call 717-849-2256 to confirm for your address.

How much does York County charge in transfer tax?

It is 2 percent in total, with 1 percent to the state and 1 percent to local governments, according to the county Recorder of Deeds. The sales contract decides whether buyer or seller pays.

Can I transfer a York house to a family member tax free?

Yes, when the deed states the family relationship, such as a transfer from a father to a son. The county advises checking with an attorney, and a Statement of Value is needed if you claim any other exemption.

How do I get a permit or license from York City?

Most applications are filed online through the city's OpenGov system. The Bureau of Permits and Inspections, at 101 S. George St., also takes appointments by phone at 717-849-2256.

How long until York County returns my recorded deed?

It takes about four to eight weeks after recording, depending on workload, because each document is scanned, proofed, indexed and verified. Include a stamped, self-addressed envelope.

What sellers should know in Manheim Township

Manheim Township is a Lancaster County municipality of 43,977 people, sitting directly north of Lancaster city. A certificate of use and occupancy and a 2 percent transfer tax round out the local rules.

Lancaster County also has a separate borough named Manheim, so check the municipality on your tax bill before relying on any local rule here. The township has no ZIP code of its own, so owners carry a Lititz, Lancaster or Leola mailing address depending on where the house sits. Communities include Neffsville, Dillerville and Landis Valley.

A listing, a sale by owner and a direct cash purchase are all open to a seller, and the paperwork below applies to each.

The school district and who bills your taxes

The Manheim Township School District covers exactly the township, so a home inside the boundary is in the district and a home outside it is not. That makes the address check simple for a buyer. Buyers with children usually ask which elementary school serves a street, and the district office can confirm that from an address. The elementary schools are Brecht, Bucher, Neff, Nitrauer, Reidenbaugh and Schaeffer.

The township itself does not bill or collect property taxes. Lancaster County assesses the property, while the elected tax collector and the school district collect the bills. Real estate tax bills combine the county and township taxes and go out by March 1. If a lender pays your taxes from escrow, send the lender a copy of the bill.

The 2027 Lancaster County reassessment

Lancaster County reassessed every parcel at current market value, and the new values apply to the 2027 tax year. The previous assessments were based on 2018 values, and the new notices should land near what a property would sell for today.

The county used valid arm's-length residential sales from 2022 through 2024, adjusted for acreage, square footage, porches, garages and bathrooms. State law requires each taxing body to adjust its millage so it does not collect more revenue only because values moved, but the tax on an individual house can still rise or fall. County and municipal millage for 2027 is set near the end of December 2026, and school millage for the 2027-2028 year is set in June 2027. The reassessment does not change 2026-27 school taxes.

The next opportunity for an annual appeal is 2028. Call the Property Assessment Office at 717-299-8381 to ask what applies to a house that sold or changed after the notices went out. Before you price your house, look up your reassessed value on the county property search site, since buyers will do the same.

Inspection and certificate of use and occupancy

The township does not require an inspection before settlement. A certificate of use and occupancy can still be requested by the parties to the deal, and the zoning ordinance has required one for every structure since 1944.

If you need a copy, contact the Code Compliance Department with the property address, the home type (single-family, townhouse or duplex) and whether any part of the basement is finished. Staff check the records and send a copy if one is on file. If none exists, the owner or an agent applies in person at the township office, pays a $50 residential filing fee and books an inspection with a code official.

Certain family transfers and property passed by inheritance are exempt from the state portion, so ask the recorder before assuming a deed is taxable.

Selling a rental in Manheim Township

Rental properties have needed a township license since 2022, and an annual license costs $50 per building. Each rental unit is inspected at least once every five years, and one- and two-unit buildings have every unit inspected.

A landlord who sells should ask the code office how to de-register or transfer the license, and should hand the buyer the latest inspection results.

Getting ready to close

Start with the paperwork you can control. Ask Code Compliance for a copy of your certificate of use and occupancy, and if none is on file, book the $50 filing and inspection so a missing certificate does not delay closing. Then gather your tax bills, your payoff statement and, if the house is rented, the license and the latest inspection report. Once you have an accepted offer, the title company prorates taxes and the deed is recorded with the Lancaster County Recorder of Deeds, where the transfer tax is paid. Confirm in writing who pays which share of that 2 percent. If you inherited the house, ask the recorder how the exemption works before the deed is drawn.

Which route suits a Manheim Township seller?

The right route depends on the house's condition and your moving date. Putting it on the market reaches more buyers but brings showings and inspection haggling, while a direct cash sale can be timed around your move.

  • Request your certificate of use and occupancy early so a missing certificate does not delay the closing.
  • Look up your 2027 reassessed value on the county property search site and compare it with the price you are weighing.
  • Subtract the 2 percent transfer tax share you agree to, plus any mortgage payoff, to estimate net proceeds.

If a buyer asks for repairs, compare the cost against a quote for selling as-is. Cash Home Buyers CA can provide that quote.

No. Manheim Township is a separate municipality that borders Lancaster city and has its own school district and township government. Lancaster County also has a borough named Manheim.

Not as a condition of settlement. The township does not inspect before closing, but buyers or lenders may ask for a copy. If none is on file, the residential filing fee is $50 and an inspection is scheduled.

What do buyers and sellers owe in transfer tax in Manheim Township?

The combined rate is 2 percent of the value transferred. The state gets 1 percent, and the township and school district share the other 1 percent. The Lancaster County Recorder of Deeds collects it.

When did the Lancaster County reassessment take effect?

The new values apply to the 2027 tax year. The next annual appeal opportunity is 2028.

Who sends the property tax bill in Manheim Township?

The elected tax collector and the school district collect the bills. Lancaster County sets the assessment, and the township does not bill or collect property taxes itself.

How much transfer tax do sellers pay in Wilkes-Barre?

A deed for a Wilkes-Barre property carries 3.5 percent in total transfer tax, which is well above the 2 percent charged in most Luzerne County municipalities. The county recorder will not accept a deed until payment is made, and the county says most sales agreements split it between buyer and seller.

Total realty transfer tax by location, from the Luzerne County Recorder of Deeds fee schedule effective July 1, 2026
LocationTotal rate
Most Luzerne County municipalities2% (1% state, 0.5% municipality, 0.5% school district)

Pittston City3.5%

On a $100,000 sale, 3.5 percent comes to $3,500 against $2,000 at the standard rate. A split contract puts $1,750 on each side, so build that into your net before you compare offers. The state's own page says both grantor and grantee are jointly and severally liable for the tax.

Which fees come with recording a Wilkes-Barre deed?

Luzerne County's schedule effective July 1, 2026 sets a deed's base fee at $87.75, covering up to four pages, four names and one parcel number. Extra pages cost $2.00 each, extra names $0.50 each and extra parcel numbers $0.50 each.

  • Deeds go to the Recorder's office at 200 North River Street. Recording runs from 9:00 A.M. until 4:20 P.M., and the lines are 570-825-1641 and 570-825-1642.
  • Every deed needs a signed, certified address for the buyer, and parcel numbers must be certified through the county Assessor's Office, which charges its own fee.
  • A Statement of Value goes in as an original plus one copy whenever the deed does not pay full tax or claims an exemption. It counts as a page at $2.00.
  • Deeds between husband and wife, parent and child, grandparent and grandchild, and siblings are generally exempt, and the deed must say why.

The Recorder's staff cannot give legal or tax advice or run title searches, so the closing agent or an attorney handles those pieces.

Do floods and old mines affect a Wilkes-Barre house sale?

They can, and buyers ask about both. Tropical Storm Agnes in 1972 pushed the Susquehanna to nearly 41 feet, about four feet above the old levees, and flooded downtown under nine feet of water. The city then built a levee system rising 41 feet, finished in January 2003 at roughly $250 million. In September 2011 the river crested at a record 42.66 feet, and the levees held in Wilkes-Barre while nearby boroughs flooded.

Mine subsidence is the quieter issue. Pennsylvania's Department of Environmental Protection says standard homeowner policies usually leave out damage from collapsed underground coal and clay mines, and it sells separate coverage. It lists residential coverage of $150,000 at $41.25 a year. Its online risk map shows whether an address sits over mine workings.

If you are selling, check the map for your street and tell your buyer what you find. The DEP also notes that a seller can cancel a policy at closing and that new owners must apply for their own.

Which Wilkes-Barre neighborhoods and schools matter to buyers?

The city has more than a dozen neighborhoods. Central City is the original 16-block downtown near the river, and it holds most of the high-rises and Public Square. North End is known for its architecture, and Parsons and Miners Mills have a quieter, more suburban feel at the northeastern edge. East End, Heights and Mayflower were developed in the 1900s, and Mayflower offers some of the best views of downtown from its high streets. South Wilkes-Barre, Goose Island, Rolling Mill Hill and the Iron Triangle lie southwest of the center.

The Wilkes-Barre Area School District runs one high school, Wilkes-Barre Area High School, which opened in 2020 and replaced three older secondary schools. Holy Redeemer High School is the Catholic option. King's College and Wilkes University are in the city, and Osterhout Free Library has three branches.

What carrying costs push Wilkes-Barre owners to sell quickly?

Holding an empty or inherited home in Wilkes-Barre means paying taxes, insurance and utilities while the property sits. The latest Census five-year survey reports median monthly owner costs of $1,272 with a mortgage and $559 without one, and 23.1 percent of residents live in poverty, so an extra house is a real strain for many families.

  • A house that sits empty still draws a tax bill and a utility bill each month.
  • The city's Susquehanna floodplain location may raise insurance questions, so keep flood and mine subsidence paperwork together for the buyer.
  • Estates need proof of authority before anyone can sign a deed, and a family transfer may be exempt from tax while a sale is not.
  • Tenants in place mean inspections and notices, so line up access dates in the contract.

A direct as-is sale removes showings and repair negotiations, but compare it against a listing using your own net figure after the 3.5 percent city transfer tax and recording fees.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Wilkes-Barre houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How do commuting and local employers shape demand?

Interstate 81 passes near the city, and the Northeast Extension of the Pennsylvania Turnpike (I-476) is close by. The Cross Valley Expressway carries PA 309 through the north of the city, and Interstate 80 lies about 10 miles south. Luzerne County Transportation Authority runs local buses, and Martz Trailways links downtown to Scranton, New York City and Philadelphia.

GUARD Insurance Group ranks among the large employers, and downtown holds regional offices for several banks and insurers. Census data for 2020 to 2024 put the mean commute at 20.7 minutes, and 58.4 percent of people aged 16 and older are in the civilian labor force. Hospitals and clinics lead the local economy: the Census counts about $2.2 billion in 2022 receipts across healthcare and social services, the biggest line it reports for the city.

What should I ask the city before listing a Wilkes-Barre property?

Call the Wilkes-Barre City code enforcement office and ask whether your property type needs a certificate of occupancy, a rental license or a buyer notice before closing. Rules for rentals and for occupied buildings differ from owner-occupied homes, and the office can say what an inspection will cover and how long it takes.

Bring the parcel number, the names on the deed and, for an estate, the letters or court papers that show who may sign. If liens or back taxes exist, request payoff figures early. An as-is purchaser can often work around those items. The seller still has to hand over a deed the Recorder will accept.

Frequently asked questions

How high is the Wilkes-Barre transfer tax?

It is 3.5 percent in total for a property inside Wilkes-Barre City, compared with 2 percent in most Luzerne County municipalities. The county says the buyer and seller usually split it, and the deed cannot be recorded until it is paid.

Who records the deed after a Wilkes-Barre sale?

The Luzerne County Recorder of Deeds at 200 North River Street records it, usually through your closing agent or title company. The base fee for a deed is $87.75 under the July 2026 schedule.

Is mine subsidence a concern for Wilkes-Barre homes?

It can be, because the region was heavily mined for anthracite. Check the state Department of Environmental Protection's online risk map for your address, and note that standard homeowner policies usually exclude this damage.

Must I fix a Wilkes-Barre house first?

Yes, an as-is buyer accepts the property with its flaws. City occupancy or rental rules may still apply, so call the code enforcement office before choosing a settlement day.

Are family transfers taxed in Luzerne County?

Transfers between spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, and siblings are generally exempt. The deed has to state the relationship, and a Statement of Value is needed when a non-family exemption is claimed.

Altoona housing at a glance

Altoona is a railroad city of about 42,300 people in Blair County, built on hillsides in the Allegheny Mountains. The July 1, 2025 estimate is 42,347 residents, down 3.6 percent from the 2020 base. Population peaked at 82,054 in the 1930 census and has dropped in every count since.

Prices sit far below the national level: an owner-occupied home has a median value of $119,900, while the figure for the United States is $332,700. About 63.9 percent of occupied homes are owned. Median gross rent is $819, and median household income is $51,250. At that price level, a repair bill can eat a large share of what the house will sell for. Get a firm estimate before deciding how to sell.

Older housing stock

The Pennsylvania Railroad founded Altoona in 1849 as a shop and maintenance site, and the housing followed the work. Many older districts mix rowhouses with single homes built for workers and managers. The manager houses are narrow and tall, resemble Victorian or Edwardian mansions, and have often been converted to double or triple family apartments.

Rowhouses share walls and rooflines between units, so a roof or drainage problem next door can affect you. Streets are numbered: Streets run northwest to southeast, and Avenues run northeast to southwest. The hillsides, the cold winters and about 136 days of precipitation a year put steady wear on roofs, gutters and basements, and buyers know it.

Neighborhoods and city limits

Learn the right section name before you write a listing.

  • Downtown and Center City: the Downtown Altoona Historic District, with multistory brick buildings from around 1900.
  • Main sections: Logantown, Fairview, Juniata, Wehnwood, Calvert Hills, the 5th and 6th Wards, Westmont, Eldorado, East End, Dutch Hill, Pleasant Valley, Hileman Heights, Mansion Park, Llyswen, Garden Heights and Highland Park.
  • Named neighborhoods: Little Italy, Gospel Hill, Toy Town, Columbia Park, Knickerbockers and Curtin.
  • Outside the city: Lakemont, Greenwood, Bellmeade and Newburg are treated as parts of Altoona but lie in Logan Township.

Logan Township wraps around the city, and a parcel's tax bill and codes office both depend on which side of the boundary it is on. For a parcel check, use the floodplain information page and the zoning and GIS map on the city website.
