Local taxes and transfer costs

Anyone who buys or sells in Altoona owes real estate transfer tax, and the Blair County Recorder of Deeds collects it. The rate adds up to 2 percent: the state takes 1 percent, and the other 1 percent is divided between the city and the Altoona Area School District.

The Blair County Assessment Office is at 423 Allegheny Street, Suite 041, Hollidaysburg, phone 814-693-3110. Request the appeal form and the yearly filing deadline there. Your closing agent can explain how the transfer tax is divided.

Selling a rental

Every owner of a leased or non-owner-occupied dwelling in Altoona must hold a Conditional Housing Permit, which becomes a Residential Rental Unit License after the unit passes inspection. Licenses are renewed on or before July 31 each year, and most units are inspected every three years.

  • An inspection takes 20 to 30 minutes, and the owner, tenant or a representative must be present.
  • Inspectors use the International Property Maintenance Code on the interior and exterior.
  • Owners usually get 45 days to repair violations, with extensions in 30-day steps, and life-safety hazards must be corrected immediately.
  • Heat must be supplied from October 1 to May 15, and smoke and carbon monoxide detectors are checked.

Landlords should confirm license status with Codes and Inspections at 1301 12th Street, Suite 103, phone 814-949-2456, and ask whether any inspection applies to the property at sale. Hand the buyer a copy of the license and the latest inspection result if you have them.

Vacant houses and open code notices

With an empty house, ask Codes and Inspections whether a property maintenance notice is open before you list. Such a notice stays with the building, and the buyer's title company will probably turn it up. Mowing the yard, boarding a broken window or correcting the violation now usually costs less than haggling over it at settlement. Gather the deed, the tax bills from H. A. Berkheimer and the county, and any permit records, before the first showing.

Collect the deed, the tax bills from H. A. Berkheimer and the county, and any permit records before the first showing.

Ways to sell a house fast

Owners here have three routes. Listing with an agent reaches the widest audience but means open houses, an inspection by the buyer and a lender's timetable. Selling privately keeps the commission and puts the paperwork on you. A cash offer closes fastest and with the least doubt, though the price reflects repairs the buyer absorbs.

Before choosing, get a rough repair estimate and ask a few buyers for written offers. Compare what each one would leave you after payoffs and transfer tax, and ask when each could close.

From offer to closing in Altoona

Paperwork comes first. The title company needs the deed and searches for liens, unpaid taxes and open notices. Get current balances from Blair County and H. A. Berkheimer, because either can appear on the settlement statement. When a mortgage is open, ask the lender for a payoff figure.

Next, decide who pays the 2 percent transfer tax. The sales agreement sets that, and it is one of the easiest items to bargain over. For a rental, add the license check with Codes and Inspections and a copy of any lease the buyer will inherit.

You sign the deed and settlement papers at closing, and the transfer is recorded in the Blair County Recorder of Deeds office. In a cash sale no lender appraisal or underwriting is involved, which leaves title work and your move-out date. Cash buyers can therefore often commit to a quick closing, useful for an inherited house, a vacant property or a move that cannot wait.

Jobs, roads and schools

Health care leads local employment, with UPMC Altoona and the James E. Van Zandt VA Medical Center. Penn State Altoona has a downtown presence. I-99 and US 22 link the city to the wider region, and a single school district, the Altoona Area School District, covers the whole city.

Frequently asked questions

Does Altoona have a transfer tax when I sell my house?

Yes. It is 2 percent in total: 1 percent to the state and 1 percent shared by the city and the school district. The Blair County Recorder of Deeds collects it.

When must Altoona landlords renew their rental license?

On or before July 31 each year. Most units are inspected every three years, and owners generally get 45 days to fix violations found.

Who collects real estate tax on an Altoona home?

H. A. Berkheimer collects the city's local real estate tax, at 7.129 mils. Blair County and the school district bill separately.

Is Lakemont inside the city of Altoona?

No. Lakemont, Greenwood, Bellmeade and Newburg are treated as parts of Altoona but lie in Logan Township, outside city limits.

Where do I ask about assessment changes in Blair County?

Call the Blair County Assessment Office in Hollidaysburg at 814-693-3110. It handles appeal forms and can tell you the filing deadline for the year.

How a home sale works in Hempfield Township

Paperwork is lighter in Hempfield than in many Pennsylvania municipalities, because the township does not ask for a certificate of occupancy at sale. What you do need is a clear picture of your septic or sewer setup, the 2 percent transfer tax and the county assessment record.

Hempfield is a large Westmoreland County township, spread over about 77 square miles, with an estimated 41,421 residents. Population is steady rather than growing, so sellers mostly compete with other established houses. About 84.7 percent of homes are owner-occupied, a typical owned home is valued at $232,100, and typical rent is $964. More than a quarter of residents are 65 or older, and that mix is why estate sales and downsizing moves are common.

However the buyer finds you, the deed ends up at the Westmoreland County Recorder of Deeds in Greensburg, where the deed is filed and the transfer tax is paid.

Location and storm history

The city of Greensburg and six boroughs sit entirely inside the township: Southwest Greensburg, South Greensburg, Youngwood, New Stanton, Arona and Adamsburg. Communities within it include Fort Allen, Grapeville, Hannastown, Carbon, Radebaugh, Maplewood Terrace, West Point and Luxor. The township is big enough that a home near Greensburg and a rural parcel miles away can have very different values.

Hempfield is the retail center for the Laurel Highlands, with U.S. Route 30 passing the Westmoreland Mall and Greengate Centre. The Hempfield Area School District serves the township.

A tornado on March 23, 2011 damaged many homes in the West Hempfield area and the Fort Allen neighborhood. A buyer may ask whether a house in those areas needed storm repairs, so have the answer ready.

Local rules when a Hempfield house sells

The township's planning and code department says a certificate of occupancy is not required to sell a home. Two other checks apply, depending on how the house drains.

  • On-lot septic. Contact the township's Sewage Enforcement Officer about any dye test the buyer or lender wants.
  • Public sewer. Call the Municipal Authority of Westmoreland County at 724-755-5800 for the sewer account and any test or final reading.
  • Permits. Sort out open permits and unpermitted work first. Zoning permits take up to 15 business days and building permits up to 30.

The code office is at 1132 Woodward Drive, Suite A, and answers at 724-834-7232. The county assessment office, at 724-830-3409, can explain whether a building permit changes the assessed value. Landlord and tenant disputes go to the Pennsylvania Attorney General's consumer hotline at 1-800-441-2555.

Township property tax is low in dollar terms. The township levies 3 mills for general purposes and 3 mills for a dedicated fire service tax. School and county taxes are separate and larger. Areas inside a street light district also pay a yearly light district assessment. The township runs a rebate program that returns part of the general township real estate tax to qualifying senior homeowners, which long-time owners of older houses may already use.

Transfer tax split

The full charge on a sale is 2 percent of the price. It is paid when the deed is recorded, and the recorder can be reached at 724-830-3518.

Your sales contract says who covers which share, and both parties answer to the recorder for the tax. State rules exempt certain family transfers and property passing by inheritance.

Have the title company show you the transfer tax line before signing. If you are selling an inherited house, ask whether the inheritance exemption covers your deed.

How do Westmoreland County assessment appeals work?

The county Tax Assessment Office sets the values that drive every property tax bill in the township. Anyone can appeal a change of assessment within 40 days of the mailing of the notice. A yearly appeal has to be on file by August 1 and only changes the next tax year's bill.

Hearings run on the second Thursday of every month, starting at 9:00 in the morning, in Suite 440 of the county building at 40 North Pennsylvania Avenue in Greensburg. Forms come from the county website or the assessment office itself.

If you plan to sell, check the assessed value before you list. Lenders look at the current tax amount. If you think the assessment is too high, file by the next August 1.

From listing to deed: what to prepare

A Hempfield sale goes more smoothly when you settle a few questions in advance. Know whether the house is on septic or public sewer, because that decides who you call for a dye test or a final reading. Find out whether any permit was left open or any work was done without one. Pull your current tax bills and any street light district assessment, since the buyer's title company will prorate them at settlement.

When an offer comes in, the title company orders the search, the contract names who pays each share of the transfer tax, and the deed goes to the Recorder of Deeds in Greensburg once you sign at closing. If a parent's estate is involved, have the paperwork showing who may sign ready before you accept an offer, because that is the item most likely to slow things down.

Keep a simple folder with the sewer account number, the code office phone number, your permit history and the county assessment notice. When a buyer or lender asks a question, you can answer it the same day instead of making calls while the closing date drifts closer.

Which Hempfield houses suit a direct cash sale?

A cash sale tends to suit worn houses, estate properties and sellers who want to pick the closing date. It is less useful for a move-in-ready home you can list quickly.

Set any cash figure against what a listing would net after commission, transfer tax, repairs and months of waiting. If you want to see a number for your Hempfield house, Cash Home Buyers CA can quote one, and you can set it beside your other choices.

A cash sale skips showings, a buyer's loan approval and most repair negotiation. You still deal with the same local items: the septic or sewer check, any open permits, the transfer tax and the recorder's filing. Ask the buyer to confirm in writing which of those they will handle, so nothing is left to the last week before closing.

A house inherited from a parent is a common fit. The heirs often live elsewhere, the property sat for a while, and nobody wants to manage repairs from a distance. Picking the closing date yourself lets the estate wrap up on its own schedule, with no lender deadline hanging over the heirs.

Frequently asked questions

Is a certificate of occupancy needed for a Hempfield home sale?

No. The township's planning and code office confirms that the sale of a home does not trigger a certificate of occupancy.

Who handles a dye test for a Hempfield home sale?

It depends on the system. For a septic system, contact the township's Sewage Enforcement Officer. For public sewer, call the Municipal Authority of Westmoreland County at 724-755-5800.

Who gets the 2 percent Hempfield transfer tax?

The state receives 1 percent, the township 0.5 percent and the Hempfield Area School District 0.5 percent. The county recorder in Greensburg collects the money when the deed goes on record.

Which school district covers Hempfield Township?

The Hempfield Area School District. It also covers Adamsburg, Armbrust, Bovard, Grapeville, Hunker, Luxor, Manor, New Stanton and Youngwood.

When must a Westmoreland County assessment appeal be filed?

August 1 for a yearly appeal, which affects the following tax year. If a change of assessment notice is mailed, the window is 40 days.

Selling a house in State College

You have three routes: a listing, a private sale, or a straight sale to a buyer who takes the place as it stands. All three end the same way, with a deed recorded in Centre County and the transfer tax paid. What changes from route to route is the prep work and the calendar.

Penn State's University Park campus sits partly inside the borough and partly in neighboring College Township, and it shapes who owns, rents and buys here more than anything else. Population is 40,844, about the same as a decade and a half ago, and the borough covers 4.56 square miles.

Who owns and who rents

Owners live in only 26.1 percent of the homes. The middle owned home is valued at $437,800, gross rent runs $1,273 a month and household income is $45,424. A household averages 2.24 people, and under 6 percent of residents are children.

With so much of the housing rented, the first thing many buyers ask is whether a house carries a rental permit or a student home license. Have those papers in hand before the first showing, and say plainly whether tenants live there now.

Transfer tax in State College Borough

The borough's transfer tax totals 3 percent of the price, against 2 percent in most Centre County municipalities. The county's rate table gives the borough a 1.5 percent local share on top of the state and school district shares.

State1.00%1.00%

No deed gets recorded until the tax is paid. Sales agreements commonly split it down the middle, yet the new owner answers for it if the amount paid is ever questioned, so settle the split before you sign.

Family transfers can be exempt, and so can a deed between ex-spouses. A deed that recites token consideration, such as $1, travels with a state Statement of Value for Department of Revenue review.

Rental permits and student home licenses

These matter in a sale because they decide what a buyer may do with the property after closing. The borough hands rental permit administration to Centre Region Code Administration, which also serves Patton, Ferguson, College, Half Moon and Harris townships and Bellefonte Borough.

  • Rental Housing Permit: required for any unit lived in by someone other than the owner or the owner's immediate family. The unit must meet the International Property Maintenance Code and the Fire Prevention Code. An imminent hazard can bring a vacate order within 10 days, and a suspended permit if the problem is not fixed within 90 days.
  • Student Home License: applies to one-family homes, one-family homes with an accessory apartment, and two-family dwellings occupied by more than one unrelated student. The borough created it with Ordinance 2029 in November 2013. An existing license can pass to a new owner with an approved transfer application and a $25 fee.
  • New student homes: a first license costs $1,000, with a $50 zoning permit for the change of use and a $25 rental permit application fee. In the R-1, R-2 and R-3 zoning districts a new student home must also meet spacing rules from existing ones, which is why a house that already holds a license is worth more to an investor.
  • Short-term rentals: the borough license costs $450 and lasts one year. It requires a rental housing permit, proof the applicant lives there at least eight months a year, off-street parking matching the bedrooms rented, and at least $100,000 of liability insurance.

Student home licenses renew every year. Write to studenthomes@statecollegepa.us to confirm a license is current before you tell a buyer it transfers.

Valley weather and what inspectors look at

The borough sits at about 1,154 feet in a mountain-ringed valley, and rain, snow and flooding are all common on the valley floor. Yearly precipitation is 41.53 inches and snowfall 43.8 inches, with snow usually falling between October and April.

Home inspectors here tend to check sump pumps, foundation moisture, gutters and furnace age. Hand over repair and roof records early, and buyers will have fewer reasons to ask for a credit.

Utilities and schools buyers ask about

New owners set up accounts quickly, so it helps to list the providers in your seller packet. West Penn Power supplies electricity, Columbia Gas of Pennsylvania supplies natural gas, the State College Borough Water Authority provides water, and the University Area Joint Authority handles sewer. Borough public works collects trash and recycling.

The State College Area School District serves the borough. Coral Street, Radio Park and Easterly Parkway elementary schools sit inside it, and Mount Nittany Middle School takes most of the borough's students apart from College Heights. Confirm your own street's assignment with the district before you name a school in your listing.

Which routes sell a State College house fastest?

The quickest routes skip showings and repair haggling. A listing reaches the most people but adds inspection requests, financing contingencies and a closing date that has to suit a lender.

An investor planning a rental may close sooner, especially when a rental permit or student home license is already in place. A direct cash purchase drops the financing step and takes the property as is, with an offer that accounts for repairs. Get price, closing date and the 3 percent tax split in writing before you commit.

What should you confirm before accepting an offer?

  • Locate your deed. If it is missing, contact the Centre County Recorder of Deeds.
  • Request a payoff figure from your lender to see what remains after the mortgage clears.
  • Settle who pays the 3 percent transfer tax before you sign.
  • Confirm whether the house has a rental housing permit, student home license or short-term rental license, and disclose it.
  • Gather receipts for roof, furnace, drainage and plumbing work.
  • Check that property tax bills are current, since unpaid balances come out of your proceeds at closing.

At the closing table the title agent totals the payoff, any tax balance and the transfer tax, and the Recorder will not accept the new deed until that tax is paid. Buyers who pay cash skip the lender's appraisal, so a clean paper trail is usually the only thing that holds up a close.

Frequently asked questions

Is State College's transfer tax really 3 percent?

Yes. Centre County's rate table puts the borough at 3.00 percent: 1.00 percent state, 1.5 percent local and 0.50 percent school district. Most other municipalities in the county total 2.00 percent. Buyers and sellers often divide it equally, but the contract decides.

Does a student home license go to the buyer?

It can. The borough lets an existing license pass to a new owner once a transfer application is approved and a $25 fee is paid. Email studenthomes@statecollegepa.us for the current application before you advertise the license as part of the sale.

Does a rented house need a rental permit to sell?

The permit is a condition of renting, so a rented house should hold a current Rental Housing Permit from Centre Region Code Administration. Check the permit status first, because a lapsed permit can worry a buyer.

Who handles trash and water in State College?

Borough public works collects trash and recycling, and the State College Borough Water Authority provides water. Sewer service comes from the University Area Joint Authority.

How can I obtain my State College deed?

Contact the Centre County Recorder of Deeds, which holds the recorded deed. The office will not accept a new deed for recording until the transfer taxes due have been paid.

Permits still apply to projects, including replacements. An old shed or fence may never have been approved, so replacing it needs a permit and a fresh look at current rules. The township and its housing

Northampton Township is a second class township of about 26 square miles in Bucks County, roughly 12 miles northeast of Philadelphia, and the Neshaminy Creek forms its entire northeastern edge. Its communities include Churchville, Holland, Ivyland and Richboro. Farmland turned into subdivisions in the second half of the twentieth century. The population was 6,006 in 1960, 35,406 in 1990 and 39,915 in 2020, so much of the housing dates from those decades.

Prices run high and turnover is slow. A typical owned home is worth $599,100, owners occupy 93.8 percent of units and median household income is $158,583. Students attend the Council Rock School District.

Route 332 crosses the township along Jacksonville Road, Almshouse Road and Newtown Richboro Road, while Route 232 runs north and south along Second Street Pike and Route 532 follows Buck Road. Tyler State Park offers 1,711 acres of trails.

Private well water

Groundwater contamination from the former Naval Air Warfare Center in Warminster has moved into Northampton Township. The Navy has identified affected private wells and committed to some remediation, but the township believes more is needed and urges owners with wells to test.

The Northampton Bucks County Municipal Authority supplies public water to thousands of residents and businesses, and a public water connection project covers 334 homes. If you are on a private well, expect questions from buyers and lenders. Practical steps include:

Assessment appeals and homestead

What you need to sell a house in Penn Hills

You need an Occupancy Permit and a passing dye test before the house changes hands. Penn Hills code enforcement requires the permit for every sale, purchase or deed transfer, whether or not anyone lives in the house. It is a municipal requirement, so it applies to a cash sale as much as to a listing.

The two steps have different owners. The occupancy application goes to the Code Enforcement Department at the Government Center, 102 Duff Road, and a plumber you hire handles the dye test. Starting both early keeps them from becoming the last item standing between you and the closing table.

The occupancy permit process

You file a three-part carbonless application, signed at the top and listing the new owner's information, and pay with it. The form posted on the municipal website is a sample and will not be accepted, so pick up the real one at the office. Payment can be cash, check or money order payable to the Municipality of Penn Hills, and cards are taken only at the office, where a service charge may apply.

If you mail the application, enclose a copy of a photo ID and name the person the inspector should meet at the property if that is not you. Inspections are scheduled Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m., and the department's own hours are 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays. The same permit is needed for every change of tenant or occupant, which matters if you are selling a rental with a tenant in place.

Call Code Enforcement at (412) 342-1192 with questions. Have the property address, the buyer's name and your preferred inspection day ready when you call, and ask how long the permit takes to issue after a passing inspection. A building permit is a separate item for new construction or home improvements, so ask before you finish any repair work you started on your own.

Penn Hills sellers pay a 3% total realty transfer tax: 1.5% to the municipality, 0.5% to the Penn Hills School District and 1% to the Commonwealth. Allegheny County collects it when the deed is recorded, on a separate check from the recording fees. The sales agreement says which side pays, so price the municipal share in early.

Penn Hills at a glance

Penn Hills is a home rule municipality in Allegheny County and one of its largest. It took home rule status in 1976. The population peaked at 62,886 in 1970 and stood at 41,059 in the 2020 census, down from 42,329 in 2010, so housing supply has outpaced demand for decades.

The municipality covers about 19 square miles, with the Allegheny River on its northern edge and Plum Creek marking the border with Plum Borough. It touches ten neighbors, among them Verona, Oakmont, Monroeville, Churchill and the Pittsburgh neighborhoods of East Hills and Lincoln-Lemington-Belmar. Neighborhood names include Lincoln Park, Milltown, Rosedale, Universal, Verona Hilltop and Frankstown Estates.

Interstate 376 crosses the south end, with Penn Hills at exit 81, and Rodi Road (PA 791) connects the interstate to Frankstown Road. PA 130 and PA 380 are the other main routes. The Penn Hills School District runs Penn Hills Elementary, Linton Middle and Penn Hills High School.

County taxes and assessments

Allegheny County uses base year values, and the current base year is 2012, so an assessment is not a present-day market price. The county portal lists parcels, and changes from appeals, permits and corrections post daily. The annual appeal window runs from July 1 to early September, so plan ahead if you think your value is wrong.

Penn Hills tax collection is split among the county, the municipality and the school district. Ask the county treasurer and the Penn Hills tax collector for a paid-to-date statement before you set a closing date. Balances still owed at sale usually come out of your proceeds, and the title company searches for them.

The county runs a Homestead exclusion under Act 50 for owner-occupied homes, with the application made through the county. A buyer who will live in the house should apply in their own name after closing.

Seller disclosure

A seller must deliver a signed property disclosure statement to the buyer before the agreement of transfer is signed. The statement must address the roof, basement, structural problems, plumbing, wiring, water and sewage, drainage and other topics listed in 68 Pa.C.S. Section 7304. Several creeks cross Penn Hills, so answer the land and drainage questions carefully.

An executor or other fiduciary who sells for an estate falls outside the chapter. Everyone else owes the buyer a truthful form, and a buyer who proves a violation can recover actual damages if the suit is filed within two years after settlement. If something on the form changes before closing, tell the buyer in writing.

Preparing for a fast sale

Tackle the municipal steps first, since they have fixed lead times. The dye test depends on your plumber's calendar, and the occupancy inspection needs a weekday slot between morning and early afternoon. With those booked, what remains is ordinary: clear title, a payoff statement and a price buyers will accept.

  • Book the dye test and, if the house has a septic system, the septic report.
  • Pick up the carbonless occupancy form at the Government Center rather than printing the sample.
  • Cut grass before inspection; the municipality treats grass over 10 inches as high.
  • Ask Code Enforcement whether any open permits or violations are on the address.

A buyer who purchases as is still needs the municipal permit for the deed to move, so ask whether the buyer or the seller handles it and put the answer in the contract.

Does Penn Hills require an inspection before I sell?

No. The form on the municipal website is only a sample and will not be accepted. Pick up the three-part carbonless form at the Code Enforcement office at 102 Duff Road, or call (412) 342-1192 about other arrangements.

Who does the dye test in Penn Hills?

A plumber of your choice does it. The plumber completes the form after the house passes, and you submit it with the $25 fee. A house on septic also needs a septic report.

When can I appeal my Allegheny County assessment?

The annual window runs from July 1 to early September. Check the county's real estate portal for the exact closing date.

How a Cheltenham sale works

A Cheltenham sale follows the normal Pennsylvania steps, with one township requirement layered in: the seller must hand the buyer zoning and use certifications issued by the township before settlement. Cheltenham is a home-rule township in the southeast corner of Montgomery County, so the Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds records the deed and the county Board of Assessment Appeals handles values.

A seller who needs to close quickly should file the township application as soon as there is a signed agreement of sale and a settlement date. The township's code says it will issue the certification statement and affidavits within 15 days of receiving the application, and no deed is registered by the township until the certifications are issued.

Cheltenham at a glance

Cheltenham is a 9.03-square-mile inner-ring suburb that borders Philadelphia on the south and east, Abington Township and Jenkintown on the north and Springfield Township on the west. It has ten districts: Glenside, Laverock, Edge Hill, Wyncote, Cedarbrook, Chelten Hills, La Mott, Elkins Park, Melrose Park and Cheltenham Village. ZIP codes are 19012, 19027, 19038 and 19095. Housing includes rowhouses, twins and split levels, and the Cheltenham Township School District runs the public schools.

For 2020 to 2024, 62.6 percent of housing units are owner occupied and the median owner-occupied value is $384,800. Median gross rent is $1,608, median household income is $109,022, and there are 14,859 households averaging 2.47 people. Population was 37,452 in 2020 and an estimated 38,498 in July 2025. Transit is a selling point, since SEPTA Regional Rail runs through the township and bus routes start at the Cheltenham-Ogontz loop. Workers average 30.6 minutes each way.

What a Cheltenham seller must deliver at settlement

Chapter 217 of the township code, titled Property, Sale of, makes it unlawful to sell without delivering four items to the buyer at or before settlement. The township issues them on forms it provides and may inspect, though it is not required to. Call the township office at 215-887-1000 on weekdays with questions.

  • A certification of the property's zoning district from the township Zoning Officer.
  • A certification that the current use does or does not comply with township ordinances.
  • An affidavit that the street address number is displayed as Chapter 114 requires.
  • For a single-family home, an affidavit that smoke detectors meet the Fire Prevention Code.

The agreement of sale must state the zoning classification and warrant that the use complies. An owner who skips the certifications and whose use violated zoning faces a summary offense with a fine up to $600 plus costs. The fire code also requires battery-powered smoke detectors in single-family dwellings when they are sold. Fees are in the township's Chapter A300.

Selling a Cheltenham rental

Cheltenham requires a rental license before an owner enters a rental agreement, and Chapter 227 requires every rental property to pass inspection against the building, property maintenance and fire codes at least once every three years. The license is a mercantile or business privilege license under the township's tax chapter.

  • Within 30 days of a transfer of ownership, the owner must give the Code Administrator written notice with the new owner's name and address.
  • The township gives at least seven days' notice before an inspection, and the owner schedules required inspections.
  • A license can be suspended or revoked for unpaid fees, uncorrected violations or refusing an inspection.
  • A summary offense under the chapter carries a fine of $50 to $1,000 per violation.

If your buyer will keep the tenants, pass along the license and inspection records. Gather the last inspection report and any correction notices before you list, because the buyer's lender and inspector will ask about the house's condition.

Permits and past work

Permits go through the township's OpenGov portal, and since March 26, 2025 the township accepts applications only there. Permits are needed for roofing, siding, decks, kitchen and bathroom renovations, fencing, sheds and HVAC. Painting, flooring and gutter replacement do not need one, and replacement windows with no change in rough opening are exempt unless the house is in a Historic District, where added review and inspection apply.

A retaining wall that disturbs the Steep Slope Conservation District, a gradient of 15 percent or more, may need zoning relief first. Each permit carries a $4.50 state UCC charge. The township code also has chapters on sump pump standards and a vacant building registry, so owners of empty houses should look at those before listing.

Getting the certifications done

  1. Sign an agreement of sale and set the settlement date.
  2. File the township's application for the Chapter 217 certifications.
  3. Wait up to 15 days for the certification statement and affidavits.
  4. Install battery-powered smoke detectors if a single-family house lacks them, and make sure the street number is displayed.
  5. Hand the buyer the four items at or before settlement.

Because the township registers no deed until the certifications are issued, apply early.

Records to gather before you list

Buyers and their lenders ask for paperwork, and Cheltenham has more of it than most townships. Pull together permits for past roofing, siding, decks or HVAC work, and any correction notices from earlier inspections. If the house has a tenant, add the rental license and the last inspection report. If a building sits in the Historic District or near the Steep Slope Conservation District, ask the township what review applies before a buyer asks you.

Having these in a folder lets you answer questions in a day instead of a week, which matters when the township has up to 15 days to issue its own certifications.

List, sell directly or take a cash offer. A cash purchase can close sooner, but the township certifications are still required before settlement, so file the application at the start. Compare offers by what you keep after the certifications, any repairs and the transfer tax, and get each offer in writing.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a township certification to sell in Cheltenham?

Yes. Chapter 217 requires a zoning district certification and a use compliance certification, plus an address affidavit and, for single-family homes, a smoke detector affidavit. Apply on the township's form, and expect the answer within 15 days.

What happens if I skip the Cheltenham certifications?

The township will not register the deed, and an owner whose use violated zoning faces a summary offense with a fine up to $600 plus costs. The agreement of sale also must include the zoning and use warranty.

How much is the transfer tax in Cheltenham?

The realty transfer tax is 2 percent. The Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds collects it at recording, with the state's 1 percent included.

Which school district serves Cheltenham?

Cheltenham Township School District serves the township, and its 2026-2027 millage is 56.68 mills, the largest piece of the bill.

Where do I apply for Cheltenham building permits?

On the township's OpenGov portal. Paper applications ended when the portal became mandatory on March 26, 2025, and each permit carries a $4.50 UCC charge.

Selling a house in Upper Merion

Upper Merion covers about 17 square miles of Montgomery County and has an estimated 36,674 residents. A single-family sale here needs no use and occupancy permit. What remains is the standard Pennsylvania sequence: disclosure form, agreement of sale, transfer tax, deed recording and tax proration.

The township sits about 16 miles from Philadelphia and takes in the villages of Gulph Mills, King of Prussia, Swedeland and Swedesburg, plus parts of Radnor and Wayne. A house in Swedesburg and a house near the King of Prussia mall draw different buyers, so the first job is matching your street to the right pool of buyers and the right sale route.

Housing and who buys

Upper Merion works as an employment center as much as a bedroom suburb, so many buyers want a short commute rather than a large yard. The Schuylkill River forms its northern and eastern edge, Valley Forge National Historical Park fills most of the western end, and the King of Prussia retail and office district sits in the middle.

Since 44.9% of occupied homes have renters, your own house may have a tenant. In that case, read the lease and its notice terms before booking showings or agreeing to a closing date.

No use and occupancy permit at sale

For a single-family dwelling, a change of ownership needs no Use and Occupancy Permit, provided the use of the dwelling does not change. Converting a house into a different use is a separate question for the township.

Permits still matter if you did work on the house. Buyers' inspectors and lenders ask about decks, finished basements, sheds, pools and replaced roofs. Pull your own records before you list:

  • Permit review takes up to 15 business days, and inspections need 24 hours' notice, so finishing open work before listing takes weeks, not days.
  • Contractors on residential jobs must be state-registered and put a Pennsylvania HIC number and an insurance certificate on the application.
  • Accessory structures have setbacks by zoning district. In R-1 and R-1A a shed or pool sits 10 feet from the side and rear lines, while R-2 and R-3 require four feet from the side and five feet from the rear.

Call the township's safety and code enforcement office if you cannot tell which zoning district your lot is in. A shed or pool that sits too close to a lot line is the sort of problem a buyer's surveyor finds, so measure before you list and fix or disclose anything that falls short.

Schools

Public school students attend the Upper Merion Area School District. Children start at one of five K-4 elementary schools: Bridgeport, Caley Road, Candlebrook, Gulph and Roberts. They move on to Upper Merion Area Middle School for grades 5 through 8 and Upper Merion Area High School for grades 9 through 12. Mother Teresa Regional Catholic School is the parochial option.

Elementary assignment depends on your street, so check with the district before naming a school in the listing.

What do I pay and file when I sell?

The state's share of realty transfer tax is 1 percent of the property's value. Add the local share and the usual total is 2 percent, with the second point going to the municipality and school district. Buyers and sellers commonly divide it. Before you sign, call the Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds and confirm the rate for your township and school district.

The seller's disclosure duty comes from 68 Pa.C.S. Section 7303. Fill out the property disclosure statement and hand the buyer a signed, dated copy before the agreement of sale is signed. The form covers the roof, basement, plumbing, wiring, storm water facilities, hazardous substances and flood risk indicators. The Schuylkill runs along two edges of Upper Merion and annual precipitation runs near 48.5 inches, so answer the water questions with care. Act 74 of 2026 amended the land item and added a flood-insurance notice to the chapter.

Behind on property taxes? Twice a year, in September and December, the county Tax Claim Bureau auctions parcels that owe taxes from two years back, and winning bidders inherit any liens. For the annual appeal deadline and forms, contact the Board of Assessment Appeals.

What happens at settlement

At the closing table the title agent totals your mortgage payoff, the transfer tax, any unpaid taxes and prorated tax for the year. You sign the deed, and the agent sends it to the Recorder of Deeds. Ask for a net sheet ahead of time so no line item surprises you.

If the house has unpermitted work, disclose what you know on the form. Applying for a permit on the open work before listing is common, because inspectors notice a deck or finished basement and lenders may ask about it.

If the house needs work before you sell

Repairs and permits go together. Decks, finished basements, sheds, pools and replaced roofs each have their own permit category, and the township can tell you which one your project falls under. Gather the permit numbers, contractor names and final inspection dates in one folder so a buyer's agent can see them at a glance. Start with the oldest items on your list, since a permit review runs up to 15 business days and then an inspector needs a day's notice.

If you would rather not manage contractors, a buyer who purchases as is will price the work into an offer and handle the permits afterward. That trade usually costs you some of the sale price, but it saves weeks and keeps your attention on the move.

Which sale route fits an Upper Merion house best?

Your time and repair budget point to the right route. A listing can tap the big pool of workers around King of Prussia, at the cost of showings, inspection requests and a financing schedule. A private sale saves an agent's fee and adds legal and marketing work. A direct sale to an as-is buyer shortens the schedule and removes repair negotiations, usually at a lower price.

  • Get proof of funds and a dated closing commitment from each buyer.
  • Request a net sheet that shows transfer tax, payoff, tax proration and any repair credits.
  • Judge each route by the money you keep, not the advertised price.

Frequently asked questions

Is a certificate needed to sell a house in Upper Merion Township?

Not for a single-family home that keeps the same use. Ask the township office first if the property is multi-unit or non-residential.

What is a typical home value in Upper Merion?

The middle owner-reported value is $455,300. Individual houses price off nearby sales, so ask an agent or appraiser for comparables on your street.

Who pays the transfer tax when an Upper Merion house sells?

Nothing in the law assigns it. Agreements commonly divide it, though the buyer answers if the amount paid is challenged. Write the split into your agreement of sale.

Can I sell an Upper Merion house with unpermitted work?

Yes, but disclose what you know. Pennsylvania's disclosure form asks about additions, remodeling and structural changes, and a seller cannot make statements the seller knows are false. Many owners apply for a permit on the open work before listing.

How quickly can a cash sale close in Upper Merion?

With no lender involved, the pace is set by the title search, the deed and the transfer tax paperwork. Get a written date from the buyer, along with a list of what must happen first.

Selling in Norristown: the code step

Norristown requires a municipal inspection and an occupancy certificate whenever a residential or commercial property changes owners, so a sale here carries a code step that many Pennsylvania towns skip. Norristown is a home rule municipality and the Montgomery County seat, packed into about 3.5 square miles along the Schuylkill River. Its 2020 population of 35,748 makes it the second most populous borough in the state.

Because the inspection must happen before settlement, sellers who start early avoid a delayed closing. The sections below lay out the sequence, the tax bill calendar and the county appeal rules.

Steps to get a property transfer approved

The process begins with zoning and ends with an Occupancy Certificate handed to the seller for use at settlement. The order is:

  • A Zoning Use Registration Permit confirms the intended use is allowed in that zoning district.
  • The seller then files a Property Transfer Permit application with the Code Department at least 30 days before the settlement date, with every field completed.
  • After fees are paid and the application is processed, an inspector contacts the owner or agent, which can take at least three business days.
  • The seller supplies a Heating Certification and a Chimney Certification from a contractor registered with Norristown.
  • If the building complies, the inspector issues an Occupancy Certificate.

The Code Enforcement Department answers questions at 610-270-0441, including whether a particular contractor is registered with the municipality.

If the inspector finds violations

Repairs must be finished before the Occupancy Certificate is issued, unless the buyer accepts responsibility in writing through a Letter of Intent. The buyer completes that form and returns it to the Code Department.

Depending on what the inspector finds, one of two temporary certificates may be issued. A Temporary Occupancy Certificate covers a violation that is not substantial and lets the purchaser live in the property while correcting it. A Temporary Access Certificate covers at least one substantial violation: nobody may occupy the building, though the owner may store belongings and enter to make repairs.

A substantial violation is one that makes a building or part of it unfit for human habitation. Examples include a significant fire or accident hazard, inadequate sanitary facilities, vermin infestation, or disrepair so deep that repair cost would exceed half the agreed purchase price. That last test is why a badly damaged house often moves to a buyer who is ready to take on the work.

Rental licensing and a sale

Norristown has more than 7,500 residential rental units, and the owner-occupied rate is 42.7 percent. Many sellers here are landlords, and many buyers plan to rent the house out.

Every rental unit needs an annual license before it can be lawfully occupied. A new landlord submits an application, the Code Enforcement Department inspects the unit under the 2012 International Property Maintenance Code with local amendments, and a license issues only after violations are fixed and the invoice is paid. Owners who stop renting can file a De-Registration Request, and any later return to renting restarts the first-time landlord process.

Zoning limits how many separate units a building may hold. In single-family zones, converting a house to two or more rentals is illegal, and a long-vacant multi-unit may lose its legal status, so confirm the approved use with the Planning and Municipal Development Department at 610-270-0450 before pricing a property as a duplex.

Real estate tax calendar

Norristown bills real estate tax once a year, and the 2026 municipal rate is 19 mills after the council raised it by 0.75 mill. The Finance Department collects municipal and county real estate taxes plus the trash fee, and it won't take partial payments on a bill.

Norristown real estate tax calendar
Payment periodWhat applies
Through April 152 percent discount on face value
By June 15Face value due

For a closing, the finance office issues tax certifications for a $35 fee and wants requests at least three weeks before settlement. Duplicate bills or receipts cost $5. The taxes phone line is 610-270-0431.

Unpaid taxes can end up with the Montgomery County Tax Claim Bureau, which holds upset sales each September and December. An upset sale buyer assumes the liens, while a judicial sale delivers parcels free and clear.

Assessment appeals

The Montgomery County Board of Assessment Appeals values every Norristown parcel for county, municipal and school taxes, and its annual appeal deadline is August 1 of the year before the year on appeal. An interim appeal must be filed within 40 days of the date on a notice of change in assessment.

Appeals must be hand-delivered or postmarked on or before the last day, and faxes are not accepted. Because postmarks can run late, use a post office counter postmark, certified mail, or delivery to the board's Norristown office on weekdays.

The assessment is presumed correct, so you carry the burden of proof with an appraisal, comparable sales or witness testimony. You or an attorney must appear at the hearing, and missing it gets the appeal dismissed as abandoned.

The town and its housing

Norristown sits on hilly ground where Stony Creek and Saw Mill Run split the town into thirds before emptying into the Schuylkill. It has four distinct areas: the West End, East End, North End and downtown. With about 50.65 inches of precipitation in a year, basement moisture and roof condition often come up during buyer inspections.

U.S. Route 202 runs through town as a one-way pair on DeKalb and Markley Streets, and the Norristown Transportation Center connects SEPTA buses, the Norristown High Speed Line, a Regional Rail line and the Schuylkill River Trail. The Norristown Area School District serves the municipality.

The 2020 to 2024 median owner-occupied home value is $213,900, and median household income is $66,701 across 12,642 households.

Transfer tax and when a cash offer helps

Pennsylvania's 1 percent state realty transfer tax is collected by the county Recorder of Deeds at recording, and local transfer tax is collected on top of it. Ask the Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds for the combined rate on a Norristown address, and plan on a Statement of Value form where the deed shows no price or claims an exemption.

A cash offer helps when the inspection cost or timeline is the obstacle. Sellers often turn to one in these cases:

  • Heating or chimney certifications and repairs would cost more than the seller can front.
  • The inspector is likely to issue a Temporary Access Certificate.
  • The house is a rental with a tenant and open violations.

Any buyer still has to work through the Letter of Intent and certificate steps, so ask who handles them before signing.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need an inspection to sell a house in Norristown?

Yes. Norristown requires a property transfer inspection before settlement, and you apply for a Property Transfer Permit at least 30 days before closing. A passing result produces an Occupancy Certificate for use at settlement.

Can a buyer take over Norristown repairs instead of the seller?

Yes, if the buyer assumes responsibility in writing by completing a Letter of Intent and returning it to the Code Department. Without that letter, repairs must be finished before the Occupancy Certificate is issued.

When are Norristown real estate taxes due?

Bills are due June 15 each year at face value. Payment through April 15 earns a 2 percent discount, and bills paid from June 16 through December 31 carry a 10 percent penalty.

How do I get a tax certification for a Norristown closing?

Submit the municipality's tax certification request form with the $35 fee at least three weeks before closing. The Finance Department taxes line, 610-270-0431, can answer questions.

When is the deadline to appeal an assessment in Norristown?

August 1 of the year before the year on appeal. Interim appeals must be filed within 40 days of the date on a notice of change in assessment.

Selling a house in Hampden Township

Hampden Township ranks among the pricier, owner-dominated parts of the Harrisburg area and is Cumberland County's most populous municipality. An estimated 35,401 people lived here in 2025, an 8.1 percent rise since April 2020. Survey years 2020 to 2024 show owners in 76.9 percent of homes, a typical owned home valued at $354,900 and rent at $1,466. The median household income is $105,434.

Sellers in Hampden often own a family home with plenty of equity, and buyers want it in good shape. A house that needs repairs, holds tenants or arrived through an estate can sit on the market, so some owners price an as-is sale before paying for fix-ups. The Cumberland Valley School District serves the township and mails its own bill, described below.

Property tax bills and due dates

Each year an owner gets three bills: one from the county that also carries the library and township charges, one from the school district, and a per capita tax on adults. Assessed values are set by the county at 100 percent of 2010 value.

Real estate bill calendar
BillIssued2 percent discountFace amount10 percent penalty starts
County, library and townshipMarch 1March 1 to April 30May 1 to June 30July 1
Cumberland Valley School DistrictJuly 1July 1 to August 31September 1 to October 31November 1

The combined county, library and township millage is 3.031 mills for 2025 (county 2.625, library 0.250, township 0.156), and the school district rate is 11.937 mills for 2024 to 2025. Apply those mills to the assessed value, not to the sale price.

  • A county bill pays for a calendar year, and a school bill pays for July through June, so the closing agent splits each at the settlement date.
  • The per capita tax is $10 at face for each resident 18 or older. It is not prorated, so someone who moves out of the township after March 1 still owes the full year.
  • Landlords must tell the tax collector about tenants over 18 under Chapter 24 of the township code.
  • The state Homestead credit on the school bill was $85.49 for 2024 for residents on file with the county assessor.

Get a balance statement for your parcel from the tax collector before you sign a sale contract. For assessed value questions, the Cumberland County Assessment Office is at (717) 240-6350.

Trash and stormwater charges

The township bills trash and stormwater, and both charges stay with the property, so clear them before closing. Weekly household pickup is $117.99 per quarter and includes one bulk item a week if you schedule it with the hauler.

The Sewer Authority set the stormwater fee by a 2015 resolution at $13.25 per equivalent residential unit each quarter. Every single-family home counts as one unit of 3,534 square feet of impervious surface. When the closing date is set, ask the township office about the sewer bill and a final reading.

Leaf collection, yard waste and bulk pickup schedules are on the township website. A clean, cleared yard helps a buyer walking the property, whether the buyer is a family or an investor.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Hampden house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Permits and certificates of occupancy

Community Development, the township department that issues permits, expects one for most work above $500. Buyers and lenders sometimes ask whether past projects were closed out. The office works weekdays until 4:30 in the afternoon, and the phone is (717) 761-0119.

  • Building permits cover residential construction above $500 in total cost. Roof re-shingling that is not structural, window replacement, siding, gutters and like-for-like kitchen or bath replacement are exceptions.
  • Most standard residential permits are processed within 15 business days.
  • Zoning permits are needed for sheds, fences, accessory buildings and added impervious coverage.
  • A certificate of occupancy proves a building passed final inspection under the Pennsylvania Uniform Construction Code. The owner, not the contractor, is responsible for making sure it was issued.

A deck, pool or addition without its final inspection can hold up a sale that depends on a lender. Cash buyers may take that risk, though it is smart to ask the department how to close the file.

Recording and transfer tax in Cumberland County

Deeds are recorded by the Cumberland County Recorder of Deeds, with records back to 1750. Visits happen on weekdays until 4 in the afternoon, by appointment only. Book one at 717-240-6370.

Pennsylvania's realty transfer tax is 1 percent, and a local share is added at the recorder's office for school districts and municipalities. Property received by heirs, with a will or without, is exempt. The Department of Revenue's Cumberland County valuation factor is 1.56 for deeds accepted in the year that began July 1, 2026. Your title company can give you the exact local percentage and who pays each part.

From accepted offer to settlement

After you accept an offer, the title company opens its search and asks for tax balances. Expect it to contact the tax collector and the township for trash and stormwater accounts, so give it the information promptly. If a mortgage is open, request a payoff from your lender.

Closing day is when you sign the deed and the settlement papers. The recorder then adds the deed to the county records. A cash buyer needs no appraisal or loan approval, so the schedule depends mostly on title work and any permit that has to be closed. Tell the buyer about the county and school bill periods early, since the settlement sheet will split each one between you at the closing date.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Hampden houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Choosing a sale route

The right route depends on how the house looks and how fast you need to close.

  • Agent listing: usually the best price for a well-kept house, with showings, an appraisal and a lender's timetable to manage.
  • By owner: no listing fee, though you do the marketing, the forms and the negotiating.
  • Cash offer: the buyer accepts the house as it stands, with no showings and no repair list, and closes on a date you pick.

If repairs were put off, an estate is open or tenants live there, measure each route by what you keep and not by the sticker price.

Before you sign a contract

Request a balance statement for each bill from the tax collector, then check the trash and stormwater accounts. Look for permits that were never finished and ask Community Development how to close them. The title company can tell you the local transfer tax share and who pays what.

With a tenant in the house, hand the buyer the lease and recall the landlord reporting rule for tenants over 18. If a relative left you the house, gather the papers that prove you can sign for the estate. Last, line up written offers and compare them on proceeds and on closing speed.

Frequently asked questions

Can a Hampden house be sold while a tax bill is unpaid?

Yes. A sale can close with an open balance. Call the township tax collector at (717) 737-4822 for your parcel's figure and give it to the title company, so it shows on the settlement statement.

Who handles a wrong Hampden assessment?

Call the Cumberland County Assessment Office at (717) 240-6350. The township tax collector only bills the assessed value the county provides, so corrections and appeals start with the county.

Does the per capita tax follow me if I sell and move mid-year?

Yes, if you lived in the township on March 1, when bills were mailed. There is no proration, so Hampden Township gets the full amount for that year and not your new municipality.

Is a certificate of occupancy needed to sell in Hampden?

It is proof that permitted work passed final inspection. If a past project needed a permit, phone Community Development at (717) 761-0119 and confirm the last inspection took place before you list.

What does the Hampden stormwater fee cost?

The Sewer Authority set it in 2015 at $13.25 per quarter for each equivalent residential unit, and a single-family home counts as one. Check today's amount with the township before closing.

Before you sell in Cranberry Township

Cranberry is a fast-growing township in southwestern Butler County, about half an hour north of downtown Pittsburgh, and its housing market looks more like a family suburb than a small town. Because it is a township with no separate city government, nearly every step of a sale runs through three offices: the township for permits and tax certifications, Butler County for assessments, deeds and delinquent taxes, and the Seneca Valley School District for school taxes. Knowing who handles what saves time at closing, and it tells you whom to call first when a buyer asks a question you cannot answer.

If you own a house here and want to sell it, you can list it, sell it yourself, or take an as-is offer from a buyer. Each path has the same tax and paperwork steps.

Cranberry housing figures

An estimated 35,244 people lived in Cranberry on July 1, 2025, up from 28,098 in 2010. Three out of four households own their home, and the median home value is above $420,000. Buyers are usually working households with mortgages, who care about school district boundaries, move-in condition and inspection results. The mean commute is 27.1 minutes.

Taxes that come due at a Cranberry sale

The township's tax page lists a real estate transfer tax of 0.5 percent that goes to Cranberry, and that figure leaves out the state and school district shares. The Commonwealth takes 1 percent on top. Ask the Butler County Recorder of Deeds for the school district portion and the total on your deed, since the recorder collects the tax when the deed is filed.

Both buyer and seller are legally responsible for the realty transfer tax, and some transfers are exempt, such as certain transfers between family members and property passed by will or intestacy. Your sales contract decides who pays.

  • County and township property tax: bills mailed March 1
  • Seneca Valley School District tax: bills mailed August 1
  • Township rate for real estate, apart from county and school: 15.75 mills
  • Earned income tax: 1 percent, split between township and school district (this one follows the owner's income, not the sale)

Your closing agent will prorate the current-year taxes between you and the buyer, so having the tax bills handy at the start speeds things up.

Tax certifications and tax sales

An elected tax collector with an office in the Municipal Center on Rochester Road collects township, county and school taxes. The same office issues the certification required when a property or mobile home is sold or refinanced, reviewing the last three years of township, county and school tax records and breaking them down for the closing. The office works with real estate agents and closing attorneys, and appointments are available.

County and township bills offer a 2 percent discount within two months of the notice date. Payments after four months carry a 10 percent penalty. Taxes still unpaid after one year go to the Butler County Tax Claim Bureau, and a sheriff's sale follows if the balance remains unpaid for an additional year.

The Tax Claim Bureau holds its upset sale on the second Monday of September for properties two years delinquent. If a sale does not happen at that stage, the parcel goes to a judicial sale, then to a repository list. A seller with unpaid taxes should settle them or ask the Bureau for a payoff figure early, because the amount can include added costs.

Butler County assessments and appeals

Butler County's Assessment Department builds the tax bills for the county, municipalities and school districts. Assessments are still based on 1969 dollars, which is why Butler County bills use mills against a base that does not track current market value.

The county assessment page has the forms an owner may need: a Board of Assessment appeal form, a commercial or industrial appeal form, a mobile home appeal form, a homestead and farmstead exclusion application, and a change of address form. Appeal hearing information and millage sheets are posted there too.

Call the Butler County Assessment office for the current filing date and to ask whether a recent sale changes how your property is reviewed. The Seneca Valley School District runs its own homestead application window, so ask the district.

Township permits and rules

Cranberry's Code Administration staff review and inspect building, zoning, sign and fire permits and enforce the Property Code. The township follows the Pennsylvania Uniform Construction Code with the 2018 International Codes, effective October 1, 2018. Inspections are booked through the township's online portal at any hour.

Look at the work done on the house before you list. Decks, sheds, pools, enclosed porches and fences all need residential permits, and a buyer's inspector will notice an unpermitted deck or a finished basement with no paperwork. The township's code of ordinances holds the fee schedule for permits, inspections and rentals.

  • Sidewalks belong to the abutting owner, who must clear debris and handle snow and ice removal
  • Home-based businesses have their own township page and rules
  • Mobile home removal permits come from the tax collector's office

Owners selling a tenant-occupied house should ask the Code Administration office what rental fees apply.

A closing checklist

  1. Gather the current tax bills for the county, township and school district.
  2. Ask the tax collector's office for the certification and the three-year breakdown.
  3. Settle or get a payoff figure for any unpaid taxes.
  4. Locate permits for decks, sheds, pools, porches and fences.
  5. Ask the Recorder of Deeds for the full transfer tax total.
  6. Have your closing agent prorate the current-year taxes.

Doing these in order keeps the closing agent from chasing paperwork in the last week, and it gives you time to fix a permit gap while the buyer is still happy to wait.

Which way to sell in Cranberry

A listing makes sense for a house in good condition that can wait for showings and a lender's appraisal. An as-is purchase suits an owner who needs a closing date: an inherited house, a relocation, a house with deferred repairs or one with unpaid taxes. In either case, compare offers by your net proceeds after transfer tax, payoffs, prorated taxes and repair credits.

Ask any buyer who is paying cash for proof of funds, the closing date, and who covers title and recording costs. Get the offer in writing before you stop marketing the house.

Frequently asked questions

Which county handles deeds and assessments for Cranberry Township?

Butler County. Its Recorder of Deeds records the deed and collects transfer tax, and its Assessment Department sets the assessment and prints the tax bills.

Who issues the tax certification when a Cranberry house sells?

The township's elected tax collector, whose office is in the Municipal Center. It reviews three years of township, county and school tax records and returns a breakdown for closing.

Which school district taxes a Cranberry house?

The Seneca Valley School District. Its tax notices are mailed August 1, with a discount through September 30 and face value through November 30, and the year ends December 31.

What happens if I owe back taxes on a Cranberry property?

Unpaid taxes go to the Butler County Tax Claim Bureau after one year. A sheriff's sale can follow, and the Bureau's upset sale covers properties two years behind. Pay or request a payoff figure before you list.

Does a deck or shed without a permit affect a sale in Cranberry?

It can. Cranberry requires residential permits for decks, sheds, pools, enclosed porches and fences, and an inspector may flag unpermitted work. Ask the township's Code Administration staff how to close it out.

Selling fast in Falls Township

An owner in Falls has three options: list with an agent, sell without one, or take cash from a buyer who accepts the house in its present state. The township asks for no home inspection, though a few resale steps must still be completed before closing.

Falls is a suburban Philadelphia township on the Delaware in Bucks County. Portions of Fairless Hills and Levittown lie inside it, and a few addresses use Morrisville or Yardley as the mailing name while sitting inside Falls. Residents numbered 34,716 in 2020, and the July 2025 estimate of 34,282 is a drop of 1.3 percent.

A typical owner's home was worth $361,900 for 2020 to 2024, and owners occupy 72.9 percent of homes. Households earn a median $93,223, and median gross rent is $1,465. Homeowners who still have a mortgage pay a median $2,154 monthly, while owners with no loan pay $808.

Resale certification

Four major components must be certified before Falls issues a certificate of occupancy for a resale: the heating system, chimney, sewer system and electrical panel. A 2021 ordinance replaced the older resale inspection with this certification, so no township home inspection is required. Open violations and unresolved permits are disclosed to buyers before purchase.

  • Who handles it: the Code Enforcement Department, which schedules use and occupancy, electrical and housing inspections and also takes permit applications.
  • Rentals: the ordinance also created a rental inspection program. Apartment complexes get a yearly look at common areas, and any unit occupied three years or more gets an interior inspection.
  • Historic area: a Historic Architectural Review Board reviews plans, so ask whether your property falls under it.
  • Flood paperwork: the township posts a flood hazard area permit application and a FEMA substantial improvement form, relevant to a house near the river or a creek.

Find out from Code Enforcement which components apply to your house. If one fails, the certificate waits until it passes, so arrange the repair or look for an as-is buyer willing to finish it.

Working through the certificate step by step

  1. Call the Code Enforcement Department and ask which of the four components your house must certify.
  2. Check for open permits on the property and close them before you list if possible.
  3. Have the heating system, chimney, sewer system and electrical panel looked at by qualified tradespeople, and keep their paperwork.
  4. Schedule the use and occupancy visit through the department once the work is done.
  5. Hand the buyer's side the certificate at closing.

In older houses, heating systems and sewer lines are where trouble usually shows up. If the repair cost looks larger than your room to negotiate, tell prospective buyers up front and see who will take the house as it stands.

Flood and water history

Water covers roughly 16 percent of the township, so expect questions about drainage and floods. Note any basement water, sump pump use and earlier claims on the disclosure form. Keep permits and invoices for any storm repairs, and ask the township whether a flood hazard permit applies to your parcel. The age of the heating system is also a fair buyer question in a township that sees real winters.

Bucks County assessments and appeals

Transfer tax and state disclosure

Pennsylvania's realty transfer tax is 1 percent, and the county Recorder of Deeds collects it with any local tax. Some family transfers and property passed by testate or intestate succession are exempt, and 15 percent of collections support the Keystone Recreation, Park and Conservation Fund. Ask the Recorder what local rate applies to your price.

Two sections of 68 Pa.C.S. matter here. Section 7312 permits a written amendment before the agreement is signed, and section 7307 makes the seller notify the buyer of changed facts before final settlement. A material defect means a problem that significantly hurts value or creates an unreasonable risk to people, and a system simply nearing the end of its life does not qualify on that ground. Municipalities cannot add disclosure demands beyond the statute, apart from ordinances that predate it.

Filling out the seller disclosure

The disclosure form covers what you know firsthand, and the law does not make you investigate. Never write something you know is untrue, and never skip a defect you are aware of. Tell the buyer in writing if conditions change before settlement. For items you cannot know, give your best available information.

Gather what backs up your answers: roof receipts, sump pump records, past insurance claims and permits. A buyer who sees records behind the form is more likely to move ahead without a price cut.

When cash makes sense

Cash suits owners who want to avoid repair bids and a buyer's financing contingency. Examples in Falls include an inherited house, a failed heating or sewer system that stalls the resale certificate, a rental unlikely to pass a township inspection, or a move on a fixed date. Compare the offer with a listing's net after repairs and transfer tax.

Getting to the closing table

The contract sets the closing date, and a cash buyer has no lender to wait on. What fixes the earliest date is the work on your side: title work, any open permits and the resale certificate steps. Start with a call to Code Enforcement, then ask the Recorder of Deeds about the local transfer tax and request tax figures from the county.

At closing you sign the deed and settlement papers, and the deed is recorded. Bring a photo ID and, if a mortgage is open, expect it to be paid from your proceeds. If the house is a rental, give the buyer the lease and tell them about the rental inspection program, since an owner who keeps a tenant in place inherits that schedule.

No. The township replaced its resale inspection with certification of the heating system, chimney, sewer system and electrical panel. Any private inspection is between buyer and seller.

What if the heating system or another component fails certification?

The certificate of occupancy waits until it is certified. Ask the Code Enforcement Department what repair or permit is needed, or sell as-is to a buyer who will finish the work.

When is the Bucks County appeal deadline?

Early August each year. Annual appeals go to the Board of Assessment Appeals, cost $75 per parcel and change the assessment from the following tax year.

Do Levittown and Fairless Hills belong to Falls Township?

Parts of both do. Pieces of Fairless Hills and Levittown lie inside the township, and the Morrisville and Yardley post office names also cover some Falls addresses.

The contract sets the date, and a cash buyer has no lender to wait on. Title work, open permits and the resale certificate steps fix the earliest possible day.

Your options for a fast sale in Lower Makefield Township

You have three ways to go: hire an agent, sell on your own, or accept a cash offer. Cash is the quickest, since settlement happens when you are ready and not when a buyer's lender signs off. The township's own sale steps are light: a moving permit, a sewer lateral inspection by the seller, and clean tax and utility balances.

Houses on this side of the Delaware are expensive, and every idle month adds up through insurance, utilities and tax bills. Owners who want out fast rarely cite price alone. Common reasons are an estate to close out, a job move, a divorce, a rental that wore the landlord down, or repairs the owner would rather not pay for.

  • Cash purchase: the house goes as it stands and the date is yours to pick.
  • Agent listing: wider exposure and often a better price, in return for showings, repair requests and a slower pace.
  • For-sale-by-owner: the commission stays with you, and so do the marketing, the contract and the haggling.

The Lower Makefield housing market

Lower Makefield lies on the Delaware in Bucks County and surrounds the borough of Yardley, which is why most addresses carry a Yardley mailing label even though they are in Lower Makefield. Children attend the Pennsbury School District, and Interstate 295 is the main highway into New Jersey.

An estimated 34,028 people live here. Owners live in 87.6 percent of occupied homes. A typical owned home is valued at $630,200 and a typical rent is $2,340. Nearly every sale is a single-family house with an owner in residence. Prices at this level make every percentage point of transfer tax and every month of carrying cost visible, so compare closing timelines as carefully as the offer price.

Winter freezes are a fact of life here, so expect a buyer's inspector to focus on roof, gutters and basement. Having recent repair records on hand helps.

Property taxes on a Lower Makefield home

Real estate tax comes from three bills: township, county and the Pennsbury School District. The 2025 combined rate is 256.403 mills, and the township levies no earned income tax.

Owners who live in the house can apply for the homestead and farmstead exclusion, which lowers the value used for school tax. Apply by March 1 for the tax year starting the next July 1. Investors should know about a 2026 Pennsylvania law: after buying a property, the owner sends contact details to the Board within 30 days, though owner-occupied homes are excused.

Costs at closing

Pennsylvania takes 1 percent of the sale value in transfer tax. Locally, the township and the school district each take a further half percent, which brings the total to 2 percent. Certain family transfers and property passed by will or intestacy are exempt. A title company can price the statement of value and the recording fees due at the Bucks County Recorder of Deeds. Mention any payoff, lien or tenant early so the figures come back right.

Run a quick net sheet first. Start with the likely list price, then subtract agent commission, the transfer tax share you would owe, repairs a buyer would demand, and the taxes and insurance you would pay while the house waits on the market. Compare that total with the cash figure in hand.

Also look at your own calendar. If you need to relocate, close an estate or end a lease by a fixed date, certainty can be worth more than the last bit of price. Cash Home Buyers CA can give you a figure to put next to your other choices, and you decide whether the numbers work.

From accepted offer to settlement

After you accept an offer, work through four items. Apply for each side's moving permit. Have a plumber scope the sewer lateral and send the findings to the township. Ask the tax office and each utility whether it has a requirement of its own. The title company then builds the settlement statement, prorates the tax bills and files the deed.

A cash sale shortens the list further. Without a lender there is no appraisal and no loan approval, which leaves the sewer lateral report and the permits as the items that set your date. Start them first. If the plumber finds a problem with the private line, the repair becomes the longest step, and you will want to know that before you promise a closing day.

No. Community development confirms a resale use and occupancy certificate is not required. It does require a moving permit for buyer and seller and a sewer lateral inspection by the seller, so call the township office to confirm.

The state takes 1 percent, and the township and school district each add one half percent. The 2 percent total is split between buyer and seller as the contract says.

The seller. The township expects the seller to inspect the private sewer line and submit the result, and its review can take time, so schedule the plumber early in your sale.

What is the deadline to challenge a Bucks County assessment?

Annual appeals close in early August, and a decision affects the following tax year. An interim appeal depends on the date shown on an assessment revision notice.

Which school district serves Lower Makefield Township?

Pennsbury School District serves the township, and its 2025-2026 millage of 204.003 is the largest part of the combined 256.403 mills on a Lower Makefield tax bill.

Selling a house in the city of Chester

Chester is a dense river city in Delaware County, and a sale there turns on three local things: an old housing stock, a city under state financial oversight, and a transfer tax higher than the usual local rate.
