Much of Chester's housing was built for a larger workforce, when the population peaked at 66,039 in 1950. The count was 32,605 in 2020, and the estimate for 2025 is 33,996. What remains is mostly rowhouses and twins on narrow lots, many a century old. Buyers and inspectors tend to look closely at foundations, old heating systems, lead paint and aging sewer laterals.

Chester is low and sits where Chester Creek and Ridley Creek reach the Delaware River, so flood exposure varies a lot by block. Damp basements, sump pumps and old drainage are routine inspection topics. Find out whether your address is in a mapped flood zone and whether the house carries flood insurance before you list, since a buyer's lender will check the same thing.

Values and rents

The city's financial recovery status

Pennsylvania designated Chester a financially distressed municipality in 1995, declared a fiscal emergency in 2020, and in 2022 the city filed for Chapter 9 bankruptcy. The recovery process is still part of local government, with a receiver and an advisory committee.

The effect on a seller lands on the tax side more than on the sale. Property tax rates and city fees can change as the recovery plan is revised, so an old tax bill is a weak guide to what the next owner will carry. Ask the City of Chester finance office for the current city millage, and ask the Delaware County treasurer for the county and school figures, when you work out your net.

None of this stops a sale. A title company wants a clean tax picture, so unpaid city bills, rubbish fees and liens should be sorted out before settlement.

Transfer tax on a Chester sale

Chester charges 1.5 percent on the city side, effective September 1, 2023, on top of the 1 percent that goes to the Commonwealth. That is 2.5 percent of the sale price in total. The Delaware County Recorder of Deeds treats Chester as one of four municipalities above the standard local rate, the others being Radnor, Upper Darby and Upper Providence.

Under state rules the grantor and the grantee share legal liability, so the agreement of sale should name who pays. Certain family transfers and inherited property are exempt. For a doubtful case, the county refers questions to the state revenue department's realty transfer tax unit.

An assessment challenge is filed at the Board in Media, on paper with an original signature. Faxed or e-mailed forms are rejected, and since postmarks can lag, hand delivery or a counter receipt at the post office is safer. If you disagree with the Board's findings, you have 30 days to go to court. The notice you were mailed gives the filing date.

Special situations

Putting the house on the market gives the widest exposure but needs showings, repairs and a lender's approval, which can stretch the timeline by months. An investor or cash purchase gives up some price for speed and certainty, and the buyer generally accepts the property with its flaws.

  • Code or permit issues: ask L&I what is open on the address

Whatever you pick, line up the offers by the check you would actually receive after transfer tax, payoffs and credits.

What to gather before closing

Collect the latest county and school tax bills, any city rubbish or rental registration notices, and written payoff figures for liens. Ask L&I whether the address has open permits. Can I sell a Chester house that has a tenant living in it?

Who do I ask about property taxes on a Chester house?

Start with the Delaware County treasurer and Board of Assessment in Media for county and school figures, and the City of Chester finance office for city charges. Both can confirm balances before closing.

Does Chester's bankruptcy stop me from selling?

No. Houses sell in Chester under the same Pennsylvania rules as elsewhere. The recovery process mainly affects city tax rates and fees, so call for current figures before you price the house.

Request the application from the Chester Upland School District between December 15 and March 1, then send it to the county Board of Assessment in Media. The county replies within 30 days.

Whichever route you pick, the township's building sewer inspection and the deed recording at the county Recorder of Deeds still have to happen before the keys change hands.

Lower Macungie sits in southern Lehigh County, about 7 miles southwest of Allentown. It has about 33,507 people, and the township grew from 16,871 residents in 1990 to 30,633 in 2010, so much of the housing is fairly recent. Nearly all of it is owner occupied, which means most sales are a family selling the home they live in. Turnover is low, so a house that needs repairs or comes with tenants stands out. The building sewer inspection

Before any sale or transfer, the township wants a building sewer inspection on file. The inspection looks at the private sewer line that runs from the house to the township's sewer lateral, a pipe the owner, not the township, is responsible for.

  • A Journeyman or Master Plumber must perform the video inspection and submit a complete Building Sewer Inspection Report, a copy of the video and proof of licensure to the township.
  • Emailed or uploaded video files are rejected. Hand in a physical copy, ideally a USB flash drive, which stays in the property file for at least five years.

  • A failed line means the owner fixes it before the sale. A passing result is valid for up to two years.

The township posts a list of plumbers whose credentials are on file. Any other plumber works too, as long as proof of licensure goes in with the report. The point of the program is to keep stormwater and groundwater out of private lines, since that extra flow adds to overflows at the Allentown wastewater plant. The ordinance also covers transfer without inspection, so call the township office at 610-966-4343 before you assume anything about timing.

Bills and taxes at a Lower Macungie closing

Four items show up on a Lower Macungie settlement: a sewer and trash certification, the sewer inspection record, and state and local transfer tax. Each runs through a different office with a different wait, so open them the day the agreement is signed.

  • Sewer and trash certification: the township's utility billing office issues it for a sale or refinance for a $50 fee, and the check has to arrive before processing starts. Sewer and trash bills go out quarterly and are due within 30 days.

Lehigh County Authority bills water on its own, which means the final water reading is a separate phone call. Some transfers owe no state transfer tax, such as certain family transfers and property passed by will or intestacy, so ask the title company whether an inherited house qualifies.

Your assessed value comes from the 2013 base year, when Lehigh County last reassessed every parcel at 100 percent of fair market value. Only new construction or demolition changes it since. To appeal, get an original signed form plus the filing fee to the Board of Assessment Appeals by August 1. A postmark or a fax will not save a late filing. If you received a Change of Assessment Notice, the date printed on it is your deadline.

A 2026 Pennsylvania law makes owners who do not live in a property send the county their contact details within 30 days of buying it. Homes the owner lives in are excused, so this lands on an investor buying your rental, not on you.

What if the house needs repairs or has tenants?

You can still sell it, and the sewer line is the first item to sort out. Order the video inspection early, because a failed line means repair work before closing and the township mails the pass or fail letter, which takes time. If a buyer will take the house as-is, ask whether that includes sewer repairs and who pays, and put the answer in the contract.

For tenants, review the lease end date and security deposit handling with your attorney, and ask the township office about any rental rules that apply to the address. Keep copies of the sewer inspection letter, the utility certification and the deed, since the buyer's title company will ask for them.

A workable order is to book the plumber first, then request the $50 sewer and trash certification, then ask the title company to total the transfer tax. A cash buyer will not wait on a lender, but the pass or fail letter and the certification still set the earliest closing date.

Yes, a building sewer video inspection by a Journeyman or Master Plumber is required before a sale or transfer. The township reviews it and mails a pass or fail letter, and a passing result stays valid for up to two years.

Who pays the transfer tax when selling in Lower Macungie?

Your sales contract settles that, though the law holds both sides liable. At recording, the county Recorder of Deeds collects 1 percent for the state plus one half of one percent for the township.

The township charges $50 for a sewer and trash certification used for a sale or refinance. Email the utility billing office and mail the check, which must arrive before processing begins.

When is the deadline to appeal an assessment in Lehigh County?

Annual appeals are due August 1. The office must have the signed original and the fee in hand by that day, and a fax or postmark does not count.

Which school district serves Lower Macungie Township?

East Penn School District serves it. High school students go to Emmaus High School, and the township has Eyer Middle School, Lower Macungie Middle School, Wescosville Elementary and Willow Lane Elementary nearby.

What is it like to sell a house in Warminster, PA?

Warminster is a Bucks County township of 10 square miles and an estimated 33,254 residents, and a sale there starts with the township's Licenses and Inspections Department, which expects a permit application for any property being sold. Applications go in online, and the department answers questions at 215-443-5423. After that, the sale follows Pennsylvania's normal disclosure, recording and tax steps.

The township has been on the map since 1711, when its borders were set, and it started as farmland under early English and Scotch-Irish settlers. Almost all of its housing came later. As recently as 1955 it had no residential subdivisions and one housing complex, and then the population jumped from 7,127 in 1950 to 34,900 in 1970. Most houses you will see on a listing sheet come from that postwar build-out.

Why did Warminster grow so fast, and what does that mean for sellers?

The Navy's presence at the Johnsville site drove the township's mid-century growth, and that shapes today's housing stock. The U.S. Navy took over an industrial site from Brewster Aeronautical Corporation in 1943, and the Naval Air Warfare Center there operated until 1996. The same site later trained astronauts for the Mercury, Gemini and Apollo programs. Today the township's larger employers include ABB, Burpee Seeds, CRC Industries, Havis and a Penn State research laboratory.

One local issue deserves a straight answer in any sale. Several of the township's groundwater wells have been contaminated with PFOS and PFOA from the former Navy site, the Navy paid for treatment systems, and the Warminster Municipal Authority now buys more water from the North Wales Water Authority. The authority supplies water and sewer to about 10,300 customers. If your house is on public water, buyers may ask about it, so keep a recent water bill and the authority's contact details ready.

  • Neighbors include Warrington, Warwick, Ivyland, Northampton, Upper Southampton, Hatboro and Horsham.
  • Villages inside the township include Davisville, Hartsville, Johnsville, Rosewood Park and Warminster Heights.
  • The township maintains 13 parks covering 420 acres, led by the 243-acre Warminster Community Park.

Start the application early. If repairs are needed, time them against your settlement date, since a closing date in the agreement of sale does not move on its own.

Which schools and transit serve Warminster?

Warminster is part of the Centennial School District. The township's public schools are Davis, McDonald and Willow Dale elementary schools, Log College Middle School and William Tennent High School. Archbishop Wood Catholic High School and Nativity of Our Lord School are the parochial options inside the township.

For commuters, SEPTA's Warminster station is the terminus of the Warminster Line into Center City Philadelphia, and City Bus Route 22 runs south from the township through Willow Grove to North Philadelphia. The DART East bus runs weekdays along PA 132. Major roads include PA 132 (Street Road), PA 263 (York Road) and PA 332 (Jacksonville Road), and the township maintains 100.83 of its 113.97 miles of public roads. PECO supplies electricity and gas, and trash service runs under a township contract.

What do I owe at closing and how do Bucks County rules apply?

Bucks County's recorder says the realty transfer tax is 2 percent, with 1 percent to the state and 1 percent to the municipality and school district, paid when the deed is recorded. It is a tax on the value conveyed, which is not always the sale price, and the sale agreement usually divides it between buyer and seller. Since January 2026 the recorder no longer takes personal checks for the tax: cash in the office, cashier's check, money order or credit card only.

Family transfers can be exempt, but you must still present the state's Statement of Value (REV-183) where the exemption is not stated in the deed. Your attorney or title agent handles that paperwork. The seller must also deliver the property disclosure statement under 68 Pa.C.S. Section 7303 before the agreement is signed, and Act 74 of 2026 adds a flood-insurance notice that sellers provide once the Insurance Department posts its flood information.

On the assessment side, the Bucks Board of Assessment Appeals set August 3, 2026 as the 2026 annual appeal deadline, which has passed, and annual appeal changes take effect the following tax year. The homestead and farmstead filing deadline is March 1 for the tax year starting July 1. Buyers must send contact information to the Board within 30 days of purchase under Act 29, so tell your buyer.

Listing suits a house in good condition on a street with recent sales, and an as-is cash sale suits a house that needs work or a seller on a short clock. Cash buyers usually offer less than a repaired, listed house would bring, in exchange for speed and fewer contingencies. Yes. The Licenses and Inspections Department says selling a property needs a permit, and applications are made online. Call 215-443-5423 before applying to confirm the permit type and fee.

Be ready to discuss it. At the Bucks County Recorder of Deeds, usually through your title company or attorney. The recorder collects the 2 percent transfer tax at recording and no longer accepts personal checks for it.

Selling a house in Radnor Township

Radnor is a Main Line township in Delaware County with high home values, a use and occupancy certificate required for every resale, and a transfer tax above the county default. Home values run above $800,000, so many buyers arrive with jumbo loans, tough appraisals and long inspection lists. About a third of households rent, which keeps investors and landlords in the buyer pool near Villanova University and Eastern University.

Wayne, St. Davids, Rosemont, Ithan, Garrett Hill and Villanova all fall in or touch the township. Strafford, Bryn Mawr and Villanova straddle township lines, so the mailing address on a listing may not match the municipality. That matters for both the transfer tax and the certificate, so check the municipality on your deed before anything is filed.

Use and occupancy certificate for a resale

Every resale needs a use and occupancy permit, and the township Engineering Department issues it. No new owner may move in until the certificate is out, so treat it as a closing item, not an afterthought.

  • The seller files the application at least 10 business days before settlement. The owner signs it, and the fee is $150.
  • Filing 10 days or less before settlement adds a $300 expedite fee.
  • The township inspects for house number display and the condition of the public sidewalk, then sends a violation notice for anything that needs repair.
  • If sidewalk blocks cannot be replaced before closing, money goes into escrow with the department, and a sidewalk permit is needed for the work.
  • Seller and buyer both sign a smoke detector and carbon monoxide certification. The township will not accept the application unless the form, the fee and the signed application arrive together.
  • The owner books an inside look at the sanitary sewer soil pipe to confirm there are no illegal connections. Sump pumps must be disconnected from the sanitary system under Chapter 235 of the township code.

Call the Engineering Department at 610-688-5600, extension 129, to book the sewer appointment. Do it the day you file, because that appointment is the step most likely to push a closing date.

Transfer tax

Delaware County's Recorder of Deeds shows the state share at 1% and the local share at 1% for most municipalities. Radnor Township is named as an exception at 1.5% local. Confirm the exact split with the Recorder before you set a net-proceeds number.

The county Recorder collects the state's 1% along with any local tax. The seller (grantor) and the buyer (grantee) are jointly liable, which is why the sales agreement should say who pays. Certain transfers between family members, and property passed by will or intestate succession, are exempt under state rules, so an inherited house moving to an heir is treated differently from a market sale.

The recording office is at the Government Center in Media. If a deed leaves the price off, the state's Statement of Value form (REV-183) carries the value to the Recorder.

Property tax due dates and appeals

Township bills go out on or before February 1, and the face amount is due May 31. Paying by March 31 earns a 2% discount, and a 10% penalty applies after May 31. The Radnor School District bills and collects its own tax separately, with school bills mailed in July.

An unpaid bill becomes a lien if it is not paid by the end of the calendar year, and the Delaware County Tax Claim Bureau adds interest and penalties. When a house sells, return the bill to the township with the new owner's name, because the Recorder can take more than 60 days to process a title transfer.

  • Assessment appeals go to the Delaware County Board of Assessment Appeals before August 1, for a value effective the following January 1.
  • An appeal does not pause the bill. You pay what is billed and receive a refund or credit if the value drops.
  • The county reassessment that ran from December 2017 to 2020 took effect in January 2021, so current values rest on that base year.
  • A tax certification from the township finance office costs $25 per parcel, and title companies typically request one.

Sewer and stormwater are billed together on a separate mailing around April 1, due May 31. The stormwater charge depends on parcel size and applies to all developed properties in the township.

Which selling route fits

Three paths cover most sellers, and each handles the township certificate differently.

  • A traditional listing suits houses in good repair. The agent coordinates the certificate, but showings, inspection requests and buyer financing set the schedule.
  • A for-sale-by-owner sale saves the commission and leaves you running the certificate, the sewer inspection and the transfer tax paperwork yourself.
  • A cash sale to a company that buys as-is removes lender timing and repairs from the buyer side. The seller still files the township application and still schedules the sewer check, so ask any buyer who does the filing and who pays any sidewalk escrow.

Compare offers on net proceeds, not headline price. Subtract the transfer tax, the $150 or $300 township fee, any sidewalk or sewer repairs and unpaid taxes before you decide.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Radnor houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

A timeline for a fast Radnor closing

Start the day you sign a sales agreement. Gather your deed, the latest township and school tax bills, and the parcel (folio) number, because the application and the tax certification both ask for them.

  1. File the occupancy application with the Engineering Department and pay the $150 fee, so you stay clear of the $300 expedite charge.
  2. Call 610-688-5600, extension 129, and book the sewer soil pipe inspection for the earliest open slot.
  3. Walk the front of the property. Check the house number and look for lifted or cracked sidewalk blocks, since those are the items the township flags.
  4. Have the buyer and yourself sign the smoke detector and carbon monoxide certification and send it in with the application.
  5. Ask the township finance office for the tax certification the title company will want.
  6. Confirm with the closing agent that the deed, the Statement of Value if needed, and the transfer tax will reach the Recorder together.

A cash buyer can skip the mortgage appraisal and underwriting wait, which are the slowest parts of a financed sale in a high-value market. The township steps above stay the same either way, so the earliest you can close is set by how fast you complete them.

Selling with taxes owed or repairs outstanding

Unpaid township or school tax does not block a sale. It gets paid from your proceeds at closing, and the title company asks for a tax certification to see what is owed. If a bill has already turned into a lien, the Delaware County Tax Claim Bureau adds interest and penalties, so the number grows the longer you wait.

Repairs work the same way. The sewer, sidewalk and house number items the township flags must be corrected or escrowed before the certificate is released. Cosmetic and structural repairs are a matter between you and the buyer, and a cash buyer who takes the house as-is simply prices them in.

Frequently asked questions

Who applies for the certificate of occupancy in Radnor?

The seller does. The application goes to the Radnor Engineering Department at least 10 business days before settlement, signed by the owner, with the $150 fee and the smoke detector and carbon monoxide form signed by seller and buyer.

What happens if my sidewalk is damaged at the time of sale?

The township sends a violation notice after its inspection. If the sidewalk blocks cannot be replaced before settlement, money is placed in escrow with the Engineering Department, and a sidewalk permit is required for the repair.

Is Radnor's transfer tax higher than the rest of Delaware County?

Yes. Most municipalities sit at the 1% default local share, while Radnor Township is at 1.5%, plus the 1% state tax. Ask the Recorder of Deeds to confirm the combined figure for your deed.

Can I sell a Radnor house that needs repairs?

Yes, but the sewer connection, sidewalk and house number items flagged by the township still have to be corrected or escrowed before the certificate is released. Cosmetic and structural repairs are between you and the buyer.

Where do I get a Radnor tax certification for closing?

From the Radnor Township finance office at 301 Iven Avenue in Wayne. The township charges $25 per certification, and you need the parcel (folio) number, the owner name and the address.

How a Mt. Lebanon sale works

A Mt. Lebanon sale follows the usual Pennsylvania routes: list with an agent, sell directly to a buyer, or take a cash offer. A few municipal and county steps sit on top. Mt. Lebanon is a home rule municipality in Allegheny County, roughly four to six miles south of downtown Pittsburgh, and its Inspection Office, tax office and county records all affect the closing date.

Line up the local pieces first, from open permits to the 2026 tax rates and the county appeal calendar.

Homes and housing numbers

Most houses here are early twentieth century commuter homes. The first streetcar line to Pittsburgh opened on July 1, 1901, the Liberty Tubes followed in 1924, and the population jumped from 2,258 in 1920 to 13,403 in 1930. About 4,400 properties sit inside a National Register historic district established in 2014, with Foursquare, Tudor, Colonial Revival, Bungalow and Dutch Colonial styles all common.

Age shows up when a buyer inspects roofs, windows, porches, masonry and basement drainage. The municipality offers an illustrated design guide for historic homes and a contractor vetting guide, which helps you decide whether to renovate before listing or sell without touching it.

Typical value of an owned home in Mount Lebanon township for 2020 to 2024 is $378,300, with 72.3 percent of units occupied by owners across 13,646 households. Median household income over the same period was $123,771.

Permits and inspections that can delay a closing

Open building permits are the most common local snag, because the Inspection Office withholds lien letters while permits are open. If you finished a deck, remodel, furnace swap or fence, confirm every final inspection is on record before you set a settlement date.

  • Work started without a permit can draw fines set by the magisterial district judge, so ask the Inspection Office how to regularize it.
  • Residential building permits generally issue within 15 business days, while zoning permits for items such as an air conditioning unit, driveway, fence or shed take up to 30 days.
  • Fences in single-family districts may reach six feet in side and rear yards, are not allowed in front yards, and cannot be solid.
  • A front porch may extend no more than 10 feet into the front yard, and new or replaced front stairs need a building permit.
  • Every private swimming pool carries an annual operation permit and a safety inspection.

On the first Wednesday of each month the office holds Inspections Consultations from 2 to 5 p.m. Appointments last 30 minutes and require preregistering at 412-343-3408.

An ordinary resale doesn't call for a Certificate of Occupancy, which covers changes of use, enlarged buildings and new construction. Call the same number to confirm anything specific to your address.

Property tax due dates and rates

A Mt. Lebanon parcel carried a combined 42.963 mills in 2026, divided among the municipality, the school district and Allegheny County. The municipal tax office, on the ground floor of the municipal building, collects real estate tax for both the municipality and the Mt. Lebanon School District.

Collection runs from June 1 to March 5 of the following year, with a discount period through July 31, a face period from August 1 through September 30, and a penalty after that. The school portion can be paid in three installments, due September 30, December 31 and February 28. Unpaid balances move to private delinquent collectors each March.

The tax office can supply a bill or receipt, and a title company will usually ask for one before closing. For address changes, the Allegheny County Treasurer handles the request.

Assessments and appeals

Allegheny County assesses every Mt. Lebanon parcel on a 2012 base year, and the last county-wide reassessment took place in 2013. The county office may change a value only for omissions, mathematical or clerical errors, physical changes such as demolitions or building permits, and the occasional interim request from a school district or municipality.

The Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review hears challenges. The annual window runs from July 1 through September 1, and the board mails residential hearing notices at least 14 days ahead. It applies a common level ratio to the market value in appeals, and that ratio is 49.3 percent for the 2027 tax year. Bring comparable sales or an appraisal.

A catastrophic loss such as a fire allows a reduction request within six months of the event. Under Act 29 of 2026, buyers of non-owner-occupied property must send contact details to the chief assessor within 30 days of purchase, and a false filing can bring a fine up to $500. If your buyer is an investor, remind them.

Transfer tax and recording

Pennsylvania's realty transfer tax starts at 1 percent of the value transferred, and Allegheny County adds municipal and school district shares so the total ranges from 2 to 5 percent across the county. The county Department of Real Estate collects both the state and local portions at recording, and the tax goes on a separate check from the recording fees.

A 2 percent total splits into 1 percent to the state, half a percent to the township and half a percent to the school district. Call the Department of Real Estate for the rate that covers Mt. Lebanon and its school district, since the local share is set by those bodies.

Some family transfers are exempt, and a Statement of Value (form REV-183) is required when the deed lists no consideration or claims an exemption. Grantor and grantee are jointly liable, so the settlement statement should show who pays.

Neighborhoods buyers look at

Buyers tend to focus on walkable blocks near Uptown, which runs along Washington Road (U.S. Route 19 Truck) and holds 182 businesses and 72 storefronts. Beverly Road forms a second commercial strip on the north side, and the Red Line light rail stops at Mt. Lebanon Station beneath Uptown, running through the Mt. Lebanon Tunnel toward the city.

Named neighborhoods include Virginia Manor, Hoodridge, Mission Hills, Seminole Hills, Beverly Heights and Washington Park. The Mt. Lebanon School District is a walking district with no school bus service, and fifteen parks cover about 200 acres.

When a cash sale fits

Cash works best when the closing date or the property's shape matters more than a retail price. A cash buyer purchases as is, so repairs and permit clean-up fall into the buyer's own plan. Typical situations include:

  • An inherited house with older systems that no one in the family wants to renovate.
  • A property with unfinished or unpermitted work that would take weeks of Inspection Office review.
  • A tenant-occupied house where the owner wants out of landlord duties.
  • A move on a short timeline, such as a job change that leaves two mortgages.

Whoever buys, ask the Inspection Office whether any permit is open before agreeing on a closing date, since municipal lien letters are part of the paperwork.

Frequently asked questions

Does Mt. Lebanon require a resale inspection before I sell?

The Certificate of Occupancy covers changes of use, enlarged buildings and new construction, not an ordinary resale. Lien letters are withheld while permits are open, so close those out first and call the Inspection Office at 412-343-3408 about your address.

When are Mt. Lebanon property taxes due?

Collection runs from June 1 to March 5 of the following year, with a discount through July 31, face value from August 1 through September 30, and a penalty afterward. School tax can be paid in three installments, due September 30, December 31 and February 28.

What starts an Allegheny County assessment appeal for a Mt. Lebanon home?

File with the county's Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review during the annual window, July 1 through September 1. Bring comparable sales or an appraisal, because the board applies the county common level ratio to market value.

What does the realty transfer tax cost on a Mt. Lebanon sale?

The state charges 1 percent and local municipal and school shares come on top, so the countywide total ranges from 2 to 5 percent. Ask the county Department of Real Estate for the figure that applies to Mt. Lebanon.

Can I sell a Mt. Lebanon house that has unpermitted work?

Yes, but work done without a permit can lead to fines set by the magisterial district judge. Ask the Inspection Office how to bring it into compliance, or discuss an as-is sale with a buyer who will take the house as it is.

Bethel Park in brief

Bethel Park is a home rule municipality in Allegheny County, about 7 miles south of Pittsburgh, with an estimated 32,074 residents on July 1, 2025. Homes are mostly owner-occupied at 76.4 percent for 2020 to 2024, the median home value is $273,400 and the median household income is $107,090. Only 92.9 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, so turnover is low and well-kept houses get noticed. Median value covers the whole borough, so use it as background, not as a price for your street.

The municipal building is at 5100 West Library Avenue. The primary ZIP code is 15102, while 15234, 15236 and 15241 serve border communities, so confirm the municipality on the parcel record before you assume which rules apply.

Housing figures

There are 14,829 households averaging 2.19 people. Median monthly owner cost with a mortgage is $1,902, and median gross rent is $1,311. Most buyers are therefore owners moving up or in from nearby, who tend to care about condition and a clean sewer lateral report.

Dye test and camera lateral inspection

A seller in Bethel Park must complete a dye test and a camera lateral inspection before any deed is transferred. The Camera Lateral Inspections Ordinance took effect on January 1, 2025, and the municipality's dye test page lays out the rules.

  • Finish the dye test and camera inspection 21 days before closing or deed transfer.
  • The municipality charges a $50 processing fee.
  • The camera lateral inspection must come from a contractor certified by the National Association of Sewer Service Companies, and the plumber must be registered through the health department.
  • A plumber holding an Allegheny County license performs the dye test, and a municipal building code official signs off if a defect is corrected.
  • A test already performed and certified within the last two years can satisfy the rule.
  • A deed cannot be transferred until needed repairs are made and pass inspection.

Paperwork has a 48-hour turnaround. Request the forms through the municipal office at 412-831-6800, extension 205. An occupancy inspection is not required for a sale. Owners who deeded a property without the test receive an official letter, and non-compliance leads to a citation.

Planning around the 21-day rule

Because the deadline sits 21 days before closing, a sale that closes in under three weeks needs the dye test and camera work done before a contract is signed. Start by requesting the forms from the municipality, hire the certified plumber, and keep the video and paperwork together for the buyer's title company.

If the camera finds a defect, price the repair in early, because the deed cannot move until the repair passes inspection. A certified test from the last two years is worth locating if you have one, since it can save you the whole step.

Checklist before you list

  1. Ask the municipal office at 412-831-6800, extension 205, for the dye test and camera forms.
  2. Hire an Allegheny County plumber and a camera contractor certified by the National Association of Sewer Service Companies.
  3. Get the paperwork back, which has a 48-hour turnaround, and fix any defect so it can pass inspection.
  4. Keep the video, the certification and the receipt for the $50 processing fee in one folder.
  5. Confirm the work is finished 21 days before the closing date.
  6. Check for open permits on past projects through Community Development.

A seller who works through this list before accepting an offer rarely has the deed held up at the end.

Mine subsidence and selling

Bethel Park sits on the Pittsburgh coal seam, and all of the borough was undermined. The Pittsburgh Terminal No. 8 Mine, also called the H Mine and the Coverdale Mine, opened around 1920 and is closed.

Raise mine subsidence early in a sale. Ask your homeowner's insurer whether the policy covers mine subsidence, and ask the buyer's title company what it will search. Buyers who know the area will ask about coverage and about any past damage you are aware of, and a straight answer up front is better than a question at the inspection stage.

Permits go to the Community Development Department on the second floor of the municipal building, or by email to the permits address on the municipality's site. Residential questions go to extension 131 at 412-831-6800. Pennsylvania adopted the 2021 I-Codes under the Uniform Construction Code effective January 1, 2026, so repairs before a sale follow the newer code. Grass over 8 inches is a code violation, so mow before photos and showings.

How Allegheny County assessments and appeals work

Allegheny County's Office of Property Assessments sets values for Bethel Park, and appeals go first to the Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review. A party who disagrees with that result can appeal to the Board of Viewers at the Court of Common Pleas.

  • Hearings take place by telephone.
  • Legal representation is optional, and an authorized representative may appear for the owner.
  • A taxing body, such as a school district or municipality, can also file an appeal on a property.
  • Special Appeals can be filed year-round in response to a written determination notice from the assessment office.

Call the Office of Property Assessments for the annual filing window, because the county sets it by ordinance. The county's real estate page also covers state and local realty transfer taxes, the municipal and school shares, and recording requirements for deeds.

Transit and getting around

Pittsburgh Regional Transit's three light rail lines run through the borough, with park-and-ride lots at South Hills Village, West Library, Lytle and Washington Junction. PA Route 88 and US Route 19 carry most commercial traffic. Interstate 79 and the Mon-Fayette Expressway stay outside the boundary, each about a 15-minute drive. Rail access is worth a line in a listing. Mean commute is 26.5 minutes, and buyers who work downtown often ask how close the nearest station is, so have the answer ready for showings and the listing description.

Ways to sell fast in Bethel Park

An owner here can list the house, sell privately or accept a cash offer. A cash buyer skips the lender's appraisal, but the sewer lateral rules still apply to the deed, so plan the dye test and camera work whichever route you pick.

Compare offers on what you keep after payoffs, repairs and any prorated taxes. Ask each buyer for proof of funds and a closing date in writing before you take the house off the market.

Do I need a dye test to sell my Bethel Park house?

Yes. Bethel Park requires a dye test and a camera lateral inspection before a deed transfers, unless one was done and certified within the last two years.

How much does the Bethel Park lateral paperwork cost?

The municipality charges a $50 processing fee. The plumber's fees are separate and depend on the contractor you hire.

Does Bethel Park require an occupancy inspection when a house is sold?

No. An occupancy inspection is not required for a sale. A $50 Certificate of Occupancy appears on the fee schedule for other situations.

Is Bethel Park built over old coal mines?

Yes. All of the borough was undermined, and part of it lies over the closed Pittsburgh Terminal No. 8 Mine.

Where do I appeal an Allegheny County assessment?

Appeals go to the Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review. Hearings are held by telephone, and later appeals go to the Board of Viewers.

Selling a house in Tredyffrin Township

Tredyffrin is the most populous township in Chester County, with 31,927 residents at the 2020 census, spread over 19.9 square miles of the Philadelphia Main Line. Its communities include Chesterbrook, Strafford, Howellville and East Howellville, plus portions of Paoli and Wayne.

Housing here ranges from colonial-era log houses and an 1818 octagonal schoolhouse to the postwar subdivisions that filled in after the population jumped from 7,836 to 16,004 between 1950 and 1960. Age and condition vary widely from street to street, so price off nearby sales instead of a township average.

Flooding and stormwater

Water can matter for a Tredyffrin sale, depending on your street. The township's 2025 annual report lists stormwater projects at Crabby Creek, Strafford Park, Bair Road, the Willis, Woodcrest and Upper Weadley Roads area, and Gregory Lane.

The township also runs flood buyouts. It received more than $697,000 to acquire the home at 595 Park Ridge Drive, demolish it and return the lot to vegetation, and more acquisitions were underway on Park Ridge Drive and Yellow Springs Road. If your home sits near Trout Creek or one of those streets, expect buyers and their insurers to ask about flood history, and gather repair records before you list.

Is an inspection or occupancy permit required to sell?

No. Tredyffrin has no resale inspection, and its Use and Occupancy permit is "not required for changes in residential ownership or tenancy." The permit applies to new residential construction. Commercial properties are different: a change of occupant, change of use or commercial alteration needs a U&O permit before occupancy.

Open permits are the practical risk. Applications go through the Clariti online portal, and final inspections must pass before a U&O is issued, so a deck or finished basement built without sign-off can surface during a buyer's inspection review. Residential plans get a maximum review of 15 business days. Email permits@tredyffrin.gov or call 610-644-1400 and press 4.

Some repairs need no building permit: painting, window replacement without structural change, replacing siding, replacing gutters, and re-roofing up to 25 percent of the roof in a 12 month span. Larger work and any change to plumbing, gas, mechanical or electrical systems does need one.

  • Removing more than five trees six inches or wider in diameter within 12 months needs a tree removal permit, unless the trees are dead or hazardous.
  • A student home is limited to three tenants and needs a special exception and registration.
  • Zoning certificates are requested by letter to the zoning officer, with the address and tax parcel.

Transfer tax and recording in Chester County

The Chester County Recorder of Deeds collects transfer tax for all 73 municipalities and the state. The usual rate is 1 percent to the state and 1 percent to the municipality, with Coatesville, Malvern and Tredyffrin as exceptions. Tredyffrin is set at 1.5 percent, so the local share here is higher than in most of the county.

Transfer tax rates and payment rules at recording in Tredyffrin

The Recorder does not take cash or credit cards for transfer tax. Tax is figured on the price or on the computed value, which the county says is usually the higher figure. Pennsylvania makes both buyer and seller liable to the state, so settle in the contract who pays. Recorded documents usually show up in the county's online records within 48 hours, and a lender has 60 days to record a satisfaction after a payoff.

How to appeal your assessment

Chester County sets assessments, and appeals go to the county Board of Assessment Appeals. An annual appeal can be filed from May 1 through August 1, or the next business day if August 1 is a weekend. The decision takes effect with the next year's tax bills. If a change notice follows a new addition or permit, an interim appeal must be filed within 40 days of the notice.

Filing costs $25 for a residential parcel, paid by check or money order to the Chester County Treasurer. Forms must be printed and delivered, with no fax or electronic copies, to the Assessment Office at 313 W. Market Street, Suite 4202, West Chester. Hearings take place in the Government Services Center on Westtown Road, and you can bring recent sales of similar homes, an appraisal and exterior photographs from the last six months. A further appeal to the Court of Common Pleas must be filed within 30 days of the Board's notice.

The county's assessment represents 100 percent of market value at the base year, so it reflects that older value, which can sit well away from what a buyer would offer.

Schools and street noise

Schools come from the Tredyffrin-Easttown School District. The township approved turning an office building at 1200 Swedesford Road in Berwyn into a new elementary school, expected to open for the 2027-28 school year. A new school near a street can change how buyers talk about that neighborhood, so check the district's attendance map before you price.

  • Note whether your street is near a turnpike, 202 or 422 interchange, since noise comes up in showings.
  • Ask the district which school your address feeds, and say so in the listing.
  • Mention commuter rail access in Paoli if you are within a short drive.

What to bring to the township and the closing

Before you accept an offer, gather the papers each office will ask for. From the Permits and Inspections office, get a list of permits on your address and confirm none are open. From your lender, get a payoff letter. From your files, pull the deed and any receipts for roof, drainage or electrical work.

At closing the title agent adds up the payoff, any tax balance and the transfer tax, then records the deed with the county. A cash buyer skips the lender's appraisal, so the schedule depends mostly on the title search and on how fast open permits get closed out.

What are your options to sell quickly?

You can list with an agent, sell it yourself, or accept a cash offer from a buyer who purchases as-is. Buyers in this township are used to renovating, so a house that needs updating still draws interest.

  • List when the house is in good shape and you can handle showings.
  • Sell for cash when there are open permits, tenants, an estate to settle or repairs you cannot fund.
  • Pull the permit history from the township before any offer, because unresolved work can slow either route.

Compare offers on net proceeds after the 2.5 percent combined transfer tax, any agent fees and repairs, and ask each buyer in writing about closing dates.

Frequently asked questions

Does Tredyffrin Township require a use and occupancy permit when I sell my house?

Not for an ordinary residential sale. The permit is not required for changes in residential ownership or tenancy, and it applies to new residential construction and to commercial occupancy changes.

What is the transfer tax rate in Tredyffrin?

The county lists 1 percent to the state and 1.5 percent to Tredyffrin, a combined 2.5 percent. Most Chester County municipalities charge 1 percent on the local side.

When can I appeal my Chester County assessment?

An annual appeal window runs from May 1 through August 1 each year. An interim appeal must be filed within 40 days of the date on an assessment change notice.

Can I sell a Tredyffrin house with open permits?

You can try, but open permits are a title and inspection problem. Ask Permits and Inspections at 610-644-1400 (press 4) which permits remain open, and finish the inspections first if you can.

Where do I record a deed after closing in Tredyffrin?

With the Chester County Recorder of Deeds. The office takes transfer tax by business check, cashier check or money order, and posts records online within about 48 hours.

Three bodies tax and record a North Huntingdon house on their own schedules, the township, the county and the school district, and the township asks for no resale inspection on an ordinary house sale. North Huntingdon is a first class township in Westmoreland County covering about 27 square miles, governed by a board of commissioners with one commissioner from each of seven wards.

The township had 31,880 residents in 2020 and an estimate of 31,697 for 2025. The Pennsylvania Turnpike (I-76) and the Lincoln Highway (U.S. Route 30) cross it, with the Youghiogheny River touching its southwestern corner.

Housing and neighborhoods

Owners live in 90.1 percent of the housing units, based on 2020 to 2024 figures, which makes this mostly a township of owned houses. The typical home is worth $232,400. Median household income is $101,200, and 94.4 percent of residents stayed at the same address from the year before, so turnover is low.

Older sections grew around settlements such as Circleville, Cavitt's Mills and Robbin's Station, and the Fullerton Inn and the McFarlane House carry federal historic register listings. Students attend the Norwin School District.

About 21.3 percent of residents are 65 or older, which makes estate sales and downsizing moves a steady source of listings.

Permits and inspections

The township's permit fee schedule has a residential occupancy permit for new construction only, at $25 and included in the building permit fee. An existing owner-occupied house changing hands doesn't go through an occupancy inspection. Commercial occupancy for a new use or tenant costs $150.

Permits still matter for projects you finish before listing:

  • Residential building permits are charged per square foot plus a state fee and review fee, and the application won't be accepted without a property survey.
  • Accessory buildings under 200 square feet skip the building permit but need a $50 zoning permit.
  • Demolition requires proof of utility shut-offs, and the township inspector checks the sewer cap before backfilling.

The Planning and Zoning Department takes questions at 724-863-3806, extension 220, and inspections need 24 hours of notice.

Property tax rates and collectors

The tax bill multiplies the Westmoreland County assessed value, divided by 1,000, by each millage rate. The levying bodies are the township, the county and the Norwin School District. The township's 2026 budget lists a general real estate rate of 10.73 mills, up from 9.23.

How to appeal your assessment

Each year you may ask the Westmoreland County Board of Assessment Appeals to review your value. Get the filing in by August 1 and any change applies to the next tax year. If a notice of change in assessment arrives, the clock is 40 days from its mailing date.

You can download the form from the county website or pick one up in Greensburg at 40 North Pennsylvania Avenue. Hearings are the second Thursday of each month at 9:00 a.m. in Suite 440.

County values feed the township and school bills alike, so a win lowers all of them at once. Planning to list with an assessment that seems high next to similar nearby houses? File before August 1.

Recording and transfer tax

Your deed gets recorded at the Westmoreland County Recorder of Deeds, and every document must carry the 10-digit parcel identifier number. Bring original signatures and a certified grantee address, plus the transfer taxes or a finished Statement of Value (REV-183), unless the deed shows a family exemption.

The state's share is 1 percent of the value transferred, and the buyer and seller answer for it jointly. The township's 2026 budget shows real estate transfer tax revenue of $650,000, so a local share applies as well. Ask the Recorder of Deeds for the combined rate on your parcel.

If a deed's transfer tax covers more than one municipality, it must state how the tax is divided.

Fire service, roads and sewer

The fire levy is shared equally among the seven volunteer fire companies inside the township, and a separate hydrant levy applies only within 600 feet of a hydrant. The fire service line appears on every tax bill.

The township maintains about 125 miles of roads, and its 2026 budget stresses roads and stormwater. Sanitary sewer service and inspections run through the North Huntingdon Township Municipal Authority, which you can contact about a lateral line before a buyer's inspector raises it.

With seven wards and three tax bills, paperwork here can scatter. Make a folder for the township bill from the Center Highway tax office, the Norwin School District bill, the county assessment notice and any receipt from Keystone Collections Group. If a delinquent balance went to the collector, call 724-978-0300 for the payoff before a buyer's title search finds it.

Then walk the property with the earlier list in hand. A new deck, a finished basement or a replaced shed may have needed a permit, and a buyer's agent will ask. Tell the Planning and Zoning Department what you did and get the permit closed if it is still open. Having these answers ready keeps a signed contract from stalling.

When a cash sale fits

Owners who value a firm closing date, or who don't want to pay for updates ahead of a buyer's inspection, often choose cash. The buyer takes the house as is, which suits these common cases:

  • A long-held house that needs a new roof, furnace or sewer line.
  • An inherited property that heirs live far from.
  • A home with delinquent township, county or school taxes that moved to a collector.
  • A landlord who wants out of a rental on a short schedule.

The order of work looks much the same on either route. Check with Planning and Zoning on any permit you pulled, collect the current township, county and school bills, and ask your lender for a payoff. The deed then goes to the Recorder of Deeds with the parcel number, original signatures and the transfer tax paid. The township's general real estate rate is 9.23 mills for 2025 and 10.73 mills in the 2026 budget, plus 1.32 mills for fire service. Westmoreland County and the Norwin School District tax the parcel separately, so check your bill for the full total.

Who collects North Huntingdon taxes?

Keystone Collections Group collects the township's occupation, local services and delinquent real estate taxes, and its phone number is 724-978-0300. Norwin School District bills its school taxes separately.

Annual appeals are due on or before August 1 and take effect for the next tax year. A notice of change in assessment gives you 40 days from the mailing date to appeal.

How quickly can a York Township, PA house sell?

Quickly, if the price matches the condition and the paperwork is clean. York Township is a large suburb of the City of York with a steady stream of buyers, and the route you choose (agent listing, owner sale or direct cash purchase) decides how much time you give up and how much price you keep.

Dallastown, Red Lion and Yoe grew out of the township's old southeastern corner, and what remains is the most populous suburb of York. The Census Bureau puts the township at 31,479 residents in mid-2025, a 5.8% rise from a 2020 starting count of 29,748. Growth keeps buyers active, yet a house with liens, tenants or deferred repairs usually waits longer on the open market than a tidy one.

What kind of place is York Township for a seller?

Mostly suburban, with older postwar tracts next to newer streets. Wikipedia dates settlement to 1748 and incorporation to 1753, and says the land stayed largely rural until after World War II. Head counts show the shift: 4,502 residents in 1950, 8,506 in 1960, 12,702 in 1970 and 29,740 in 2020.

About 25 square miles in size, the township contains Queens Gate, Spry and Tyler Run, three census-designated places, and answers to a Board of Supervisors. Many residents drive to work, with an average trip of 24.9 minutes.

Survey figures for 2020 to 2024 sketch the likely buyer pool and the likely sellers:

  • 12,939 households of about 2.3 people each.
  • Seven in ten homes are lived in by their owners, so roughly three in ten are rentals.
  • Household income in the middle of the range is $80,190, and 38.7% of adults 25 and over hold a four year degree.
  • Nearly a quarter of residents (22.5%) are 65 or older, which feeds downsizing and estate sales.

What are houses worth in York Township?

The Census Bureau's middle value for an owner occupied home is $260,800. Owners in the middle pay $1,914 a month in housing costs with a mortgage and $768 with none, while renters in the middle pay $1,389. A township wide figure hides a lot, so a dated ranch and a fully updated home in a newer plan will price far apart.

Which permits and inspections can affect a York Township sale?

The township's Building and Zoning Department issues permits, enforces codes and handles property maintenance. It applies the statewide Uniform Construction Code, adopted locally through Ordinance 2004-7 on May 11, 2004. A finished basement, deck or shed built without a permit may come up when a buyer's inspector or lender looks the house over, so check the file before you list.

  • Plan review is allowed up to 15 business days for a residential building permit and 30 for a commercial one.
  • A zoning permit is due in 10 days, unless a special exception or variance must go before the Zoning Hearing Board.
  • Building inspections are booked on weekdays between 7:30 a.m. and 2:15 p.m. with a day's notice, by calling (717) 428-5641.
  • Plumbing jobs go to a plumber licensed by York Township under Resolution 93-2; swapping a fixture or a water heater on the same fuel needs no permit.
  • Anyone running a business from home registers each year and pays $25.

Zoning and code staff answer questions on weekdays until 4:00 p.m. at (717) 741-3861, and the township asks you to call for an appointment first. The department also lists a LERTA tax assistance program for certain deteriorated areas, worth a question if your parcel might fall inside one.

How does recording work after a York Township closing?

The York County Recorder of Deeds records the deed, since the township does not. County fee notes set the base charge for a deed at $86.25, which covers four pages and four names. Pages past the fourth cost $2 each, extra names cost $0.50 each, and each parcel identification number on the paper adds $20.

Filing a PA Realty Transfer Tax Statement of Value costs $2. Business checks, personal checks and cash are accepted, and a bounced check brings a $50 charge. The county also posts a Common Level Ratio for each stretch from July 1 to June 30; the 2025 to 2026 figure was 1.98.

Pennsylvania taxes the transfer at 1 percent of value, and the Department of Revenue notes the buyer and the seller answer for it together. Municipal and school shares can sit on top, so ask your title company or the county recorder what the total comes to on your deed. Some gifts to family and property passing by will or intestacy are exempt.

Which selling route suits a York Township house?

Three routes cover most cases.

  • Agent listing. Best exposure for a house in good order. You pay a commission, host showings and wait on the buyer's loan, appraisal and inspection.
  • Owner sale. You keep the commission and take on pricing, marketing, contracts and negotiation, and the transfer tax and recording costs still apply.
  • Cash offer. A direct buyer buys the property in its present state, so cleanouts, repairs and tenants stop being obstacles. The price usually runs below a fully prepared retail sale, so compare it against your net after commission and fix-up.

The cash route tends to suit inherited homes, tenants who will not leave, long deferred repairs or a hard deadline such as a job move. To see the gap, request a written offer for your York Township address and set it next to a listing estimate.

What paperwork should a York Township seller gather first?

Begin with the deed and the newest tax bill, then pull permit records for any work done on the house. Request a payoff statement for each mortgage or lien, since those get paid from your proceeds at closing. If the house came from a relative, the estate papers need to show who may sign.

Then walk the property the way an inspector would: roof, furnace, electrical panel, sump area and outbuildings, noting anything built without a permit. Decide whether to repair, offer a credit or sell as is. Once you know the repair bill, choosing between a listing and a direct offer comes down to arithmetic.

Frequently asked questions

What is the typical timeline to sell in York Township?

Listed houses commonly take weeks to a few months depending on price, condition and the buyer's loan. A cash sale can close sooner because no lender or appraisal is involved, and the seller often sets the closing date.

Is a permit required before selling a York Township house?

No permit is needed just to sell. Earlier unpermitted work is the concern, because a buyer's inspection can raise it. Call the Building and Zoning Department at (717) 741-3861 to ask what the township file shows.

Which office records the deed for a York Township sale?

The York County Recorder of Deeds. Its base fee for a deed is $86.25 for four pages and four names, plus charges for added pages, names and parcel numbers.

Who owes Pennsylvania's realty transfer tax?

Buyer and seller are both liable, per the Department of Revenue. The state takes 1 percent of the value, and local shares can be added; your sales agreement sets who pays what.

Can a house that needs repairs still be sold here?

Yes. A direct buyer takes it in its current condition, while a financed buyer tends to ask for repairs or a lower price after inspection. A repair estimate up front lets you compare what each path would net.

A 93.3% same-house rate means most owners stay put, so houses that do come up often belong to long-term owners, estates or retirees. If you have owned the house for decades, get a repair estimate before you pick a price.

Code Enforcement and what the township requires

Phone the township Code Enforcement office at 610-534-4803 well ahead of settlement. Sellers are expected to contact it for the details that apply to their address.

Owners of rental units must hold an annual certificate of use for each dwelling unit, whether occupied or empty. If you are selling a duplex or a house that was rented, confirm that the certificate is current so it does not become a closing problem.

  • Ask what inspections or forms apply to a sale at your address.
  • Ask whether any open violations, stormwater issues or unpermitted work are on file.
  • Ask for the current fee list, since permit and certificate charges are set locally.
  • Keep sidewalks and shared driveways clear of snow and ice within 24 hours after snow stops. The township enforces that rule, and buyers walking a property in winter will notice.

The township also keeps a code book, a zoning map and a stormwater management ordinance, which matter if a buyer plans an addition or paving.

Transfer tax on a Ridley sale

Expect the county default here: 1% goes to the state and 1% to the township. Ridley is not on the Recorder of Deeds list of places charging a higher local rate. Ring the Recorder to confirm the combined 2% before you lock in your closing figures.

State rules make buyer and seller jointly liable. Some transfers are exempt, among them certain family transfers and property passing through an estate. Even so, put who pays in the contract.

  • The Recorder of Deeds is in Room 108 of the Government Center at 201 West Front Street in Media, phone 610-891-4152.
  • Recording hours are 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., a full hour before the 4:30 p.m. office close.
  • Ask your closing agent how the recording fee and the two taxes are paid, because the office takes them separately.
  • A deed that leaves off the full price needs the Statement of Value (REV-183) attached.

Deeds for many municipalities are filed in the same office, so make sure yours names Ridley Township. A mistake there changes the local tax line.

Property taxes, assessments and stormwater

Three bills reach a Ridley homeowner: Delaware County, Ridley Township and the Ridley School District. Call the Delaware County Assessment Office for the current appeal deadline and form, and ask the township treasurer for the tax certification before closing.

Delaware County's countywide reassessment took effect in January 2021, so values across the county were reset to the same base year. If you think your assessed value is too high you can appeal, though the bill stays due while the appeal is pending.

Stormwater is its own cost. The township's stormwater management ordinance was last updated in September 2022, and a stormwater fee schedule sits on its code page. Ask how the fee is billed on your parcel and whether any credit applies.

Schools and access

Students living in the township generally attend the Ridley School District, and Our Lady of Angels Regional School is the nearby Catholic option. Families often filter searches by district, so put the school assignment near the top of a listing. Parts of Morton and Secane lie inside the township, so check the school district on your tax bill.

Highway access helps resale. Interstate 95 crosses the southern part of the township, U.S. 13 follows Chester Pike, and SEPTA bus routes 37, 113 and 114 serve the area.

Which way to sell

List the house if it is updated and you can price it against recent sales nearby. Lean toward cash if the house is dated, an estate is involved, or you must move by a set date.

  • For an estate sale, confirm who has legal authority to sign the deed before listing.
  • For a tenant-occupied house, confirm the annual certificate of use and the lease terms.
  • For a quick sale, ask the buyer to put the closing date and who pays transfer tax in writing.

Whatever route you pick, gather the tax bills, the deed and any township notices before you call anyone. With 73.7% of Ridley homes owner-occupied and few households moving in a given year, a clean file and a firm closing date set one offer apart from another.

Steps to close in Ridley

  1. Call Code Enforcement at 610-534-4803 and ask what your address needs before settlement.
  2. Confirm the rental certificate of use is current if anyone has lived in the house as a tenant.
  3. Clear snow and ice from sidewalks and shared driveways, and settle any open violation or unpermitted work item the township has on file.
  4. Request the tax certification from the township treasurer, and ask the county about the current appeal deadline if you plan to contest the assessment.
  5. Have the closing agent record the deed at the Recorder of Deeds in Media, with the recording fee, the state tax and the local tax paid separately.

A cash buyer shortens the financing portion of this list, but the township and recording steps stay. Plan them around the office hours above, since recording ends at 3:30 p.m. and a late-day closing can push the filing to the next business day. Ask your closing agent which day the deed will actually reach the office.

Frequently asked questions

Does Ridley Township require an inspection before I sell?

Call the Code Enforcement office at 610-534-4803 to find out. Sellers are told to contact that office for the necessary information before settlement, so the answer for your address comes from them.

What is the transfer tax rate in Ridley Township?

The county default of 1% state and 1% local applies, and Ridley is not among Delaware County's higher-rate exceptions. Confirm the figure with the Recorder of Deeds before you finalize your closing numbers.

Can I sell a Ridley rental property with tenants?

Yes. The township requires an annual certificate of use for each rental dwelling unit, occupied or not, so keep that current. Review the lease for how the buyer takes over the tenancy.

Which school district serves Ridley Township?

Students living in the township generally attend the Ridley School District. Parts of Morton and Secane lie inside the township, so check the school district on your tax bill.

Where is the Delaware County Recorder of Deeds?

In Room 108 of the Government Center, 201 West Front Street, Media. Recording hours run 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., and the office phone is 610-891-4152.

Is a quick sale realistic for an Easton house?

Yes. An Easton owner has three paths: hire an agent, handle the sale personally, or take an offer from a cash buyer who purchases as-is. Pick based on repairs needed, who occupies the house and your deadline. Deferred repairs, a tenant lease or a clouded inheritance are the common reasons an owner here looks at cash.

Easton is the seat of Northampton County, at the eastern end of the Lehigh Valley where the Lehigh River meets the Delaware. Phillipsburg, New Jersey, sits across the river, so some buyers commute over the bridges. The population was 28,127 in 2020 and 30,402 in July 2025. Owners live in 44.5% of the city's homes, so a good share of the houses you compete with are rentals.

Housing costs and income

The typical owner's home is worth $196,300 for 2020 to 2024, against a typical household income of $69,348. Citywide medians blur big differences between a renovated Downtown block and an unrenovated College Hill one, so price your house against recent sales close to it.

Easton is divided into four districts: Downtown, College Hill, South Side and West Ward. Lots are small and houses sit close together. Older ones often need a look at the roof, gutters and plumbing after a hard winter.

City offices that touch an Easton sale

Start with Code Enforcement, then the Historic District Commission, then the rental licensing desk if anyone rents the house. Code Enforcement administers the city Property Maintenance Code and the Pennsylvania Uniform Construction Code. Ask it whether any permits on your address remain open.

  • Permits: building, enlarging, altering, repairing, moving or demolishing a structure, changing its use, or installing electrical, gas, mechanical or plumbing systems all need one.
  • Historic review: facade and signage work may also need a certificate of appropriateness from the Historic District Commission.
  • Occupancy cap: a single housekeeping unit may hold no more than three unrelated people, and an Occupancy Limitations Certificate states the limit for each dwelling unit.
  • Rental paperwork: an owner who rents files each tenant's name and address with the Rental Licensing Officer, and a moving permit comes from the Finance Department.
  • Fire check: the fire inspector will do a free fire safety inspection if you doubt a building has the required smoke detectors.

For a rented house, put the lease, rental license papers and tenant form in one folder. The buyer's attorney will want those papers, and having them ready saves days.

Taxes and recording steps

You will see separate tax bills from the city, the county and the school district. Easton levies 24.95 mills on the value the Northampton County Assessment Office sets. Residents also pay a city earned income tax of 1.45% plus 0.5% to Easton Area School District, for 1.95% in all.

The county mailed 2026 bills in mid-January. The discount ended March 31, and the face amount was due June 1. Taxes still owed when business closes on January 31 of the following year go to the Tax Claim Bureau. Clear any balance from the sale proceeds.

State realty transfer tax runs 1% of value. Pennsylvania law makes the person conveying and the person receiving jointly responsible for it. The Recorder of Deeds, at (610) 829-6210, collects it with any local tax at recording, and the city's tax list includes a real estate transfer tax. Ask for the combined rate at your price before you sign a contract.

Think the assessed value is high? The Assessment Division, second floor of the courthouse at 669 Washington Street, can give you the present appeal deadline. School homestead exclusions come from Act 72 of 2004, so an owner-occupant should ask the school district how the exclusion is handled when the deed changes.

What an Easton seller must tell the buyer

A seller of one to four dwelling units in Pennsylvania must give the buyer a written property statement under 68 Pa.C.S. section 7303. It must be filled in, signed and dated, and it is due ahead of the sales agreement. The state form runs through 16 topics, among them the roof, the basement, hazardous substances and title defects.

A seller who willfully or negligently falls short owes the buyer's actual damages, and a suit has to begin within two years after final settlement (section 7311). Executors and other fiduciaries selling for an estate fall outside the chapter (section 7302). Selling for cash does not alter these duties, so fill the form out honestly.

How a cash sale runs from first call to closing

You contact the buyer with the address and the facts that affect value: condition, tenants, open permits or code notices, and who holds title. The buyer weighs those facts and offers a price for the house in its present state. If you accept, a title search begins, and any lien, unpaid tax or estate question surfaces at that stage.

Before closing, gather the deed, the latest city, county and school bills, any lease and rental license records, and payoff letters for loans. An heir or executor should also bring the estate attorney's paperwork. Closing day means signing the deed and settlement statement. Whatever you owe in taxes or on liens is paid first from the price, then the deed is filed downtown in the Recorder of Deeds office. You hand over the keys when the funds clear, and you choose the date within what title work allows.

When cash is the better route

Cash fits best when condition, occupancy or timing would stall a listing. Typical Easton situations:

  • A house left by a relative that no heir wants to keep.
  • A rental where the unit or the license paperwork needs attention.
  • Open permits or code notices that scare off buyers who depend on a mortgage.
  • Roof, plumbing or heating damage after a hard winter.
  • A job transfer, divorce or court date that fixes your move.

A cash sale skips loan underwriting, a lender's appraisal and the repair haggling that often follows an inspection. Your closing date is limited mainly by title work. Weigh any cash figure against the likely net from a listing once repairs, concessions and transfer tax are subtracted. To get a figure for an Easton address, call or text with the details, including tenants and any open code items.

Frequently asked questions

What controls the speed of a cash closing in Easton?

Title work and the date you choose control it, since there is no loan to underwrite. Once title is clear, the deed is filed and your payoffs are taken out of the price.

Who owes the Pennsylvania transfer tax in Easton?

The 1% state tax is the joint responsibility of whoever gives the deed and whoever receives it. Your sales agreement decides how the cost is divided, and the Recorder of Deeds collects any local share with it.

Is a tenant a problem when selling in Easton?

No, but paperwork matters. Owners who rent keep tenant names and addresses on file with the Rental Licensing Officer, so give the buyer the lease and those records.

Where is a deed recorded for an Easton property?

The Northampton County Recorder of Deeds files deeds and mortgages and takes the fees and transfer taxes at the same time. The office number is (610) 829-6210.

Can I sell an inherited Easton house?

Yes. Realty transfer tax does not apply to a transfer by will or intestate succession, and an executor selling for the estate need not give the disclosure statement. Settle title questions with the estate's attorney before setting a closing date.

Hazleton housing at a glance

Hazleton is a compact Luzerne County city where homes are affordable and about half are rented. It has an estimated 30,286 residents, up from 25,340 in the 2010 count. Around 51.1 percent of homes are owner-occupied, the typical owned home is valued at $151,600, and rent is $1,089. Households earn a median $46,177.

The city posts major notices in both English and Spanish. If your buyer or tenant speaks mainly Spanish, plan on bilingual paperwork and a translator at the closing table.

Sellers here include longtime owners of older rowhouses, landlords with several units, and heirs to a house they do not plan to keep. The housing stock is narrow, older homes on steep, close lots, and many have stayed in one family for generations. That is why a good share of Hazleton sales involve an estate, several heirs or deferred maintenance.

Weather and what inspectors look at

Hazleton sits on a high plateau, and the weather shows up in building codes. The city's codes list a frost depth of 42 inches, a ground snow load of 40 pounds per square foot and a design wind load of 115 miles per hour. Buyers and inspectors look closely at roofs, chimneys, gutters, foundations and basement moisture, so a recent repair record helps your price.

If you have had work done in the last few years, pull the receipts and any permits now. A roof or foundation repair with paperwork behind it answers the first question most buyers ask.

City rules for rentals, permits and inspections

Several city rules can affect how a Hazleton sale closes. City Hall at 570-459-4960 can point you to the Code Enforcement Office. A residential rental unit must be registered with that office within 30 days after a new owner takes title, with one application and one license per property.

  • An owner who lives more than 10 air miles outside the city must appoint an agent who lives within 10 air miles.
  • Building permits are required for interior renovation, new siding, a new roof, sidewalks, sheds, fences, paving and concrete work.
  • Residential permit applications can take up to 15 days, and every outstanding fee and fine, including property taxes, garbage, water and sewer, must be paid before a permit is issued.

Land Bank, code violations and the new charter

If the house is vacant, blighted or tax-delinquent, the City of Hazleton Land Bank may take an interest in it. Ask City Hall whether any code or fee balance is attached to your property before you sign a sale contract.

Hazleton voters approved a Home Rule Charter. Call the Code Enforcement Office and ask whether it changes any permit or inspection step that applies to your sale.

Recording and transfer tax in Luzerne County

Your Hazleton deed is filed with the Luzerne County Recorder of Deeds. Pennsylvania taxes the transfer at 1 percent of the property's value, and a local share is collected alongside it. Seller and buyer are jointly liable, so the closing statement should show who covers what.

Inheritance transfers are exempt, which helps an heir putting a house in their own name. For deeds accepted during the year that began July 1, 2026, the state's Luzerne County valuation factor is 1.14. The Recorder's office or your title company can give you the local rate and the recording fees.

Getting an inherited or tenant-occupied house ready to sell

Many Hazleton houses reach the market after a death or a long stretch with tenants. Start with the paper trail. Confirm who has authority to sign, find out whether any code or fee balance sits against the property, and ask the city whether a rental registration is current. If the house is vacant, check on the Land Bank question first, since a blighted or delinquent property gets different attention from the city.

Next, line up the inspection. Occupancy inspection fees climb quickly when notice is short, so ask for the date early. Fifteen days of notice costs the least, and a request inside 72 hours costs the most. If a tenant is in place, tell them about the inspection and agree on access in writing.

Last, settle the bills. Property taxes, garbage, water and sewer all have to be paid before the city issues a permit, and a buyer's title company will find any balance at closing anyway. Clearing them first keeps the sale on schedule.
