A cash buyer does not need a lender's appraisal or a financing contingency, so the usual delays from a mortgage underwriter drop out. You also skip showings, open houses and rounds of repair requests after an inspection. The house sells as it is, which matters when it has old wiring, a damaged roof or tenants who have left belongings behind.

Some steps remain either way. The deed still goes to the Luzerne County Recorder of Deeds, the transfer tax still applies, and the city's rental registration and occupancy rules still follow the property. Ask the buyer in writing who handles each of those, and keep copies of every city notice you receive until settlement is done.

If the buyer will rent the house out, they will need to register it with Code Enforcement after taking title, and an out-of-area owner must name a local agent. Mentioning that up front saves a scramble in the weeks after closing.

Which sale path fits a Hazleton house?

Hazleton owners usually pick one of three paths.

  • Use an agent for a sound house and a seller who can wait out financing and inspections.
  • Sell yourself to keep the commission, taking on pricing, showings and contracts.
  • Take a cash offer for an inherited, vacant, damaged or rented house, bought as-is on a closing date you pick.

Total the repairs, taxes owed, rental registration items and holding costs before you decide. With a cash sale, those repairs and the occupancy inspection run are part of what the buyer takes on, which is why it fits houses a lender would not finance.

Must I register a Hazleton rental after buying it?

Yes. The Code Enforcement Office wants rental units registered within 30 days of a change in ownership. An owner living beyond a 10-mile air radius of the city must name an agent who lives inside it.

Can I get a Hazleton building permit with city bills unpaid?

No. The city requires every outstanding fee and fine, including property taxes, garbage, water and sewer, to be paid before it issues a permit.

What does a Hazleton occupancy inspection cost?

The fee is $75 per dwelling unit with 15 days of notice, $150 with less and $300 inside 72 hours. Extra certificate copies cost $5, and a no-show adds $50.

Does an inherited Hazleton house trigger transfer tax?

Not on the inheritance itself, which state rules exempt whether or not there is a will. The heirs' later sale to a buyer is a separate transfer with the 1 percent state tax plus the local share.

Which district covers Hazleton schools?

The Hazleton Area School District does. Three of its schools sit inside city limits, and Hazleton Area High School is in Hazle Township.

Selling a house in Upper Macungie Township

Upper Macungie is a Lehigh County township about 11.5 miles southwest of Allentown, 60.8 miles northwest of Philadelphia and 99.2 miles west of New York City. Its forms cover basements, decks, kitchens, bathrooms, roof re-shingling, water heaters, HVAC replacement, pools, oil tank removal and sheds, along with a Business Use and Occupancy application. Call the department and ask what, if anything, your address needs at transfer.

Pennsylvania enforces the 2021 ICC code series, so work started now must meet it. If you have an unfinished project from an earlier contract, ask the township which code applies to it.

  • Zoning permits are issued when a use or structure conforms to the zoning ordinance.

Once you sign an agreement of sale, a title company searches the record and a closing date is set. At settlement the closing agent pays off your mortgage and any tax balance from your proceeds, collects the transfer tax, and files the deed at the Recorder of Deeds in Allentown.

Before that day, collect your deed copy, a payoff letter from your lender and recent township and school tax bills. A cash buyer skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting, so the schedule then depends on the title search and on how quickly any open permits are closed.

How can I sell quickly?

Most owners weigh a traditional listing against a direct sale to a buyer who pays cash and takes the house in its current state. With so much newer housing around you, buyers compare condition closely, and a dated or worn property may fit a cash buyer better.

  • A listing suits a recently updated house and an owner who is fine with weeks of showings and lender timelines.
  • A direct sale suits an inherited house, a tenant-occupied one, or a seller with a fixed moving date.
  • Collect permit records for any finished basement, deck or kitchen project, because buyers and title agents ask for them.

Get each offer in writing and compare what you would actually net after transfer tax, fees and repairs.

Is a resale inspection part of closing on an Upper Macungie house?

No residential resale inspection applies. Call the Permit Department to learn whether your address needs anything, and close out any open permits before listing.

Which school district serves Upper Macungie Township?

Parkland School District. Students in grades 9 through 12 attend Parkland High School, and most middle schoolers attend Springhouse Middle School. Confirm your attendance zone with the district.

What is the cutoff for contesting an Upper Macungie assessment?

August 1 each year for annual appeals. The Board needs the original signed form and fee in its hands by then, and it gives no credit for a fax or a postmark.

How much transfer tax applies when an Upper Macungie house sells?

The state takes 1 percent, and the county adds a local portion when the deed is recorded. Call the Recorder of Deeds at 610-782-3162 to confirm the local figure for your property.

What if my Upper Macungie land is enrolled in Clean and Green?

Talk to the county Assessment Office before signing a contract. The program taxes qualifying land on its use value and generally starts at ten acres, and the county posts a conveyance form for land that changes hands.

What should I know about selling a house in Whitehall Township?

Whitehall is a home rule township in Lehigh County, so the rules that matter most to a seller come from the township building on MacArthur Road. The big one is a mandatory resale inspection, and it shapes how fast a sale can close.

The township covers about 12.6 square miles on the north side of Allentown, with the Lehigh River marking its eastern edge. The Census Bureau estimates 29,405 residents for July 2025, a gain of 0.8 percent over the 2020 base. Owners live in about 62 percent of homes, and the 2020 to 2024 midpoint for home value is $262,100. Households count 11,664, with a median household income of $75,658.

Local history explains the housing stock. Farming and then the Lehigh Canal, iron furnaces and the "Cement Belt" built villages such as Hokendauqua, Cementon, Fullerton and Egypt, and after World War II the township became an Allentown suburb. The villages merged under a single Whitehall post office identity in 1968, and voters adopted the home rule charter in 1974.

Does Whitehall Township require an inspection before I sell?

Yes. The township's FAQ says it requires an inspection for the resale of your property, and its permits page adds that a change of use or occupancy, including a home sale, needs a certificate of occupancy.

The township says each time a property is offered for sale or lease it needs a fresh inspection and a new certificate, even when a rental has several tenants in a year. Its Certificate of Occupancy Application and Guide lays out the steps:

  • Submit the inspection request form with the fee to the Bureau of Development at 3219 MacArthur Road.
  • An inspector contacts you within 1 to 3 business days, and the visit is set within 5 to 10 business days.
  • If nothing is wrong, the clear certificate is issued within 1 to 3 business days.
  • Payment is by cash, check or money order only. The form says cards are not accepted.

Add those windows up and the paperwork alone can take two to three weeks, so ask for the inspection as soon as you pick a settlement date.

What does the Whitehall inspection cost, and what do inspectors check?

Whitehall Township charges listed on the township inspection form (revised May 2023) and FAQ page
ItemCharge

Call the township at 610-437-5524 to confirm amounts before you mail a check, since the form carries a 2023 revision date.

The township describes the visit as a targeted safety inspection that is narrower than a full home inspection. Items on its checklist include working smoke detectors on every level and in each sleeping area, a carbon monoxide alarm near bedrooms where a fireplace, attached garage or fuel-burning heater exists, GFCI outlets in kitchens, baths and laundry areas, handrails on stairs of four or more risers, a 100-amp minimum electrical service, a concrete basement floor and visible house numbers at least four inches tall. Missing items are the usual reason for a failed first pass.

What happens if the inspection finds problems?

You have two paths. Fix the violations and have the inspector return, or sell as is with a conditional certificate. The guide says repairs must be corrected and reinspected within 30 days or before settlement.

For an as-is sale, the seller gives the inspection report to the other party, and a notarized Buyer or Seller Acceptance Form goes back to the township with the added fees. The conditional certificate allows the transfer only. Nobody can move in until all required repairs pass inspection, and the deposit comes back once a clear certificate is issued inside the allotted time.

This matters for homes that need work. Heirs, landlords and owners with deferred repairs often cannot finish a punch list before closing, which is why buyers who purchase as is tend to pair well with the conditional certificate route. Ask any buyer, cash or financed, who will sign the acceptance form and who will complete the repairs.

What transfer taxes and recording steps apply in Lehigh County?

Pennsylvania charges a realty transfer tax of 1 percent of the value, and the state holds both grantor and grantee jointly and severally liable. County recorders usually collect it alongside any local transfer tax, so the deed cannot be recorded until the tax is paid.

  • The Lehigh County Recorder of Deeds sits at the courthouse, 455 W. Hamilton Street, Room 122, in Allentown, with weekday hours of 8:00 AM until 4:30 PM. The phone is 610-782-3162.
  • Transfers between spouses, parent and child, grandparent and grandchild, and siblings are generally exempt, and a family exemption has to be stated on the deed.
  • A Statement of Value (REV-183) accompanies any transfer that does not pay the full tax, does not state full consideration or claims an exemption.

Ask the Recorder or your closing agent for the local rate that applies to a Whitehall address, because the municipal and school district share is set locally.

How do rental properties change a Whitehall sale?

Landlords face one extra rule. The township requires every non-owner-occupied property to name a local responsible agent whose office or home is within 10 miles of the township boundary. That person must be reachable in an emergency and authorized to accept legal service for the owner.

The inspection request form asks whether the property will be a rental and, if so, for the agent's name, address, daytime and after-hours phone numbers. Tenants who leave before closing also trigger paperwork, because the township asks for a moving permit when anyone moves into, out of or within the township. The FAQ prices that permit at $5 and says it is issued at the Township Tax Office from 8:00am to 4:00pm.

An owner with a tenant in place can still sell, but the inspector needs access to every room, attic and the exterior, so plan notice to the tenant early.

How do schools and neighborhoods affect resale in Whitehall?

Buyers looking at Whitehall compare it with other Lehigh Valley suburbs, and the Whitehall-Coplay School District is the main draw. It serves the township and neighboring Coplay, and ninth through twelfth graders attend Whitehall High School. Several parochial and private schools sit inside the township too, including Good Shepherd Catholic School, Lehigh Valley Lutheran School and St. Elizabeth Regional School.

Shopping and commuting add appeal. The Lehigh Valley Mall is the largest shopping mall based in the Lehigh Valley, and MacArthur Road (PA 145) carries retail traffic past an interchange with US 22, the Lehigh Valley Thruway. PA 329 crosses the northern part of the township, and LANta buses serve the MacArthur Road corridor. As of 2018 the township maintained about 97.6 miles of its own roads, with PennDOT handling roughly 23 miles.

Frequently asked questions

Can I sell my Whitehall house without a certificate of occupancy?

No. Whitehall Township requires an inspection and a certificate of occupancy for a resale, and the new owner cannot occupy the property until one is issued. A conditional certificate is available for as-is sales.

How much is the Whitehall resale inspection?

The township's form lists $65 for a single-family home and $35 per apartment unit. An as-is sale adds a $100 deposit for a house, per the form revised in May 2023, so confirm the current amount with the township.

Can I sell a Whitehall house as is if it fails inspection?

Yes. The seller or buyer signs a notarized acceptance form, pays the added fees and receives a conditional certificate that allows the sale only. All listed repairs must pass inspection before anyone occupies the home.

Who pays the transfer tax on a Whitehall home sale?

The state says buyer and seller are both liable for the 1 percent state tax, and the contract decides how the cost is split. The deed is not recorded until the tax is paid, so your closing agent usually collects it at settlement.

Do I need a local agent if my Whitehall house is a rental?

Yes. Non-owner-occupied properties must have a responsible agent within 10 miles of the township. The inspection request form asks for that person's contact details whenever the property is a rental.

Selling fast in Spring Township

A direct cash sale is the fastest route for a Spring Township house, but the township's property transfer inspection has to be scheduled either way. Spring Township is in Berks County, west of Reading, and it requires an exterior inspection of every single and multiple family dwelling before title changes hands. That inspection is the step that most often decides the calendar, so it comes first here.

The housing market is steady. There are 11,495 households, 75.3 percent of homes are owner-occupied, and the median owner-occupied value is $286,900. Median rent is $1,416 and median household income is $94,837. About a quarter of homes are rented, so some sellers are small landlords who should check lease dates before setting a closing date.

The property transfer inspection

This is a required exterior check under the township's Property Transfer Ordinance 341, in effect since August 1, 2007. The Code Enforcement Officer must inspect before title transfers. The seller, the buyer or either side's agent can file the application.

The application goes to the Code and Zoning Office no later than 30 business days before settlement. The fee is $150 per property, and it rises to $250 if the application arrives fewer than 15 business days before settlement. After a complete application, the officer inspects within 10 business days.

  • Utility and storm drainage easements and road rights-of-way must be clear of obstructions, including landscaping.
  • Fences, pools, spas, sheds and decks must be permitted and sit within setback and yard rules. Pool fencing needs a self-closing, latching gate.
  • Sanitary sewer connections must control inflow and infiltration, and sump pump discharge must be properly placed.
  • The number of dwelling units, bedrooms and smoke detectors is checked against township records.

Inspection fee and timing

The inspection covers only exterior, observable conditions, and nobody has to be home as long as the inspector can reach the backyard. Add a note with a phone number to the application if you want to be there.

If the inspection finds problems

Seller and buyer both sign the report to confirm they read it and agree to correct what it lists, and the township then issues a Property Transfer Certificate once the deficiencies are done. That can happen before or after settlement.

You do not have to fix everything before closing. If the buyer is willing to take on the repairs, an addendum to the agreement of sale normally settles who is responsible and how the money works. Order the inspection soon after you decide to sell, because the report has to be disclosed to the buyer and an early look leaves time to permit anything that was built without approval.

Common findings are an unpermitted shed or deck, a fence in an easement, or a pool without the right barrier. Fixing a pool gate or moving a fence is usually quick, while an unpermitted deck may need a permit application first, so start those items early. Those are fixable, and a cash buyer who plans to renovate will often accept them as part of an as-is purchase.

Township rules that can surprise a seller

Spring Township reviews more than 700 permits a year and enforces its fence, shed and pool rules closely. Fences in a front yard are limited to 4 feet and must be open style, rear-yard fences can reach 6 feet, and sheds are not allowed in required front or side yards.

Residential grass and weeds may not exceed 8 inches. After a verified complaint the township sends a notice, cuts the property after 7 days if the owner does not, and bills the owner, and unpaid amounts become a lien on the real estate. Sidewalks must be cleared of snow and ice within 24 hours after it stops, with the same lien risk. Clear both before you list so the inspection comes back clean.

Taxes and transfer costs

County and municipal tax payments can be made online through the Berks County Treasurer, and Wilson School District taxes are paid at Fulton Bank. Call the township tax collector's office for a payoff figure before closing. School real estate tax is paid separately from county and township tax.

Pennsylvania charges a 1 percent state realty transfer tax, collected with any local share by the Berks County Recorder of Deeds when the deed is recorded. Ask the Recorder for the combined local rate, and expect the buyer and seller to split it unless the sales agreement says otherwise.

Schools and location

The Wilson School District serves the township, with five elementary schools, two middle schools and Wilson High School. Spring Township borders Wyomissing, Sinking Spring and Adamstown, and U.S. 222, U.S. 422 and Route 724 cross it. A house near a main road or the bypass reads differently from one in a quiet subdivision, so say which you have in any listing or offer discussion. Terrain varies, with creeks to the north and hills toward the southwest, so lot grade and drainage can come up in an inspection.

A step-by-step plan for a Spring Township sale

  1. Walk the exterior and list anything built without a permit, such as a shed, deck, fence or pool barrier.
  2. File the transfer inspection application with the Code and Zoning Office at least 30 business days before settlement to hold the fee at $150.
  3. Clear easements and rights-of-way of landscaping, and mow grass and weeds to under 8 inches.
  4. When the report arrives, read it with the buyer, sign it, and agree in an addendum who handles each item.
  5. Call the tax collector for a payoff figure, and ask the Recorder of Deeds for the local transfer tax rate.
  6. Wait for the Property Transfer Certificate, which the township issues once deficiencies are done, before or after settlement.

A cash buyer removes the mortgage appraisal step, though the township inspection still applies. If time is short and you file with fewer than 15 business days to go, expect the $250 fee. Keep the signed report, any permits you pull and the addendum together, because the title company and the buyer may both ask to see them. If tenants live in the house, give them notice that an inspector will be on the grounds, and check lease end dates before you agree to a settlement day.

Frequently asked questions

Yes. Ordinance 341 requires an exterior property transfer inspection by the Code Enforcement Officer before title changes. Apply at least 30 business days before settlement to pay the $150 fee.

What is the late fee for a Spring Township transfer inspection?

The fee is $250 instead of $150 when the application arrives fewer than 15 business days before settlement. The inspector still responds within 10 business days of a complete application.

Do I have to fix every item before closing?

No. A buyer can agree to make the corrections, and an addendum to the agreement of sale usually covers it. The Property Transfer Certificate is issued once the deficiencies are completed, before or after settlement.

Who can file the transfer inspection application?

The seller, the buyer or either side's agent. It goes to the Code and Zoning Office, and nobody has to be home as long as the inspector can reach the backyard.

Which school district serves Spring Township?

The Wilson School District serves the township, with five elementary schools, two middle schools and Wilson High School. School real estate tax is paid separately from county and township tax.

Selling a house in McCandless

McCandless is a home rule municipality in Allegheny County, officially the Town of McCandless, in Pittsburgh's North Hills. A sale there carries a 2.5 percent combined transfer tax. The town also issues its own lien letter and points sellers to the sanitary authority for a dye test.

About 29,709 people live here, and the population has been flat for decades, so your listing competes with a mature, established housing supply. Hilly ground defines most streets, and Pine Creek runs through a valley in the middle of town with a floodplain along it. Homes near the creek deserve a floodplain check, so ask the town whether your lot sits in the mapped floodplain before you write the listing description.

Public schools belong to the North Allegheny School District. Buyers often search by named plan or community, such as Meadow Oaks, Guyton Farms, Greybrooke, Bennington Woods, Pin Oak, Briarwood, Park Meadows, Foxcroft Village, Sample Manor, Colington Square, Royal Manor, Pinnacle Pointe, Longvue Acres or Allison Park. Several ZIP codes cover the town, so confirm the municipality on the tax bill, not the postal city, before checking local rules.

What the transfer tax is when you sell in McCandless

The total realty transfer tax on a McCandless sale is 2.5 percent. That combines the state's 1 percent, a 1 percent municipal share and a one half of 1 percent North Allegheny School District share, based on the county's published rate table.

The county collects the tax when the deed is recorded. Buyer and seller are both liable, and contracts decide the split. Build the rate into your net sheet before you compare offers. Some transfers, including certain deeds between family members and property passed through an estate, are exempt from the state portion, so ask the county's Real Estate office how an exemption is documented.

Lien letter, dye test and utility liens

A seller should order a municipal lien letter and arrange a dye test. The lien letter costs $30 by mail or $35 if the results are emailed, and the request needs the owner's name, property address, parcel number and the reason, such as a sale. Checks are payable to the Town of McCandless.

The sanitary authority and the water authority can each file liens for unpaid service, so call both before the closing. The town's tax office handles the lien letter request at 412-364-0616.

How real estate taxes are billed in McCandless

The deputy tax collector, Jordan Tax Service, collects both Town and North Allegheny School District real estate tax. Beginning in 2026, owners receive two separate invoices, one for the Town and one for the school district.

  • The Town millage for 2026 is 1.236 mills.
  • The North Allegheny School District rate is 20.43 mills for the 2025 to 2026 school year, or $2,043 per $100,000 of assessed value.
  • Allegheny County lists 6.43 mills.
  • Taxes unpaid after December 31 are delinquent and can lead to a lien on the property.

An installment plan with three equal payments is open only to owners with a homestead or farmstead exclusion. The first payment is due August 31, followed by October 31 and December 31, and late installments carry a 10 percent penalty. Owners approved for the Act 77 senior citizen discount receive 30 percent off the Town portion. Pay tax on time even while an appeal is pending, because the higher amount must be paid once a deadline passes.

Payments cannot be left in the Town Hall drop box. Send them to Jordan Tax Service or use the options printed on the statement. Jordan representatives also sit at Town Hall on select dates, which are posted on the Town calendar, and owners should bring the full tax statements. Earned income tax and business privilege tax are handled separately by the Keystone Collections Group.

Appealing your Allegheny County assessment

The annual appeal window runs from July 1 through September 1. The Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review hears appeals, and it sends residential hearing notices at least 14 days ahead.

If you miss the window, ask the Office of Property Assessments about the next annual period and about special appeals tied to a change notice. A documented appeal can support a price discussion with a buyer, so gather comparable sales before you file.

Steps before closing

Begin by requesting the municipal lien letter, since the town's tax office needs your name, address, parcel number and the reason for the request. Book the dye test with the sanitary authority at the same time, because a failed test can mean sewer lateral work that has to be sorted out before settlement. Then call the sanitary authority and the water authority and ask whether any unpaid service could become a lien.

Look at your tax position as well. Taxes unpaid after December 31 are delinquent, and the Town and school district now send separate invoices, so make sure both are current. When an offer comes in, the title company prorates the Town and school taxes and the county records the deed. If a lender pays your taxes from escrow, tell them about the sale.

Listing or cash purchase in McCandless

Cash works best when the house needs repairs or the closing date matters more than the last dollar of price. A listing suits a house in good condition in a popular plan, where several buyers may compete.

  • Get the lien letter and dye test started before you accept any offer.
  • Compare offers after the 2.5 percent transfer tax, any payoff and the unpaid portion of the year's Town and school taxes.
  • Ask each buyer how they treat the dye test result if the sewer lateral needs work.

A cash sale skips showings, a buyer's loan approval and most repair negotiation. The town's lien letter, the dye test and the transfer tax still apply, so ask the buyer to confirm in writing who orders each one. If the dye test shows a problem with the sewer lateral, you can fix it before closing, price the repair into the offer, or ask the buyer to take the house as it is.

Hilly lots and older drainage are common here, so a buyer's inspector will look at the basement and the ground around the foundation. Have repair records ready, along with your latest tax statements from the Town and the school district, so the buyer sees a clean file from the first conversation.

What is the total transfer tax in McCandless?

2.5 percent. The state charges 1 percent, McCandless charges 1 percent, and the North Allegheny School District charges one half of 1 percent.

How do I get a lien letter from the Town of McCandless?

Mail a request with the owner's name, address, parcel number and reason, along with a $30 check. The email option costs $35. Write the check to the Town of McCandless.

Who collects real estate tax in McCandless?

Jordan Tax Service collects both Town and North Allegheny School District real estate tax. Owners receive two separate invoices starting in 2026.

Which school district serves McCandless?

North Allegheny School District. McCandless is also part of the shared Northland Public Library.

When can I appeal my Allegheny County assessment?

The annual appeal window runs from July 1 to September 1. If you miss it, contact the county's Office of Property Assessments about later options.

Selling a house in Susquehanna Township

Susquehanna Township lies north of Harrisburg in Dauphin County and uses the ZIP codes 17109 and 17110. It is a first-class township. A sale here involves three offices: the township for permits, the county treasurer for tax bills, and the Dauphin County recorder for the deed.

Knowing which office holds which record saves phone tag. Each is covered below, plus the steps that tend to slow a closing and what a cash sale does and does not skip.

The local housing market

The township counts 28,434 residents, up 6.2 percent from the 26,762 of April 2020. Homeowners occupy 62.9 percent of the housing, and the middle owned home is valued at $227,100. Median rent is $1,487, household income is $84,832, and the 11,894 households average 2.26 people.

Close to 37 percent of homes are rented, so landlords shop alongside owner-occupants. If the house is occupied, tell each buyer up front who lives there and on what lease terms.

Permits and building codes

Residential permits go to the municipal office at 1900 Linglestown Road in Harrisburg, and the number for questions is 717-909-9251. Every application needs a site plan.

Pennsylvania enforces the 2021 International Construction Codes, so repairs you do now follow that edition. For existing houses, code enforcement uses the 2021 International Property Maintenance Code, which the township adopted on July 14, 2022, effective July 19, 2022.

A contractor who disagrees with a ruling can appeal to the Joint Uniform Construction Code Appeals Board. It hears cases as needed on the fourth Tuesday of each month at 5 p.m. in the Hampden Township Municipal Building in Mechanicsburg.

The township has also been working on a Linglestown Road Overlay zoning amendment. If your house sits along that corridor, call the township about the final text before you list.

Who bills property tax and what transfer tax applies?

In this township the Dauphin County Treasurer acts as tax collector. The office is at 101 Market Street, Room 105 in Harrisburg, phone 717-780-6550.

Dauphin County realty transfer tax split on a Susquehanna Township sale
RecipientShare of sale price
State (Department of Revenue)1.0%
Municipality0.5%
School district0.5%
Total2.0%

The county Recorder of Deeds can confirm that split and keeps deeds dating to 1785. It sits in the courthouse at 101 Market Street, Room 102, phone 717-780-6560. Recording fees can be paid in cash or by check. Transfers between family members are generally exempt.

Before closing, find out from the treasurer exactly what your parcel owes. Whatever it is gets subtracted from your proceeds by the title company.

Zoning questions and township meetings

Susquehanna became a first-class township by Dauphin County Court order on January 2, 1952, and a nine-member Board of Commissioners elected by ward runs it today. Zoning decisions can be appealed to a Zoning Hearing Board, and a separate Township Authority also meets regularly.

Agendas and minutes for all three bodies are posted in the township's online Agenda Center. A seller facing a zoning question can read what has already been decided on similar properties before spending money on an application.

What to line up before closing

Title agents and buyers ask for the same handful of records, each from a different office. Begin gathering them the day a contract is signed.

  • A copy of your deed from the county recorder, and a payoff letter from the bank that holds your loan.
  • The current tax balance from the treasurer's office.
  • Permit records for decks, additions or finished space, from the municipal office on Linglestown Road.
  • Lease copies and tenant contact details, if anyone rents the house.

An inherited house adds one more step. Whoever holds legal authority over the estate must sign, so settle that question before a buyer fixes a closing date.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Susquehanna houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes owed

A tax debt will not stop a sale, only reduce what you walk away with. The title search turns up the balance, and settlement pays it out of the sale money. Call the treasurer early and ask for the figure in writing.

If you are well behind and the house is already headed toward a tax sale, a quick sale for cash can be the way to stay ahead of that deadline. Mention any other claims against the parcel to the closing agent, an unpaid contractor bill for example, since those get cleared at the same settlement.

Sellers who are current on taxes have an easier path: a clean balance letter means the title search finishes faster and the settlement date is less likely to move.

How a sale unfolds, step by step

  1. Both sides sign an agreement of sale naming the price, the settlement date and the person who covers transfer tax.
  2. A title search combs the record for liens, mortgages and tax balances.
  3. The buyer's inspector or lender asks for permit records, so the township office gets a call from your side first.
  4. At settlement you sign over the deed, the loan and any tax debt are paid off, and the remainder is yours.
  5. The new deed is filed with the recorder at the Harrisburg courthouse.

With a cash buyer there is no bank appraisal or underwriting queue, and that queue is where many closings stall. The search, the payoff and the recording still take their normal time.

Selling a tenant-occupied house

Because so many homes in the township are rented, an occupied sale is common. Start by reading the lease for its end date and its notice terms. A buyer who plans to live in the house will need the tenant out by closing, and an investor may want the lease to stay in place.

Give showing notice in writing and keep the tenant informed about timing. A cooperative tenant makes inspections and the final walk-through much smoother, and a direct buyer who takes the house as is will usually work around an existing lease instead of asking you to clear it first.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Practical ways to sell quickly

A direct sale skips open houses and lets you choose the closing day. A listing reaches the widest group of buyers. Plenty of local sellers are juggling an inherited house, a tenant or repairs they would rather not fund.

  • Pull your deed copy from the county and request a loan payoff before talking to buyers.
  • Walk the house against the 2021 maintenance code and fix peeling paint, broken steps and loose railings.
  • Write into the offer who pays the 2 percent transfer tax.
  • Put a listing's likely net, after commissions and repairs, beside a direct offer, and count the weeks as well as the dollars.

On either route the deed is recorded in Harrisburg and the county tax split stays the same.

Frequently asked questions

Who bills real estate tax in Susquehanna Township?

The Dauphin County Treasurer, at 101 Market Street, Room 105 in Harrisburg. The phone number is 717-780-6550.

What transfer tax comes with a Susquehanna Township sale?

Two percent of the price: 1 percent to the state and half a percent each to the municipality and school district.

Where is a Susquehanna Township deed recorded?

In Dauphin County. The Recorder of Deeds is in the courthouse at 101 Market Street, Harrisburg, and the office holds deeds back to 1785.

Which building codes does the township follow?

Pennsylvania's Uniform Construction Code governs building work, and the township uses the 2021 International Property Maintenance Code for existing buildings, effective July 19, 2022. Residential permit questions go to 717-909-9251.

How much has Susquehanna Township grown?

The population was 24,036 in 2010 and 26,736 in 2020, and it is now estimated at 28,434. That is growth of about 6.2 percent since the 2020 base.

Selling a house in Swatara Township

Swatara Township is a Dauphin County township just south of Susquehanna Township in the Harrisburg area. A sale there means dealing with a township codes office, a private real estate tax collector and the county recorder. The municipal building is at 599 Eisenhower Boulevard in Harrisburg.

The township runs along the Susquehanna River and takes its name from Swatara Creek, so water is part of the conversation for houses near either one.

The local housing picture

The population is 27,936, and owners live in 69.9 percent of homes. The middle owned home is valued at $214,400, rent runs $1,252 and household income is $80,444. The township has 10,640 households of 2.47 people on average.

Roughly 88.3 percent of residents lived at the same address a year earlier. Long-time owners may never have sold before, so the sections below name each office you will meet on the way to the closing table.

How the codes office affects a sale

Building and zoning permits come from the township's codes department. Approved Code Services, Inc. does the plan reviews and construction inspections as the township's sole third-party agency, and property maintenance complaints under the International Property Maintenance Code run through the same department.

New construction, additions and alterations call for a building permit. Routine maintenance, repairs and like-for-like equipment replacement generally need none. Stormwater management permits and quarterly waste fee exemption requests also go through the department.

If an inspector flags unpermitted work, phone the department at 717-564-2551 before you reply. The office is open weekdays from 8 until 4:30. Yard waste is easy to clear before showings, and the township runs a fall brush collection each year.

Real estate tax collector and transfer tax

Real estate tax is collected at a separate office, 6400A Chambers Hill Road in Harrisburg, and the municipal building does not accept those payments. The collector takes payment for the current year only. Tax certification requests go to that office at 717-832-4908.

Keystone Collections Group, with a Dauphin County office on Vartan Way, collects local services tax and earned income tax instead. Knowing the split helps when a title agent asks which office issues which certificate.

Realty transfer tax on a Swatara Township sale
Taxing bodyRate on sale price
Department of Revenue1.0%
Township0.5%
School district0.5%
Combined2.0%

The county recorder describes the 2 percent as divided among the state, the municipality and the school district. Deeds are recorded at the Dauphin County Courthouse, 101 Market Street, Harrisburg, where the deed index starts in 1785.

Schools and flood questions

Central Dauphin School District covers the township, and Swatara Middle School plus Lawnton, Rutherford and Chambers Hill elementary schools are among its buildings. Confirm which school your address feeds before naming one in a listing, since attendance can vary by street.

A house near the creek or the river can raise questions that an interior lot does not. If your property sits close to the water, ask your agent or a surveyor to confirm its flood zone status, and be ready with any repair history, including invoices for pumps, drainage work or waterproofing. Buyers and their insurers tend to ask, and a folder of records answers the question before it becomes a negotiating point.

What to collect before closing

A clean closing depends on a short list of documents, and most of them come from offices named on this page.

  • A tax certification from the township's tax collector, so the title agent sees what has been paid this year.
  • A payoff letter from your lender, and a copy of the deed from the county Recorder of Deeds.
  • Permit paperwork for additions, decks and alterations, available through the Building and Codes Department.
  • Sewer and stormwater bills, which the township lists on a separate online payment page from real estate tax.
  • Receipts for work done since you bought, because buyers who finance will have an appraiser and an inspector look at condition.

Order the tax certification early. It comes from a different office than the municipal building, and the title agent cannot finish the search without it.

If you owe tax or have unpermitted work

Two problems come up often with older township houses. The first is a tax balance. That collector handles the current year only. Ask what is due now and hand the figure to the title agent. Anything still unpaid is settled out of your sale money.

The second is a project done without a permit, perhaps a finished basement or a new deck. Phone the codes department before a buyer's inspector spots it. Staff can say whether a permit was required and what it takes to close the matter. If the cleanup is too much, tell buyers openly, because someone purchasing as is can price it into the offer.

From signed contract to the closing table

Every route follows one sequence. The agreement of sale comes first, then a title search of the record, then any lender or inspector review, then settlement. On that day the closing agent retires your mortgage, clears tax balances and sends the deed to Harrisburg for recording.

Without a lender in the chain, a cash closing can be set around your moving date. Whoever buys should give you a written date, the title company's name, and an explanation of what happens if the date slips.

Tenant-occupied and inherited houses

Houses that come with a tenant or an estate attach a few extra tasks. If someone rents the property, give the buyer a copy of the lease early and agree on whether the tenant stays or leaves before closing. If the house came to you by inheritance, confirm who has the legal power to sign the deed, and gather any tax and sewer bills that arrived in the previous owner's name.

An as-is buyer is often the simpler answer for these properties, since there is no need to empty or repair the house before the sale can move ahead.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Which routes work for a quick sale?

Three paths are open: an agent's listing, a private sale, or a direct sale to an investor or cash buyer. Listing may bring the highest price, but you give up control of the calendar to showings, repair requests and a lender.

  • Listing: suits a sound house and a seller with time for financing and inspections.
  • Private sale: avoids a commission and leaves pricing and paperwork with you.
  • Direct purchase: no financing, no showings and a closing day you choose, with the price adjusted for repairs.

On any route, line up a tax certification, a lender payoff letter and your deed copy. Get every buyer to write down who covers the 2 percent transfer tax. Without it the deed cannot be recorded.

Frequently asked questions

Where does Swatara real estate tax get paid?

At the township's real estate tax collector at 6400A Chambers Hill Road, Harrisburg, or online through the link on the township's tax page. The municipal building does not accept real estate tax payments.

What does the transfer tax cost on a Swatara sale?

Two percent overall. The recorder breaks it into 1 percent for the state and one half percent apiece for the township and the school district.

Are permits needed for repairs before a Swatara sale?

New construction, additions and alterations generally need a building permit, while routine maintenance and replacement of existing equipment generally do not. Call the Building and Codes Department at 717-564-2551 if you are unsure.

Who collects Swatara's earned income tax?

Keystone Collections Group, which keeps a Dauphin County office on Vartan Way in Harrisburg. This is separate from the real estate tax collector.

What school district serves Swatara Township?

Central Dauphin School District. Its schools include Swatara Middle School and elementary schools in Lawnton, Rutherford and Chambers Hill.

What comes first when a Horsham homeowner decides to sell?

Horsham Township asks every seller of a residential property to complete a township inspection and certification before settlement, so build that step into your timeline from day one. The rest of the sale follows the usual Pennsylvania pattern, with Montgomery County handling assessment, recording and transfer tax.

Horsham is about ten miles north of Center City Philadelphia, with an estimated 27,882 residents. Roughly 71.5 percent of homes are owner-occupied, a typical owned home is valued at $473,100, and typical rent is $1,573. At those values, a delay of even a few weeks costs real money in carrying costs and interest.

A fast sale to a cash buyer, a listing and a for-sale-by-owner deal all need the township certification below, because the rule attaches to the property transfer and not to the type of buyer.

Horsham property transfer certification

The township requires an inspection of every residential property before a transfer. The application and fee go to the Horsham Township Municipal Building at 1025 Horsham Road within the 90 days before settlement.

  • A township inspector checks the curb and sidewalk in front of the property.
  • The street address must be posted and easy to see from the road.
  • The seller certifies that working smoke detectors are in the house.

Schedule the inspection early enough to fix a cracked sidewalk slab or a missing house number before settlement. Questions go to the Code Enforcement department at (215) 643-3131.

The township also issues tax certifications through its tax collector. Send your contact details, the parcel number, the property address, the owner's name and a $30 check per parcel made out to Horsham Township, plus a stamped return envelope if you want it mailed. A title company normally handles this, but a seller handling the sale directly will need to order it.

Commute and neighborhood notes for your listing

Buyers here shop by commute and by corporate campus, so say so in your listing. Easton Road (Route 611) runs north to south through the eastern side, Horsham Road (Route 463) crosses the center, and Welsh Road (Route 63), Limekiln Pike (Route 152) and Bethlehem Pike (Route 309) frame the edges. The Willow Grove interchange of the Pennsylvania Turnpike sits just south in Upper Moreland Township.

SEPTA bus Route 55 follows Route 611, and a weekday rush hour shuttle called h.o.p.s. connects the office parks to the Fort Washington station on the Lansdale/Doylestown Regional Rail line. The township's villages include Horsham, Hallowell, Prospectville and Maple Glen, and the Hatboro-Horsham School District serves the area.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Horsham house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Montgomery County assessments and tax sales

The county Board of Assessment Appeals sets the values behind county, township and school bills. Yearly appeals are due August 1 and change the tax year after. That same August 1 date applies to real estate tax exemption applications. State law requires annual appeals to be decided by October 31 so changes reach the rolls and taxing bodies by November 15.

The board advises mailing deadline filings with a hand-cancelled postmark, a Certificate of Mailing or certified mail, because postal delays can mark a timely envelope late. You can also hand deliver in Norristown on weekdays between 8:30 a.m. and 4 p.m. The board's phone line is 610-278-3761.

If the house carries unpaid taxes, the county Tax Claim Bureau enters the picture.

Montgomery County Tax Claim Bureau sales
Sale typeWhen heldWhat a buyer gets
Upset saleEach September and DecemberThe property subject to its liens
Judicial saleAt least once a year, in August and DecemberThe property free and clear

Clear any delinquency before listing so it does not surface at closing.

Selling with unpaid taxes

Unpaid taxes do not block a sale, but the balance has to be cleared at or before closing. Ask the title company for a payoff figure early, and settle it from your sale proceeds if you cannot pay it beforehand. Once a delinquency reaches the Tax Claim Bureau, the house can end up in an upset or judicial sale, and you lose control of the timing and the price.

If you are behind and short on time, a cash sale with a closing date you pick can get the balance paid before the next sale date. Keep the Bureau's September and December upset sale dates in mind when you plan, and call the county before then to confirm your exact balance.

Also check for unpaid township items. A title company will flag them, but finding them yourself first means no surprises on the settlement statement.

Steps from decision to settlement

Here is the order most Horsham sellers follow. Start by calling Code Enforcement and asking for the transfer inspection application. Book the inspection and fix whatever it turns up, which is usually a curb, a sidewalk slab or a house number. Order the tax certification if you are not using a title company. Review your assessment, and if you think it is too high, remember that the appeal deadline is August 1 and only changes the following tax year.

Once you have an accepted offer, the buyer's title company orders the search and prepares the settlement statement. Read the statement line by line. Sellers here handle large transfer tax bills at these values, so confirm who pays each share before you sign. After settlement, the deed is recorded in Montgomery County.

Because the township certification must be submitted within the 90 days before settlement, avoid filing it too early. An application filed months in advance may have to be redone if closing slips.

When is a cash sale the better choice in Horsham?

A cash sale helps most when the property does not fit a conventional buyer's loan, or when the seller cannot wait through showings. Examples are a house with deferred roof or mechanical work, an estate property that needs to close before the next tax bill, or a seller relocating out of the area.

Because Horsham values are high, compare any cash figure with a full net sheet: list price, agent commission, transfer tax, repairs to pass the township inspection, and carrying cost. If you would like a cash figure for your Horsham house, Cash Home Buyers CA can provide one to set against that sheet.

A cash buyer skips the showings and the loan approval, so the closing date can follow your schedule. The township certification still applies, since the rule follows the property. Ask the buyer to confirm who will schedule the inspection and who pays for any sidewalk or address fix, and get that agreement in writing before you commit to a closing date.

Frequently asked questions

Is an inspection required to sell a house in Horsham Township?

Yes. The Residential Property Transfer Certification Program requires an inspection of every residential property before transfer, covering the curb, the sidewalk and the posted address, plus a seller certification of working smoke detectors. Submit it within 90 days before settlement.

How much does a Horsham tax certification cost?

The township's tax collector charges $30 per parcel, paid by check to Horsham Township. Include the parcel number, property address and owner name, and say how you want the certification returned.

What date closes the yearly Montgomery County assessment appeal?

August 1, and the result applies to the next tax year.

Which school district serves Horsham?

The Hatboro-Horsham School District serves the township, along with neighboring Hatboro. Its schools include Keith Valley Middle School and Hatboro-Horsham Senior High School.

Can I sell a Horsham house with unpaid property taxes?

Yes, but the unpaid amount must be cleared at or before closing. Taxes that reach the county Tax Claim Bureau can put the property into an upset or judicial sale, so settle the balance before then.

Monroeville at a glance

Monroeville is a home rule municipality east of Pittsburgh in Allegheny County, with 28,640 residents in 2020 and an estimate of 27,685 for 2025. The population has been flat to slightly down since 1980, so most houses sit in established neighborhoods and many were built decades ago. Owners live in 68.7 percent of homes, and the typical value is $209,800. Households average 2.20 people and 23.2 percent of residents are 65 or older, so plenty of houses hold more room than their owners use.

The Gateway School District serves the municipality. The borough of Pitcairn sits entirely inside Monroeville near its south-southwest edge, so check the parcel record to see which municipality's rules and tax rates apply to a given address.

Housing numbers

These are the figures buyers and appraisers tend to start from.

Housing measureMonroeville figure

Owners without a mortgage pay little each month, so a long-held home can be cheap to keep and still need costly repairs. That is often when an owner starts weighing an as-is sale.

Occupancy permit when you sell

Monroeville requires a residential occupancy permit tied to the sale. An inspection has to be completed before the new owners move in. The fee is $100 for a single-family dwelling or townhome, and a second reinspection can add $50 under the municipal fee schedule.

The application works like this:

  • The current owner or the owner's agent files it.
  • It lists the property address, the buyer's name, who will meet the inspector and whether the electricity is on or off.
  • It has a line to mark the house as being sold as is.
  • The permit is issued in the name of the new owners who will live there.

The municipality's number is 412-856-3340. Call before you list so the inspection can be scheduled early, and leave the electricity on if you can. An inspector can't check the furnace, outlets or water heater in a dark house, and a second visit costs money and days.

If the house is a rental

Rental units need their own occupancy permit, and an inspection must be completed before a tenant moves in. The fee is $75 for multi-family units and $100 for a single-family dwelling or townhome, and the permit is issued in the tenant's name. Units occupied before inspection can face penalty fines under the municipal ordinance.

A tenant in place changes the sale. Ask the municipality whether the permit on file is current and hand that paperwork to a buyer who plans to keep the tenant. An investor who will rent the house after closing applies under the rental rules separately from the sale permit. If the tenant is moving out anyway, put the move-out date in writing so the sale inspection can happen in an empty house.

Transfer tax at closing

Monroeville sits at the higher end of the county table. The municipality takes 1 percent and the Monroeville-Gateway school district takes one-half percent. Add the state's 1 percent and the total is 2.5 percent of the sale price. The tax is paid to the county at the deeds office with its own check, apart from recording fees. Some family transfers are exempt, and form REV-183 covers deeds that show no price.

The charge appears on your settlement sheet in any sale, so request the exact total from the title company early. Who pays what is set by the sales contract, so read that clause closely before signing.

How to appeal your assessment

A challenge to your valuation starts with BPAAR, the county's first appeal level, and all of its hearings take place by phone. You can speak for yourself, send an attorney or appoint a representative. A losing party may carry the case to the Board of Viewers in the Court of Common Pleas.

The Gateway school district or the municipality can file an appeal against an owner too, and the owner is free to attend or skip those hearings. If you plan to sell, a lower assessment matters less than the price a buyer will pay, but it does cut your bill while you hold the house.

From first call to closing

Start with a phone call to 412-856-3340 to learn what the occupancy inspector checks. Then pull together your lender's payoff figure, any lien letters and the parcel record. Decide between a listing, a cash offer and an investor purchase as is. When a contract is signed, file the occupancy form naming the buyer and book the inspection.

If the inspector marks problems, either repair them or write down who will pay for them. At the table you sign the deed, the county gets its transfer tax, and the title company settles your payoff before sending you the remainder. Mark the sale as is on the form and in the contract so the two documents agree.

Before you talk with a buyer, collect:

  • The address and the exact name on your deed.
  • Your lender and any other lien holders.
  • The power status, on or off.
  • Any tenant, plus the lease end date.

Selling quickly

Speed depends on the inspection, the title and the buyer's financing. A cash buyer removes the loan approval step, but the municipal occupancy inspection still applies.

  • Order the occupancy inspection early and fix any items it flags.
  • Pull the county parcel record for the owner of record and school district.
  • Collect mortgage and lien payoffs, and leave the power on for the inspector.
  • Weigh a listing, a cash offer and an as-is investor sale against what repairs would cost.

With cash there is no bank appraisal or underwriting queue, the stage where financed deals most often slip. Closing day is short: you sign the deed, the title company clears the mortgage and any liens, and the remaining proceeds are yours.

Prepare the house and the commute pitch

Houses with outdated wiring, old roofs or deferred upkeep are the ones most likely to snag on the occupancy inspection, so walk through yours before a buyer does and note anything that looks unsafe. Small fixes done up front cost less than a delayed closing.

Monroeville sits where I-376, the Pennsylvania Turnpike at Exit 57, U.S. 22, Business 22 and PA 48 meet. Two Pittsburgh Regional Transit bus lines run to downtown Pittsburgh from park-and-ride lots here, and the Westmoreland Heritage Trail follows an old rail line to Trafford and Murrysville. A listing can highlight the commute, since buyers who work downtown weigh drive time heavily when they compare houses across the eastern suburbs.

Frequently asked questions

What is the occupancy permit fee when selling a house in Monroeville?

$100 for a single-family house or townhome, with a possible $50 charge if a second reinspection is needed. The buyers can't move in until the inspection is done.

How much is the transfer tax on a Monroeville sale?

It totals 2.5 percent. The state takes 1 percent, the municipality 1 percent and the Monroeville-Gateway school district one-half percent.

Is Monroeville a city or a borough?

It is a home rule municipality. The area began as Patton Township in 1849, became a borough in 1951 and adopted its charter in 1974.

Which school district serves Monroeville?

The Gateway School District serves students from kindergarten through grade 12. The county transfer tax table calls it the Monroeville-Gateway district.

Can I appeal my Monroeville property assessment?

Yes. Go through the county's BPAAR board, which hears cases by phone. You may appear alone, use an attorney or name an authorized representative.

Selling fast in Springettsbury

A cash buyer will usually close a Springettsbury house faster than any other route. The township lies east and northeast of the city of York, and the steps that set the calendar are tax certification, payoff letters and title work.

The township is home to the York Galleria mall and a large Harley-Davidson manufacturing campus. It includes East York, Pleasureville, Yorklyn and Stonybrook, and the housing mixes 1930s homes in East York with postwar subdivisions such as Fayfield and Haines Acres and newer developments.

There are 10,202 households, 72.5 percent of homes are owner-occupied, and the median owner-occupied value is $243,900. Median rent is $1,339 and median household income is $86,335. About 85.8 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, and more than a quarter of homes are rented, so some sellers are landlords with tenants to consider.

Which school district is your house in

Springettsbury is split between the York Suburban and Central York school districts, and your tax bills follow whichever one serves your address. The township tax collector bills school real estate tax for both districts inside the township.

Why it matters: the split changes your sale paperwork. School tax is billed separately from the county and township bill, on a different date, and a closing company needs the right district and the right year to prorate it correctly. Pull your latest school tax bill, since it names the district, and keep it beside the parcel number for the title company.

How the tax certification works

Your closing company requests a Real Estate Tax Certification from the township Tax Collector. It shows whether York County, township, street light and school taxes are paid, with the year, face amount, discount and penalty for each. The request form carries the property address, parcel number, owner, buyer and settlement date and says whether the deal is a sale or a refinance.

The fee is $20, payable by check to the Springettsbury Township Tax Collector. Delinquent taxes from prior years go through the York County Tax Claim Bureau instead. A sewer account certification request form also exists, so ask the title company whether a sewer certification is on its list.

Property rules the township enforces

Springettsbury employs a full-time Codes Enforcement Officer who responds to complaints about property maintenance. The issues that come up most often are:

  • Signs of the wrong size, type or location.
  • Cars, RVs, tractors, construction equipment and boats parked on grass, plus abandoned or junk vehicles.
  • Weeds, tall grass, trash, uncleared sidewalks, dilapidated buildings and unsafe structures.

Owners are asked to correct a violation voluntarily, and a finding can sometimes be appealed to the Zoning Hearing Board. If a violation stays open, the township can pursue legal action and the District Magistrate can impose fines for each violation. Transfer tax and recording

Pennsylvania takes 1 percent of the value as realty transfer tax, and local governments may add their own share. The York County Recorder of Deeds gathers the whole amount when the deed is recorded. Some family transfers and property passed by will or intestate succession are exempt.

Before you estimate your net, ask the Recorder for the combined Springettsbury rate and the recording fees. The sales agreement names who pays, but if the tax goes unpaid both sides answer for it.

Ask any buyer who covers the tax certification fee, the sewer certification and the recording costs, and ask for the closing date in writing.

Selling a rental or an inherited house

A house with a tenant leaving, or one passing through an estate, adds a few questions. Check the lease end date first and plan the closing day around it. If a family member inherited the property, ask the Recorder of Deeds or the title company whether an exemption applies to your deed, because transfers by will or intestate succession can be exempt from the state tax.

Whoever signs the deed needs clear legal authority, and the title company will want to see it before it books settlement. Gather the deed, the school tax bill that names the district, and any township notices into one folder. A cash buyer usually moves faster when those papers are ready on day one, and you avoid last-week surprises over who pays a certification fee or a recording cost.

If open code notices exist, decide whether you will correct them or sell as-is with the price adjusted. Telling the buyer early is better than having a lender or an inspector raise it later.

Steps to a Springettsbury closing

  1. Find the district on your latest school tax bill and keep the bill with the parcel number.
  2. Check your address for open code notices or permit questions by calling the township office, and fix what you can before listing.
  3. Ask the closing company to send the tax certification request form with the settlement date, and have a $20 check payable to the Tax Collector ready.
  4. Pay any prior-year delinquent tax through the York County Tax Claim Bureau, and ask the title company whether a sewer certification is needed.
  5. Get the combined local transfer tax rate and recording fees from the York County Recorder of Deeds, and settle in the contract who pays.
  6. If you are a landlord, check lease dates before you agree to a closing day.

Call the township office to ask about open violations or permits on your address before listing. The code officer responds to complaints and permits, so clear any open notices first.

How much is the tax certification in Springettsbury?

The fee is $20, paid by check to the Springettsbury Township Tax Collector. The closing company sends the request form with the parcel number, owner, buyer and settlement date.

Which school districts serve Springettsbury Township?

York Suburban and Central York both serve parts of the township. Their tax bills go out July 1 for York Suburban and July 15 for Central York.

When are Springettsbury county and township tax bills mailed?

County and municipal bills are mailed February 15. School bills are separate, and the collector goes by postmark date for mailed payments.

Where do I pay back taxes on a Springettsbury house?

Delinquent taxes from prior years go to the York County Tax Claim Bureau at 717-771-9232. Current-year bills are paid to the township Tax Collector, who goes by postmark date.

What makes selling a house in Williamsport, PA different?

Williamsport is the seat of Lycoming County and the commercial center of north central Pennsylvania, so its housing market follows college calendars, hospital hiring and the river as much as it follows the wider region. Renters make up most households here, which affects who buys and what they expect from a property.

The Census Bureau estimates 27,384 residents for July 2025, down 1.3 percent from the 2020 base. Only 43.0 percent of housing units are owner-occupied for 2020 to 2024, the median home value is $154,300 and median gross rent is $855. The city counts 11,320 households with 2.14 people each, a median household income of $48,851 and a poverty rate of 25.4 percent.

Population peaked at 45,729 in 1930 when lumber money built the mansions on West Fourth Street. It stood at 27,754 in the 2020 census. That is a drop of about 40 percent from the 1930 peak.

What fees does the Williamsport Bureau of Codes charge?

The city's Bureau of Codes publishes a fee schedule, and several lines apply to owners who are selling or renting a property. It is open Monday to Friday from 8:00am to 4:00pm, closed for lunch from 12:00pm to 1:00pm, at 200 Reighard Ave., and the main number is (570) 327-7517.

Most permits issue within 15 business days of a completed application, except new construction or major reconstruction. Ask the Bureau which occupancy or certification letter your buyer or lender expects, and request it early.

How does the Williamsport rental inspection affect a sale?

If the house has tenants or is used as student housing, the rental inspection fee schedule applies, and the Bureau lists inspection of rental properties among its core duties. A landlord selling a unit should find out whether the inspection is current and whether a re-inspection is open.

  • Gather any inspection reports and repair receipts for the buyer.
  • Check the unit count, because the fee grows with each unit in a building.
  • Sobriety houses, rooming houses and student residences have their own license line at $60 plus $15 per room, capped at $500.
  • Zoning matters for conversions. Variances and special exceptions each carry a $500 application fee, so confirm the legal use before you advertise a duplex or apartments.

A purchaser paying cash for a tenant-occupied building can accept the inspection history as is, yet the closing agent will still want clean paperwork on each unit.

Which Williamsport neighborhoods and schools shape buyer interest?

Williamsport's neighborhoods each draw a different buyer. Downtown runs between Hepburn Street and Basin Street, and Millionaires' Row along West Fourth Street is a National Register historic district. Newberry lies west of Lycoming Creek, Vallamont sits north of Rural Avenue, Grampian Hills spreads around Grampian Boulevard, Park Avenue and East End fill in the south and east, and West Hills occupies the hillside and hilltop.

The Williamsport Area School District serves the city with Cochran, Hepburn Lycoming and Jackson primary schools, Curtin and Lycoming Valley intermediate schools, a middle school and Williamsport Area High School. The district was recognized for its music program, and Stevens Primary School closed in 2022. Lycoming College and Pennsylvania College of Technology are both in the city, which keeps a steady pool of student renters and staff buyers.

Little League Baseball began here in 1939, and the Little League World Series is held every late summer in neighboring South Williamsport, a draw for visitors.

How do floods and winters affect a Williamsport house?

Water is the first thing buyers ask about. The West Branch Susquehanna River borders the city on the south, and the March 1936 flood crested at 33.9 feet and reached High Street. June 1972, when Hurricane Agnes struck, set the wettest month on record at 16.80 inches. A flood control levee and the Susquehanna Riverwalk now run along the river.

Winter is the second factor. Williamsport averages about 36 inches of snow a season, January is the coldest month, and the first freeze typically arrives around October 16, so roofs, gutters and heating systems get tested every year. Yearly precipitation averages roughly 43 inches over about 136 days, which keeps basement moisture on every inspector's list.

Gather your flood insurance history, any basement repair records and roof dates before you talk with a buyer. Those documents answer the questions that slow offers down.

How is a Williamsport deed recorded and taxed?

Pennsylvania imposes a 1 percent realty transfer tax on the value transferred, and county recorders collect it along with any local tax. Both buyer and seller are jointly liable, and the contract decides who pays what. Some family transfers and transfers by will or intestate succession are exempt.

The Lycoming County Recorder of Deeds keeps land records back to 1795, with images online at the county's search portal. The county lists eleven school districts for transfer tax purposes, and Williamsport is one of them, so the local share can be divided between the municipality and the school district. Ask the Recorder or your title company for the exact local rate and the current recording fee before closing.

To add or remove a name, a new deed must be drawn and recorded. The county suggests a real estate attorney or title company for that job.

A short checklist saves weeks in a city with several overlapping offices: the Bureau of Codes on Reighard Avenue, the county Recorder downtown and the title company handling settlement.

  • Pull the parcel number and the names exactly as they appear on the deed.
  • Collect rental inspection letters, re-inspection results and any open permit paperwork.
  • Photograph the basement, roofline and any river-side flood marks, and keep insurance claims on hand.
  • Confirm the zoning use, particularly for duplexes, rooming houses and student residences.
  • Decide how you want to split the 1 percent state transfer tax and any local tax with the buyer.

With those items in a folder, you can compare a listing, a private sale and an as-is purchase on the same footing, and a buyer's questions get quick answers.

What do getting around and local jobs mean for Williamsport sellers?

Interstate 180, US 15 and US 220 meet at Williamsport, and Harrisburg is about 85 miles away. River Valley Transit runs local buses, Fullington Trailways connects downtown to Harrisburg, New York and Philadelphia, and Williamsport Regional Airport in Montoursville has flights to Washington Dulles. The Census puts the mean commute for 2020 to 2024 at 15.8 minutes.

Major employers include UPMC Susquehanna, Penn College, the school district and several manufacturers, including a large Lycoming Engines plant. The city sits in Marcellus Shale gas country, which has added another layer to the local economy. For sellers, that mix means buyers include nurses, instructors and plant workers who value short drives and move-in-ready homes.

A rental property inspection costs $85 per building plus $15 for each additional unit in the building. A re-inspection visit costs $30.

Who records the deed on a Williamsport sale?

The Lycoming County Recorder of Deeds records it. Pennsylvania's 1 percent state realty transfer tax is collected there, together with any local tax and recording fee, and the deed is not recorded until payment is made.

Does flooding affect selling in Williamsport?

It can, because the city borders the West Branch Susquehanna River and has a flood history, including a 33.9 foot crest in 1936. Have your insurance and repair records ready, and any buyer will still ask about them.

How long does a permit take in Williamsport?

What drives a sale in East Hempfield

East Hempfield is a suburban township just west of Lancaster city. Three local facts decide what you take home: a countywide reassessment now in progress, the Hempfield School District's rate, which is the biggest slice of the bill, and a township transfer tax.

The township shares the Lancaster mailing designation with five other suburbs, so plenty of East Hempfield houses carry a Lancaster address. School and county tax bills

County and township real estate taxes in East Hempfield are collected by the Lancaster County Treasurer. The Hempfield School District sends its own bill. Its 2026-27 rate is 19.8786 mills, a 4.1 percent increase over last year.

Transfer tax

On top of the Commonwealth's 1 percent, the township charges 1 percent of the property's value for its general purposes. It adopted the ordinance in 1987 under the state Tax Reform Code and the Local Tax Enabling Act. Payment is due when the deed goes in for recording, and in any case within 30 days after the document is accepted.

Buyer and seller are jointly liable under the Department of Revenue's rules. The ordinance exempts several transfers, such as a transfer to an heir from a decedent and some transfers to the trustee of an ordinary trust, as long as the Recorder of Deeds receives a copy of the trust instrument. Family transfers are on the state exemption list too.

Before choosing an asking price, call the Lancaster County Recorder of Deeds for the full transfer tax on your deed, school district share included.

The 2027 countywide reassessment

The county's Property Assessment Office covers more than 195,000 parcels in 60 municipalities and 17 school districts. Its previous reassessment took effect January 1, 2018, at market value on that date and a 100 percent ratio. The next, for 2027, is in progress, and during 2025 and 2026 assessors may inspect from outside and photograph exteriors.

The purpose is to even out values between properties, not to raise money. Taxing bodies have to lower their rates to stay revenue neutral, so a bigger assessment on your house is not the same as a bigger bill. Buyers will still set your assessed value beside similar houses.

  • Yearly appeals must be in by August 1.
  • In a reassessment year the window is 40 days from the date on the notice.
  • Once 2027 is over, the following yearly appeal chance is 2028.

No form freezes or eliminates property taxes for seniors, so disregard any video or mailer that claims one does. Call the Assessment Office at 717-299-8381 to learn about the programs that do exist.

Township permits and inspections

The township has a Building Code Official who reviews permits and carries out inspections, plus an inspector for property maintenance. Code Administrators Inc. performs inspections and needs 24 hours' notice. Residents can also file code enforcement complaints and request records research.

Before listing, dig out permits and final inspection records for any deck, finished basement or new furnace. It is simpler to settle gaps with the township while the house is still yours. Selling a rental or an inherited house

If tenants live in the house, tell the buyer early and share the lease and rent history. Showings follow the lease terms, so plan the schedule with the tenant. For an inherited house, the title company will want proof of who can sign for the estate before it prepares the deed. The township's transfer tax ordinance exempts a transfer to an heir from a decedent, but the later sale to a buyer is taxable.

In either case, settle open items with the township first. A permit that was never closed, or a property maintenance complaint, is easier to resolve before a buyer finds it during a title search.

Common ways to sell

A listing suits a house in good condition inside a well-regarded school district. An as-is sale fits an estate, a house needing major repairs, a rental with a difficult tenant, or a move that cannot wait on showings and a buyer's financing. Weigh offers by what remains after transfer tax, any unpaid tax, prorated school and county bills and repair credits. Insist that offers come in writing.

What a cash sale skips

With a cash buyer there is no mortgage approval, no lender appraisal and no financing contingency, which removes the usual reasons a closing slips. You also skip staging, repeated showings and repair requests after an inspection. The paperwork on your side stays the same: tax certification, transfer tax at recording, and any open permit or tax balance.

For an estate house, a vacant property or a tenant problem, that trade can justify a lower price. Ask every buyer how much time they need, who pays for title work and recording, and whether they will accept the house as it stands.

  3. Gather permits and final inspections for work done on the house.

A cash buyer has no lender timeline, so this list usually moves faster than it would in a financed sale. Add one more habit: keep copies of everything you send, because a lost envelope can cost days.

No. East Hempfield is a separate township in Lancaster County, though it shares the Lancaster mailing designation with five other suburbs. Permits and zoning come from the township.

The Hempfield School District sends its own bill at 19.8786 mills for 2026-27. County and township taxes go through the Lancaster County Treasurer.
