Email the Lancaster County Tax Collection Bureau with the owner name, address, 13-digit parcel number and settlement date, and mail a $25 check payable to LCTCB Real Estate Tax Group.

What is the appeal window for my East Hempfield assessment?

Annual appeals are due by August 1. In a reassessment year, you have 40 days from the notice date. After the 2027 reassessment, the next annual appeal opportunity is 2028.

Does the township require an inspection before I sell?

Its code office handles permit review, inspections through Code Administrators Inc. and code enforcement. Call the code office before you list to learn whether anything further applies to your address.

Selling a house in Upper Dublin

Upper Dublin is a first-class township in Montgomery County, covering 13.3 square miles north of Philadelphia, with 26,665 residents at the 2020 census. It was farmland until the 1950s, then filled in with postwar subdivisions, so many houses are mid-century builds with the maintenance that comes with them.

Many addresses use a mailing name other than Upper Dublin: Ambler, Dresher, Fort Washington, Jarrettown and Maple Glen, with small slices of Abington, Ardsley, North Hills, Oreland and Willow Grove. They use ZIP codes 19001, 19002, 19025, 19034, 19038, 19075 and 19090, and none of them is a separate municipality. Property records and tax bills go through the township and county regardless of the postal name.

The Fort Washington Office Park, at a Pennsylvania Turnpike interchange, is the township's main job center. For a seller in Maple Glen or Fort Washington, a short commute to it is an easy point to make in a listing.

Point-of-sale requirements

Upper Dublin has a point-of-sale process. Every property being sold must submit a Property Transfer Application under Ordinance 10-1228. The steps run alongside your sale, so start early.

  • A township official inspects the exterior for sidewalk compliance and correct house numbering. Anything found must be fixed before the sale.
  • The property file is checked for open permits. Every open permit must be finalized before the sale.
  • The file is also reviewed for zoning hearings tied to the property.
  • You sign an affidavit that smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and sump pumps are present.
  • Open Notices of Violation must be resolved before the sale.
  • Curbs and aprons are inspected and documented. A failed curb or apron does not stop the sale, but it is marked for replacement under the property maintenance code.

Permits and applications go through the township's online OpenGov portal at upperdublin.net/permits. Paper applications are no longer available, so file everything there. Leave time for both the inspection and any sidewalk repair it turns up.

Storm repairs, flooding and open permits

Nearly all of the township drains through Wissahickon Creek into the Schuylkill River, with only small corners draining to Neshaminy Creek and Pennypack Creek, so low lots near those streams deserve a closer look. An EF2 tornado from the remnants of Hurricane Ida struck the Fort Washington and Maple Glen areas on September 1, 2021, and buyers sometimes ask about repairs from that storm.

If your house had storm repairs, keep the permits, invoices and final inspection records together. Every open permit must be closed out before the sale, so storm-era work that never received a final inspection is the kind of thing that stops a closing. The township's Code Enforcement department can tell you which permits on your address are still open.

Ask for a copy of the property file before you list. It also shows past zoning hearings tied to the address, which the township reviews at transfer.

The Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds lists the realty transfer tax at 2 percent. Pennsylvania's share is 1 percent, and the rest is local. Both parties to a deed are jointly responsible to the state, so decide in the contract who pays.

If you are behind on taxes, the Tax Claim Bureau holds an upset sale each September and December of parcels whose taxes from two years earlier remain unpaid. Buyers at an upset sale take on all liens, and the Bureau advertises each property beforehand. Paying the delinquent bill first, or selling before your parcel is listed, keeps the house out of that sale.

Selling with open items on the house

Delays in Upper Dublin often trace back to the township file. A closing agent cannot finish until permits are final, violation notices are cleared and the sidewalk is sound. Walk the front of the house and the curb yourself first. Check that the house number is visible, that sidewalk squares are level, and that smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and the sump pump are all in place.

Then call Code Enforcement and ask what the file shows. Bring the permit numbers for any deck, basement finish or roof work, and ask for the inspection history so you know which approvals are missing before a buyer's agent does. If a repair is needed, schedule it right away, since the inspection and any sidewalk work take time and the sale cannot close until they are done.

What are my options if I need to sell fast?

You can list, sell privately, or take a cash offer from a buyer who buys houses as-is. The township's transfer requirements apply to each route, so the real question is who finishes the paperwork and how soon.

  • List when open permits are closed, the sidewalk is sound and the house shows well.
  • Choose a cash sale when you inherited the house, face repairs, or have a closing date to meet. Confirm the buyer will handle the sidewalk, permit and affidavit steps with you.

Whichever route you choose, call Code Enforcement first, get the property file, and make sure the 2 percent transfer tax is set out in writing.

Frequently asked questions

Does Upper Dublin require an inspection to sell a house?

Yes. Every property sold must file a Property Transfer Application, and a township official inspects the exterior for sidewalks and house numbers. Open permits and open violations must be cleared before the sale, and you sign an affidavit about smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and sump pumps.

What is the transfer tax in Upper Dublin?

The Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds lists the realty transfer tax at 2 percent, which includes the state's 1 percent. Both buyer and seller are liable under state law, so the sales contract should say who pays.

When is the deadline to appeal an assessment in Montgomery County?

August 1 each year for annual appeals. The same deadline applies to exemption applications, and the Board advises hand delivery or a post office counter postmark.

Can I sell an Upper Dublin house that has open permits?

Not until the permits are finalized. The township's transfer review checks the property file, and every open permit must be closed before the sale, so schedule the missing inspections first.

What happens if I do not pay my property taxes before selling?

Unpaid taxes become a lien and can lead to a Tax Claim Bureau sale. The Bureau runs an upset sale each September and December for parcels with taxes unpaid from two years earlier, and buyers there take on the liens.

Shaler Township, in Allegheny County, also has its own pre-closing checklist that every seller has to clear, and that checklist drives the schedule whichever route you choose.

The township's Selling Your Home guide spells out what the seller does, what the closing company orders, and what the buyer sets up afterward. Knowing it in advance keeps a fast sale from stalling in the last week.

With 95.8% of residents in the same house a year earlier, many sellers are long-time owners who are downsizing or settling an estate, and a cash buyer who takes the house as it stands suits them well.

Township requirements before closing

Shaler requires a dye test, a backflow preventer check and a final water reading from the seller, plus four township letters the closing company orders. Every document on the list is required for closing.

  • Dye test. The home is tested to confirm that downspouts and rain leaders are not tied into the sanitary sewer. Results stay valid for three years. Request the test at least 14 days before closing.
  • Backflow preventer. At least two weeks before closing, call the Hampton Shaler Water Authority at (412) 486-4867 for a visit to confirm a dual check valve and thermal expansion tank are in place.
  • Final meter reading. Sellers and landlords schedule a final reading and send a copy to the closing company so escrowed funds can be released.
  • Trash account. Close the account with the hauler and leave the recycling cart for the new owner.

If the dye test fails, the plumber notifies the township and the owner. Repairs can go to any contractor, but the township's building inspector must hear about it at least 24 hours before work starts so the work can be inspected.

Pennsylvania's realty transfer tax is 1 percent of the property's value, and local governments add their own share. The Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds collects all of it when the deed is recorded. Buyer and seller are both legally liable, though the sales agreement normally says who pays.

Some transfers are exempt, including certain moves between family members and property passed by will or intestate succession. Both can affect a Shaler house, depending on the street. The township keeps FEMA flood maps on file and zone maps for Girtys Run, Little Pine Creek and Pine Creek, which flood periodically. The building and zoning office at 300 Wetzel Road will review the maps with you and help work out which flood zone a property is in.

Part of the township sits over land that was mined in the past. If the property will sit empty for longer than three weeks, the owner can apply for a trash waiver good for up to six months and renewable. A seller who knows the house will be vacant before closing should ask about it.

Is a cash offer a good fit?

It is worth pricing when the house needs work, the dye test or backflow check looks like a problem, or the family wants a closing date it can plan around. A cash buyer is usually willing to take on the township checklist, but ask who pays for the dye test, the $50 letters and any repairs before you sign.

Compare the offer against a listing net of commission and the transfer tax. If the gap is small, the speed may be worth it. If it is large and the house is in good shape, a traditional listing may still make sense.

  4. Tell the closing company to order the No Lien Letter, the Zoning Compliance Letter and the Dye Test Certificate.

If you are selling a vacant or inherited house, shut off service through the water authority and ask about the trash waiver while the property sits empty. The township's requirements apply to every sale, so the same checklist covers an as-is cash purchase.

Three years from the test date, and the township keeps the result on file. Request the test at least 14 days before closing so a failed result can be fixed in time.

The closing company orders it from the township for $50. It confirms that no municipal liens are unfiled against the property, and the water authority issues its own separate lien letter.

The township charges $50 for it. The closing company can use three years of tax receipts instead, so keep those handy, and call the township tax office at 412-486-9700 for copies.

How a Bethlehem Township sale works

A sale in Bethlehem Township goes through an agreement of sale, a township resale inspection that produces a certificate of use and occupancy, settlement and a recorded deed. The township sits entirely in Northampton County, so the county recorder of deeds and assessment office are the same for every parcel. The township office at 4225 Easton Avenue handles the resale paperwork through its Community Development Department.

The neighboring City of Bethlehem is a separate government with separate sale rules. This page covers only the township, even if your mailing address says Bethlehem.

The township at a glance

Bethlehem Township is a suburban municipality of 14.43 square miles of land northeast of the city, with an estimated 26,769 people in July 2025, up from 23,730 in 2010 and 25,868 in 2020. Its villages include Brodhead, Butztown, Farmersville, Middletown, Prospect Park and Wagnerville. Students in grades nine to twelve attend Freedom High School inside the township. Buyers reach the Lehigh Valley mainly by US 22, PA 33 and PA 191, and the average commute is 26.1 minutes.

The township resale inspection

This is a Certificate of Use and Occupancy inspection that the Code Enforcement Officer performs for the resale of residential property and whenever a rental changes tenants. The application is in the township's Forms and Documents list under the Property Resale/Lease Inspection Program.

  • The form asks for the premises address, the reason (residential resale or change of tenant) and the type of building, such as single-family dwelling, townhouse or condo.
  • It records the settlement date and whether the agreement of sale is attached.
  • It names a contact for scheduling: seller, buyer, or the agent or attorney.
  • The owner signs permission for the inspection.

The inspection checks general compliance with the township's property maintenance, building and zoning rules under Ordinance Nos. 6-78 and 06-23. It is not a home inspection, the electrical portion looks only at GFCI protection, and the certificate carries no township liability for the condition of the house. Call the Code Enforcement Officer at (610) 814-6467 with questions.

Submitting the application

File the application once you have an agreement of sale and a settlement date, and attach the agreement if you can. Name one person for the inspector to contact so the visit is not delayed by phone tag. Whoever is named, the owner's signed permission has to be on the form.

Walk the house first. Since electrical review is limited to GFCI protection, the cheapest fix before the inspector arrives is to check the outlets near water. Items that fall under property maintenance, building or zoning rules are easier to repair before the visit than after a buyer has read the report.

Permits for past work

Zoning permits cover small outdoor projects, while construction permits cover structural, mechanical and interior work. The township says its lists are not all-inclusive, and it enforces the Pennsylvania Uniform Construction Code and the 2018 International Codes. Call the Permit Department at (610) 814-6435 if you are unsure.

  • Zoning permit only: detached garages and sheds under 1,000 square feet, decks under 30 inches above grade, patios, fences, driveway expansions and retaining walls of 48 inches or less.
  • Construction permit: structural changes, plumbing, electrical, HVAC and replacement water heaters, replacement windows, decks 30 inches or higher, pools, hot tubs, finished basements, living space conversions and patio roofs.

Finished basements and replacement water heaters are on the permit list, and both are common in older houses. If a previous owner did that work, ask the Community Development Department whether the permit was closed out before the resale inspector arrives.

Checking zoning and parcel facts

The township's Interactive Mapping System shows parcel number, lot dimensions and zoning for any address. Tax values, sales data and ownership records come from Northampton County, whose public records site is ncpub.org. The land use code on that site is a tax code, not the township's zoning.

Zoning matters at resale because the township sorts every land use into permitted by right, special exception or conditional use. A use that predates the ordinance may be grandfathered as nonconforming, and variances go to the Zoning Hearing Board. Boundary and survey questions go to the Northampton County Recorder of Deeds.

Selling a vacant or foreclosure property

The township requires vacant properties and properties in foreclosure to be registered, and it administers the program through Hera Property Registry. Owners, mortgagees and trustees register online and pay a registration fee.

If you inherited an empty house or fell behind on a mortgage, register it first and then deal with the resale inspection. Most code enforcement actions start with a concern raised by a resident or owner, and the township does not accept anonymous complaints.

Open permits, taxes and appeals

Open permits are the usual snag. After a complete building permit application, the township has fifteen business days to respond, and the work needs a Certificate of Occupancy or Compliance after final inspections. If past work was done without a permit, ask the Community Development Department how to close it out before you list.

Pennsylvania charges a 1 percent realty transfer tax on the value transferred, with seller and buyer jointly liable, and the county recorder of deeds collects it along with any local share. Ask the Northampton County Recorder of Deeds for the combined rate on your deed. For assessment appeals and the annual filing date, call the Northampton County Assessment Division, since that office sets the deadline.

From agreement to settlement

  1. Sign the agreement of sale and set the settlement date.
  2. Submit the Property Resale/Lease Inspection application with the signed owner permission.
  3. Let the Code Enforcement Officer inspect, and repair anything on the list tied to property maintenance, building or zoning rules.
  4. Close out any open permits with Community Development.
  5. Collect the Certificate of Use and Occupancy for the buyer.
  6. Ask the Recorder of Deeds for the transfer tax total, then settle and record the deed.

Keep copies of every permit and inspection record. The next owner, a lender or a title company may ask for them.

Choosing how to sell

You can list with an agent, sell on your own or take a cash offer. Each route still needs the township inspection and a certificate for the buyer. A cash buyer who accepts the house as is will usually still want the certificate in hand at settlement, so schedule the inspection around the closing date you agree on.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a township inspection to sell in Bethlehem Township?

Yes. The Code Enforcement Officer performs required inspections for the resale of residential property, and the buyer receives a Certificate of Use and Occupancy. Submit the Property Resale/Lease Inspection application once you have an agreement of sale and a settlement date.

Is the Bethlehem Township inspection the same as a home inspection?

No. Its purpose is general compliance with property maintenance, building and zoning rules. Electrical review covers only GFCI items, and the township takes no responsibility for the home's condition.

Does the City of Bethlehem sale inspection apply to my township house?

No. The city's rule covers property inside city limits. A house in Bethlehem Township uses the township's resale program, even though the mailing address says Bethlehem.

Which county records a Bethlehem Township deed?

Northampton County. The Recorder of Deeds there records the deed and collects the Pennsylvania transfer tax with any local share.

What if my Bethlehem Township house is vacant?

Register it. The township runs a vacant and foreclosure property registry through Hera Property Registry, and owners, mortgagees and trustees must register online and pay the fee.

Moon Township at a glance

Moon Township sits on the south bank of the Ohio River in western Allegheny County. The 2020 census counted 27,261 residents, and the July 2025 estimate is 26,756, a slip of 1.8 percent after 12.7 percent growth in the 2010s. The ZIP code is 15108. Workers spend about 28.2 minutes getting to their jobs on average.

A separate Moon Township exists in Beaver County, so confirm Allegheny County when you search property records. Crescent Township and Coraopolis lie to the north, Findlay and North Fayette townships to the west and south, and Robinson Township to the east. The Moon Area School District serves the township, and Crescent Township sits in that district too, which helps when you compare nearby addresses.

What shapes the market here

Pittsburgh International Airport opened in Moon in 1951, with Parkway West, I-376 and I-79 exits nearby. The passenger terminal moved to neighboring Findlay Township in 1991, but a large share of the runways and the cargo area remain inside the township. Robert Morris University has its main campus here, and University Boulevard is the business corridor. The 911th Airlift Wing, the 171st Air Refueling Wing and the National Weather Service forecast office are also based in the township.

Houses close to University Boulevard or the airport face different noise and traffic than those on quiet interior streets, and buyers will ask which kind yours is.

Getting a hillside house ready

Moon's winters hover around the freezing line and moisture arrives in every season, with about 41.80 inches of precipitation a year. A hillside lot has to shed that water, and buyers and inspectors look for signs of trouble. Before you list, check:

  • Roof condition and gutters, since water has to move off a hillside lot
  • Basement dampness and sump pump history
  • Retaining walls, steps and driveway surfaces that heave in winter
  • Furnace age and the efficiency of the heating system

Receipts for roof or drainage work give you something concrete to show.

Rental inspections

Moon requires a rental inspection before each change of occupants. The township's rental packet asks for an inspection request form, an affidavit, an inspection agreement and a rental registration, with a $20 fee per unit. The Fire Marshal's office then schedules the appointment, and owners must report the names of all occupants within 30 days of move-in. An investor buying to rent would go through the same steps.

If you are selling a house with a tenant, a buyer who keeps that tenant should check that the paperwork is on file.

The Mooncrest Historic District

Mooncrest was built in 1943 as housing for defense workers, and its homes were sold to private investors in the mid-1950s. A property there needs a Certificate of Appropriateness before the township will issue a building permit. The township's Mooncrest Historic Overlay Advisory Committee advises the Board of Supervisors on those certificates.

Building permits are required for alterations, additions, porch roofs and sheds, and rules cover windows and doors along building fronts, dryer vents, coal chutes and roofing materials. Call the township office at 412-262-1700 to ask whether an address falls inside the district, and hand a buyer the permit and inspection records.

Transfer tax and appeals

Moon charges one-half percent for the township and one-half percent for the Moon Area School District. With the state's 1 percent, a sale carries 2 percent in transfer tax. You pay it at recording by its own check, apart from recording fees. Family transfers can be exempt, and deeds that show no price need a Statement of Value.

An owner who disputes an assessment can go to the county's BPAAR board, whose hearings are held by phone. Gather recent sales of similar Moon houses and photos of any condition problems before the hearing, and ask the county for the current filing window. A lower assessment lowers your bill while you hold the house, though it does not change what a buyer will pay.

Ways to sell quickly

Speed comes down to inspection readiness and whether the buyer needs a lender. Moon owners usually compare three routes:

  • List on the open market and wait for a buyer who will live there, the route that can bring the top price for a house in good shape.
  • Sell as is to a cash buyer, a fit for estates, tenant-occupied houses and properties needing repairs.
  • Sell to a neighbor, a relative or an investor you already know.

A house in the Mooncrest district or with a rental history should come with its permits and inspection records, since buyers will ask.

What happens after you accept an offer

With a cash buyer the path is short. You agree on a price and a closing date, the title company searches the deed for liens, and you gather your mortgage payoff if you owe one. No lender appraisal or underwriting stands between signing and closing. At the table you sign the deed, the 2 percent transfer tax is paid with its own check, and the title company sends you whatever remains after payoffs.

With a listing, the same steps follow a buyer's loan approval and appraisal, which adds weeks and gives a buyer room to renegotiate if the house falls short. If your Moon house is a rental, finish the inspection and registration before the sale so the buyer inherits clean paperwork.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Paperwork to line up before you list

Start with the basics a title company will ask for: the deed, your mortgage lender's name and any lien or tax notice. Then make a short list of anything done to the house that needed a permit, such as an addition, porch roof or shed, and find the paperwork. In the Mooncrest district, add the Certificate of Appropriateness for exterior work.

Next, decide how you want to be paid and how fast. Estates and tenant-occupied houses often suit a cash buyer, while a house in good shape may earn more on the open market. Whichever you pick, ask the township office at 412-262-1700 about open inspections or registrations so nothing surprises you after you accept an offer.

Is Moon Township the same as Moon, Pennsylvania?

Yes. Moon Township is in Allegheny County and is the place most people mean. A separate Moon Township exists in Beaver County, so confirm the county when you search property records.

What is the transfer tax on a house sale in Moon Township?

Two percent altogether: 1 percent to the state, one-half percent to Moon Township and one-half percent to the Moon Area School District.

Do I need a rental inspection to sell a Moon house with a tenant?

Moon inspects a rental before each new occupant, charging $20 a unit, and wants a rental registration within 30 days of move-in. A buyer keeping the tenant should check that the paperwork is on file.

What is the Mooncrest Historic District?

It is a historic overlay area built in 1943 as defense worker housing. A Certificate of Appropriateness must come before any building permit there, with an advisory committee making recommendations to the supervisors.

Which school district serves Moon Township?

The Moon Area School District. Crescent Township also sits in that district, which helps when comparing nearby addresses.

What a Lebanon seller needs to know first

Lebanon packs about 26,479 people into 4.17 square miles of older homes, many of them rented, with a typical owner's home valued at $156,500. At that price level, repairs, taxes and closing costs take a large share of any sale.

The city is Lebanon County's seat, 26 miles east of Harrisburg and 88 miles northwest of Philadelphia. Most homes here are rented, so landlords make up a big part of both the selling and the buying side. A seller of a tenant-occupied property should expect investors to ask for the rent roll, the rental license and the last inspection results. With rent near $992 against a $156,500 home value, the rental market is a major buyer of Lebanon houses.

A Lebanon owner can use a broker, post the sign personally or take a cash bid for the house. In every case the deed is filed at the courthouse on South 8th Street, and the county treasurer keeps the tax payment records.

City of Lebanon rental license rules

Every dwelling unit or rooming unit offered for rent in the city must have a rental license, and each parcel with rental units needs its own application. A buyer inherits the license history, so it pays to have your file in order.

  • A $25 penalty is added every 60 days a fee stays unpaid after billing.
  • Renewal is delayed or denied if money is owed to the city or code violations are open.
  • The owner must keep a contract with a trash hauler on file, and a property manager must be within 20 miles of the city limit.
  • Grass and weeds cannot exceed 12 inches, snow and ice must come off sidewalks within 24 hours after a snowfall ends, and inoperable or unlicensed vehicles cannot sit on a premises more than 5 days.
  • Smoke alarms and carbon monoxide detectors are required, and a license revoked for unsafe conditions costs $100 to reinstate.

Questions go to the city's code enforcement office at 717-639-2800, option 2, at 735 Cumberland Street. For a rental, put copies of the current license and any violation notice in your file before you answer a buyer.

Permits and zoning

The city's Building and Zoning Division, part of Public Works, runs permits and zoning. A zoning permit is required for building or altering a structure, adding an addition, demolishing or moving one, and putting up fences, decks, sheds and garages. It is also required for a change of use, a swimming pool or hot tub deeper than 18 inches, and a sign.

Construction inspections are done by outside code inspection firms under contract, and the city asks for at least 24 hours' notice. A deck or shed that an earlier owner added without a permit is something an inspector may catch. Settle that question before listing, or ask the zoning office what the city would require.

The city zoning ordinance defines 10 districts. A Zoning Hearing Board hears variance and special exception requests.

How do county taxes and the Tax Claim Bureau affect a sale?

The Lebanon County Treasurer collects the county real estate tax, the city tax and now the Lebanon City School District bill, so one office can tell you whether anything is owed on a city parcel. The Tax Claim Bureau charges $15 per parcel for a tax certification, and a mailed request must include a stamped return envelope.

Delinquent taxes pass to the Tax Claim Bureau each January. The owner is sent a certified letter showing the balance, interest and costs, along with the date to pay in order to avoid a sale. About 17 months after that first notice the bureau mails a notice of sale. Buyers at the upset sale take the property subject to judgments, liens and mortgages, and bidders must pre-register for a $25 fee.

If you are behind on taxes, pay or arrange the balance before closing. Once a property is on the sale list, the process follows a fixed bureau and court calendar.

Assessment appeals and recording the deed

Assessment appeals are due each September 1 by 4:30 at the Board of Assessment Revision. A notice that arrives late waits for the following year. The filing fee for a residential property of one to four units is $50 and is not refunded. You or an authorized representative must attend the hearing, and the board can raise, lower or keep the assessment.

Filings go to the Assessment Office at 400 South 8th Street, Room 118. Owners can also view their records free on DataScout, using the control number and web password printed on the tax bill.

The Recorder of Deeds is in Room 107 of the same courthouse, open on weekdays, and accepts cash or check only. Most documents come back the following business day, and the Assessment Office must certify the parcel identifier before a deed records. The state transfer tax is 1 percent, and the recorder's office adds any local share when it collects.

Steps for a Lebanon sale, start to finish

The order below keeps a sale from stalling at the courthouse.

  1. Call the treasurer's office to find out whether any county, city or school tax is owed on the parcel.
  2. If you rent the house out, gather the current rental license, any violation notice and the last inspection results.
  3. Ask the zoning office about any deck, shed, fence or addition built without a permit.
  4. Request a $15 tax certification from the Tax Claim Bureau if the title company asks for one, and include a stamped return envelope with a mailed request.
  5. Bring the deed to Room 107 of the courthouse on South 8th Street with cash or a check, after the Assessment Office certifies the parcel identifier.

A cash buyer skips the lender appraisal, but every step above still applies. Ask who handles each one before you sign.

Which Lebanon houses suit a cash offer?

A cash sale suits a house with heavy repairs, a rental carrying open code items, a vacant building or an estate. It is also useful when tax delinquency puts the house on a calendar you cannot move.

Price comparison matters here because the median value is modest. Add up the commission, repairs, transfer tax and months of ownership on a listing, and compare that net with a cash figure. To ask for an offer on a Lebanon house in its present state, contact Cash Home Buyers.

Frequently asked questions

Does Lebanon require a rental license?

Yes. Every dwelling unit or rooming unit offered for rent in the City of Lebanon must have a license, with a separate application for each parcel that has rental units.

When are Lebanon County assessment appeals due?

September 1 each year, filed with the Board of Assessment Revision at the Assessment Office on South 8th Street. A residential appeal costs $50.

How long can Lebanon County delinquent taxes sit before a sale?

Unpaid taxes move to the Tax Claim Bureau every January, and owners have until the last working day of the next June. A notice of sale follows about 17 months after the first notice.

Where is a Lebanon deed recorded?

At the Lebanon County Recorder of Deeds, Room 107 of the courthouse at 400 South 8th Street. The office takes cash or check and can also accept electronic recording.

Which school district serves the City of Lebanon?

The Lebanon School District, which covers the city and West Lebanon Township. The county treasurer now collects its tax bill for city parcels.

What do I need to do to sell a house in Warrington, PA?

In Warrington Township the seller must obtain an Occupancy Certificate before settlement, which means applying at least 30 days ahead, paying $140 per residential unit and passing an inspection. The township puts this duty on the seller or landlord, and a real estate agent or other representative may file on the seller's behalf. After that, the sale follows the usual Pennsylvania disclosure, tax and deed-recording sequence.

Warrington is a Bucks County township of 13.7 square miles with an estimated 26,261 residents. Its motto calls it the Gateway to Historic Bucks County, and the township was founded in October 1734 and named for Warrington, England. Its population grew from 2,336 in 1950 to 25,639 in 2020, so a large share of its houses date from the 1980s through the 2000s, the years when the count rose from 10,704 to 23,418.

How does the Warrington occupancy certificate work?

The certificate is a township inspection that confirms a home meets safety and property maintenance requirements before it changes hands. The Permits Office takes applications online or by mail or drop-off at the township building, and the applicant is responsible for making sure the fee is paid and the inspection is scheduled.

The township's program page sets out these terms:

  • Apply at least 30 days before settlement so there is time to fix problems the inspection finds.
  • The residential fee is $140 per unit. Confirm commercial fees before you submit.
  • A certificate is valid for 60 days from the date it is issued, so do not schedule the inspection months before closing.
  • Homes with fire sprinkler systems need a separate inspection and certification by a registered third-party agency, and that sprinkler certification is valid for six months.
  • The township publishes a residential inspection checklist, so you can walk the house before the inspector does.

If a sale falls through and the certificate expires, you would have to apply again for the next buyer. Build that risk into your timeline if your buyer needs financing.

What is the Warrington area like for buyers?

Warrington is a suburb of winding creeks and commuter roads, and buyers compare it on schools, drive time and storm drainage. Natural features include the Little Neshaminy Creek, Mill Creek, Park Creek, Fretz Valley, Griers Hill and Prospect Hill. Villages within the township are Warrington, Neshaminy, Tradesville, Eureka, Frog Hollow and Palomino Farms.

Public schools are part of the Central Bucks School District: Barclay, Mill Creek and Titus elementary schools, Tamanend Middle School and Central Bucks High School South. Neighbors include New Britain, Doylestown, Warwick, Warminster, Horsham and Montgomery townships.

  • US 202 runs through the western part of the township as a parkway, and PA 611 (Easton Road) crosses the eastern side.
  • PA 152 (Limekiln Pike), PA 132 (Street Road), Lower State Road and County Line Road connect the neighborhoods.
  • The township maintains 83.51 of its 102.37 miles of public roads.
  • SEPTA City Bus Route 55 follows PA 611, and the DART South bus runs weekdays along the same corridor to Doylestown.

Warrington has also had a local fight over land use. In 2010 a pharmaceutical company proposed the largest warehouse facility in Pennsylvania near residential neighborhoods in the township, residents objected loudly, and the company chose a site in Northeast Philadelphia instead. Buyers who care about open land and traffic remember that history, and the township's zoning rules decide what can be built near your street. If a buyer asks about nearby development, point them to the township's Planning and Zoning staff, who work with the Bucks County Planning Commission on zoning updates, and keep a copy of your own survey and any permit records for the closing file.

The humid continental climate brings about 47 inches of precipitation a year, with July the wettest month and seasonal snowfall of 30 to 36 inches. Wet basements and roof wear are therefore the questions inspectors ask most.

What taxes and disclosures apply when I sell in Warrington?

Bucks County's recorder says the transfer tax on a Pennsylvania sale is 2 percent, 1 percent to the state and 1 percent to the municipality and school district, paid when the deed is recorded. The recorder no longer accepts personal checks for it; cash in the office, a cashier's check, a money order or a credit card will do. Sellers and buyers usually divide the tax by agreement, and a family transfer may be exempt with a Statement of Value form where the deed does not state the exemption.

The disclosure rule is in 68 Pa.C.S. Section 7303. Before the agreement of sale is signed, you deliver a signed property disclosure statement covering the roof, basement, drainage, plumbing, wiring and similar items. Act 74 of 2026 adds a flood-insurance notice that sellers provide once the Insurance Department posts its flood information, which matters in a township with several creeks.

For assessment, the Bucks Board of Assessment Appeals set August 3, 2026 as the 2026 annual appeal deadline, and that date has passed. Annual appeal changes apply to the following tax year. The homestead and farmstead exclusion filing deadline is March 1 for the tax year that starts July 1. A new owner must send contact information to the Board within 30 days of buying, so remind your buyer.

Should I fix the house, list it or sell as-is in Warrington?

Warrington's high median values reward a well-presented house, but the 30-day occupancy lead time and a sprinkler certification, if you have one, can slow a quick listing. A cash buyer who accepts the house as-is still has to see the township certificate handled before settlement, so ask how that works before you agree to a date.

  • Apply for the occupancy certificate as soon as you have a contract, not at the closing table.
  • Walk the township checklist yourself and fix cheap items first.
  • Compare a listing net sheet with a cash offer that states who pays for repairs the inspector requires.

The township charges $140 per unit for residential properties. Commercial fees differ, and the township asks you to confirm the amount before submitting.

How long does a Warrington occupancy certificate last?

It is valid for 60 days from the date it is issued. If settlement slips past that window, you will need a new certificate.

Who applies for the certificate when a house is sold?

The seller or landlord is responsible, and an agent or authorized representative can file for the seller. The certificate has to be in hand before settlement.

Owners in Warrington report a midpoint value of $553,100 for 2020 to 2024, the highest of the four townships in the same QuickFacts table.

Yes. Houses with fire sprinklers need a separate inspection and certification by a registered third-party agency before the occupancy certificate can be issued, and the sprinkler certification lasts six months. The township posts a list of registered agencies.

For questions on the inspection, call the Community Development Department at 610-635-3512. The office takes calls on weekdays and returns voicemail left after hours the next business day.

Taxes and closing costs

The realty transfer tax on a Lower Providence sale is 2 percent in total: 1 percent to the Commonwealth and 1 percent local. The local share is divided evenly, one half of a percent to the township and one half to the Methacton School District. The state holds buyer and seller liable together, and most contracts divide the cost between them.

A few recurring tax facts matter at the closing table:

  • The township's 2026 real estate levies are 2.1298 mills for the general fund, 0.3727 for the library, 0.7485 for debt service, 0.7614 for emergency services and 0.241 for parks, which together equal 4.2534 mills. County and Methacton school taxes are billed in addition.
  • Tax bills go out on March 1. Payment before April 30 earns a 2 percent discount, and a 10 percent penalty applies after July 1.
  • When your lender pays taxes out of escrow, send each bill along to the lender.

Deeds between certain relatives and property that passes by inheritance can be exempt from the state tax. Before signing, ask the Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds what paperwork proves the exemption.

Can I appeal my Montgomery County assessment before I sell?

Yes. Annual appeals go to the Montgomery County Board of Assessment Appeals, which accepts them through August 1 by postmark. It will not take a fax or an email.

For a single-family house the processing fee is $50, payable to the county treasurer, and you send three copies of your evidence, for example an appraisal, comparable sales or photographs. All appeals must be heard by October 31, and the board grants rescheduling only in extraordinary circumstances. A homestead or farmstead appeal costs nothing. The board's office phone is 610-278-3761.

A lower assessment helps the next owner more than the seller, but a documented appeal can still support a price discussion with a buyer.

Selling when you are behind on property taxes

Township, school and county taxes that go unpaid are handed to the Montgomery County Tax Claim Bureau. If taxes from two years back are still owed, the Bureau can sell the parcel. Its upset sales are held each September and December. Whoever buys at an upset sale inherits every lien on the property, whereas a judicial sale delivers it free and clear.

Settle a delinquency before it reaches that stage. Selling before the bureau acts lets the closing pay the arrears from proceeds. Call the bureau at the Norristown office to confirm the payoff figure before you accept an offer.

Steps from decision to closing

Begin at the township. Submit the resale certificate application through the online permit portal and pay the filing fee. Fix anything the inspector flags, because a failed visit means a follow-up, and the third re-inspection onward costs extra. Request the tax certification from the elected tax collector, and ask the sewer authority and the trash hauler for their account certifications.

Once an offer is accepted, the title company handles the numbers. It splits the tax bill by days of ownership, totals any payoff and lists both transfer tax shares on the settlement statement. Tell your escrow lender about the sale so that account closes cleanly. Afterward the deed is recorded at the Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds. Hold on to every certificate, since the buyer's lender can ask to see them.

Cash offer or listing: how to choose

Three things decide it: how fast you must move, what repairs the house needs and how much certainty you want. A listing reaches more buyers, but it brings showings, repair requests after the buyer's inspection and loan contingencies. Cash buyers rarely have a lender to please, so your preferred closing date usually works.

  • Find out which party books and pays for the township resale inspection, and write it into the contract.
  • Weigh each offer by what you keep after the 2 percent transfer tax, any payoff and your share of the certification costs.
  • Confirm that the buyer will accept the house with its current sewer, trash and tax accounts settled at closing.

Start the township certificates the day you decide to sell, since they are the one piece of the sale fully in your hands.

Frequently asked questions

Does Lower Providence Township require an inspection when I sell?

Yes. A residential sale needs a resale use and occupancy certificate. It costs $100, with an initial inspection and one follow-up visit included, and you apply online through the township permit portal.

How much is the transfer tax on a Lower Providence home sale?

It totals 2 percent of the value transferred. Pennsylvania takes 1 percent, and the other 1 percent stays local, divided between the township and the Methacton School District. The county recorder collects when the deed is filed.

Which school district serves Lower Providence?

Methacton School District. Arrowhead, Eagleville and Woodland elementary schools serve parts of the township, and Methacton High School is in neighboring Worcester Township.

When are Lower Providence property tax bills due?

Bills are mailed March 1. Paying before April 30 earns a 2 percent discount, and a 10 percent penalty applies to payments made after July 1.

When is the Montgomery County assessment appeal deadline?

August 1 every year. Your form, three copies of supporting papers and a $50 check for a single-family home all need a postmark or delivery by that day.

Steps to sell a house in Plum Borough

Plum requires a Residential Occupancy Permit whenever the occupancy of a home changes, which includes a sale. The owner files a Residential Occupancy Transfer Application with the Community Development office, pays $100 and then schedules an inspection. Once the house passes, the borough issues the permit.

Timing is the part to plan. The application has to be signed by the owner and submitted at least five business days before the inspection date you request.   • Limit: the borough requires the permit for a change in ownership or residents, but no more than once every two years regardless of how many changes occur.

Transfer tax for a Plum seller

Selling in Plum triggers a 2% realty transfer tax. The borough gets half a percent, the Plum School District gets half a percent and the Commonwealth gets 1%. You write a separate check for it when Allegheny County records the deed, apart from the recording fees.

Your sales agreement settles who pays. Close relatives transferring a house may only have to add a sentence to the deed naming the relationship; other exemptions go through the state's Statement of Value.

Plum Borough at a glance

Northeast of Pittsburgh, with the Allegheny River along its northern side, Plum borders Monroeville, Penn Hills, Oakmont and, across the river, Cheswick, Springdale and Lower Burrell. It covers 28.57 square miles of land, which makes it the state's second-largest borough by area. Postal mail may carry a Pittsburgh address, even though the borough is outside the city limits.

The estimate for July 2025 is 26,225 residents, about 3.4% below the 2020 base of 27,147. The 2020 census counted 11,869 housing units, 4.7% of them vacant.

Zoning and permits

Unpermitted work tends to surface when a buyer or inspector looks around. Zoning certificates cover front yard fences, sheds, detached garages, carports, gazebos and similar structures under 200 square feet.

If you added a deck or shed yourself, ask Community Development whether a permit or certificate is on file before the inspection. Fixing a paperwork gap before the occupancy visit is simpler than doing it after a buyer raises the question. The department also administers subdivision, conditional use and variance requests, which matter if the lot is large enough to split.

Plum parcels carry values from the Allegheny County Office of Property Assessments, set to a 2012 base year, so treat them as something other than today's market price. Ask the county treasurer and the Plum tax collectors for a paid-to-date statement before closing. Any balance owed gets paid from the sale proceeds, and a title search will show open amounts. The statement covers the roof, basement, structure, plumbing, electrical systems, heating and cooling, water and sewage service, land and drainage, hazardous substances and title issues. It also asks about the condition and location of storm water facilities and whether the owner or someone else maintains them.

The seller doesn't need to carry out special testing but may not say anything known to be false or leave out a known material defect. Delivery can be in person, by first class mail, by certified mail or by fax. A disclosure can be amended in writing before the agreement is signed.

  • Condominium sellers disclose only about their own unit.

Choose the route first, then line up the permit. A listing reaches the most buyers, a sale by owner saves the commission, and a cash sale tends to shorten the schedule.   • Check the borough's inspector checklist and fix small items beforehand.

  • Ask the settlement agent for the 2% transfer tax figure and the payoff before you accept terms.

What happens on closing day

With the permit issued, you sign the deed at the table. Recording follows, the transfer tax goes in on its own check, and the title company settles your loan and any open tax before handing you what is left. Paying cash removes the lender's appraisal and approval, so the schedule depends chiefly on the inspection and the title search.

A house sold within the past two years needs a call to Community Development about the permit limit, so the application doesn't stall. For a rental, put the tenant's move-out date in writing so the inspector walks an empty house. Before you set a date, collect the deed, your lender's payoff figure and any permit paperwork for decks, porches or sheds, and keep the $100 check ready so the application can go in the same day you decide to sell.

Does Plum Borough require an occupancy permit to sell a house?

Yes. A Residential Occupancy Permit is required when the occupancy of a home changes. The owner files the application with a $100 fee, an inspector schedules a visit, and a passing inspection gets the permit.

How far ahead must I apply for the Plum occupancy inspection?

Apply at least five business days before the inspection date you want. The owner signs the application, and the check is payable to the Borough of Plum. An inspector then contacts you to set the day and time.

How much is the transfer tax in Plum Borough?

It is 2% in total: 0.5% to the borough, 0.5% to the Plum School District and 1% to the state. Allegheny County collects it when the deed is recorded.

Can Plum require a new occupancy permit every time ownership changes?

Not more than once every two years. The borough caps the permit at one every two years regardless of how many changes happen. Ask Community Development how that rule applies if the home changed hands recently.

When can I appeal my Allegheny County assessment?

The annual window opens July 1 and closes in early September. Watch the county's real estate portal for the exact dates if you think your value is off.

Work you did on the house is a separate question. Collect your permit history before listing and gather receipts for projects that needed permits. The Codes and Permits office is at 1001 Stump Road, open weekdays 8:30 to 4:30.

Assessments, homestead and appeals

The county Board of Assessment Appeals sets the values that drive your county, township and school bills. If you think yours is too high, the appeal deadline is August 1, a year before the tax year you are contesting, and exemption applications are due the same day. Hearings wrap up by October 31, and decisions go to owners and taxing districts by November 15.

The homestead exclusion lowers the taxable value of the home you live in. File by March 1 and it applies to school taxes from the following July 1. File by December 15 and it applies to municipal taxes, in municipalities that take part, from the following January 1. Selling wipes the exclusion off the parcel on its own, so you have nothing to file and the new owner starts a fresh application. If the county denies a claim, you have 40 days to appeal.

Unpaid taxes put a parcel at risk of the county's upset sale, which runs each September and December for properties still delinquent from two years back.   • Sell to an owner-occupant and clear the taxes at settlement.

Paying cash removes the lender appraisal, the loan approval and the financing contingency. Those are where financed deals most often get delayed or renegotiated. An as-is buyer accepts the condition of the house, but unpaid taxes and liens still get settled at the table. Ask for the closing date in writing, and ask who covers recording costs.

Getting the house and paperwork ready

Gather three things first: your deed, your newest tax bill and whatever permit records the Codes and Permits office holds for the property. Then walk the house and jot down what you know about the roof, basement, plumbing, heating, wiring and drainage. That list turns into your disclosure statement, and a dated receipt for any repair backs it up.

Unpaid years? Phone the tax claim bureau. Have a mortgage? Request a payoff figure from the lender. If your deed will claim an exemption, ask for the Statement of Value form now so it is not the last thing holding up settlement.

You then pick a route. An open-market listing can reach the highest price but brings showings and a buyer's lender. A cash buyer offers a firmer closing date and fewer strangers walking through. Selling fast in Exeter Township

Three routes are open to an Exeter owner: an agent, a sale by owner, or a cash buyer who purchases as-is. The township borders Reading in Berks County. A cash offer makes the most sense if the house needs repairs or you have a deadline.

Exeter is a second class township with 25,466 residents at the 2020 Census and an estimated 26,069 in July 2025. Only Reading and Spring Township are bigger in Berks County. Owner-occupied homes make up 87.1 percent of the total, so few houses are rentals. The typical owned home is valued at $281,800 and median household income is $100,083. About 93.6 percent of residents had not moved in the past year. Monthly cost is typically $1,919 with a mortgage, and rent is typically $1,632.

Names such as Reiffton, Jacksonwald, Stonersville, Lorane, Neversink, Limekiln, Baumstown and Stonetown show up in addresses, yet none is its own municipality. The township issues your zoning and your permits.

Zoning, historic and lodging rules

Read the zoning code, the historic resource rules and the short-term lodging provisions before you sign anything. The code is online. The Building, Zoning and Engineering department posts forms for building, plumbing, zoning and sign permits, along with a complaint form and a flood plains map.

  • Historic resources: the zoning code sorts historic properties into Classes I to IV and routes changes to them through the Planning Commission and the Board of Supervisors. Class I status requires the owner's written consent and binds heirs and later owners. After a historic resource is demolished through neglect, the township may withhold building and occupancy permits for a year.
  • Short-term lodging: a license from the Zoning Officer lets a property serve as short-term lodging, capped at 90 days per calendar year. Anyone who wants nightly rentals must apply.
  • Floodplain: the township document center holds a flood plains map. Look up your parcel on it.

Tell buyers early if the house is a listed historic resource or lies in a mapped flood area. The Exeter Friends Meeting House, the Mordecai Lincoln House, Boonecroft, Levan Farm, Mill Tract Farm, Snyder Mill and the John Bishop House are on the National Register, and the Daniel Boone Homestead is in the township, so a house nearby may prompt questions.

Berks County assessments and appeals

Berks County last reassessed countywide for the 1994 tax year, which means assessments may be far from today's sale prices. Assessment records are kept at 400 E. Wyomissing Avenue in Mohnton, though that office neither bills nor collects. Your municipal tax collector knows what you owe.

A reduction requires proof that the assessment exceeds current market value, because the law presumes it correct. High taxes or trouble paying do not count. School districts and municipalities can appeal too, often to raise a value.

No age-based or special form freezes or removes property taxes for seniors. Homestead and farmstead exclusions do exist, and the school district supplies the forms.

Recording a deed in Berks County

Recording a document that conveys real estate in Berks County starts at $88. The Recorder of Deeds is on the third floor of the Berks County Services Center, 633 Court Street, Reading. Personal checks are not accepted for transfer tax, and a Statement of Value counts as one extra page when fees are added up.

The state's rate is 1 percent of value, and both parties on the deed are liable. The recorder forwards the state portion to the Department of Revenue and passes any local portion to the municipality or school district. Some family transfers and property that passes by will or intestacy are exempt. For the total at your sale price, phone the Recorder of Deeds.

Homestead exclusions and tax bills

Homestead and farmstead exclusions exist in Berks County, and the school district supplies the forms. If you claimed one, tell your buyer that a new owner must apply for their own. The Assessment Office holds the records but does not send a bill, so for what you owe, call the municipal tax collector. Ask for the balance in writing so the title company can pay it at settlement.

An annual appeal is a long shot for most sellers, because the law presumes the assessment is correct and you carry the burden of proof. If you already filed and the house sells, tell the buyer, since the result affects the bill they inherit.

Pennsylvania seller disclosure

Section 7308 of 68 Pa.C.S. does not oblige a seller to inspect the property. It does bar the seller from stating something known to be false or omitting a known material defect. Section 7306 lets a seller answer items outside their knowledge using the best information at hand. Owners choose cash to avoid showings, repair lists and a long wait. Collect the deed, recent tax bills, permits, warranty papers and any lease. Look up your parcel on the township's flood plains map. If the house is near one of the listed historic sites, ask the Building, Zoning and Engineering department whether any historic resource rule touches your lot. These small steps keep a deal from stalling after you have already agreed on a price.

From signed offer to closing

Once an offer is accepted, the title company researches the deed history and looks for unpaid taxes or liens. Get any balance from the municipal tax collector, and ask your lender for a payoff if a mortgage is open. Cash buyers have no lender timetable, so the closing date turns on title work and your move.

At closing you sign the deed and settlement papers, and the deed goes to the Berks County Recorder of Deeds. For a rental, bring the lease. For a house that belonged to a relative who has died, bring the papers showing who may sign for the estate.

Is Exeter Township part of Reading?

No. Exeter Township is its own municipality in Berks County and borders St. Lawrence borough and Birdsboro. Check your tax bill, since the township, not the city, sets your zoning.

Can I contest my Exeter assessment while the house is listed?

Yes, in the June 15 to August 1 annual window or within 40 days of a change notice. The proof must show the assessment is above market value.

What school district covers Exeter Township?

Exeter Township School District, which also takes in the borough of St. Lawrence. Its buildings are Lorane, Owatin Creek and Jacksonwald elementary schools, Reiffton Elementary School, Exeter Junior High and Exeter Township Senior High.

Can an Exeter house be used for short-term rentals?

Selling in Upper Moreland follows the usual Pennsylvania path, with one local advantage: the township's code enforcement department requires no use and occupancy certificate and no inspection when a residential or commercial property is resold. You sign an agreement of sale, deliver your disclosure statement first, pay transfer tax at recording and settle through a title company or attorney.

The township is in Montgomery County, about 13 to 15 miles north of Center City Philadelphia, with an estimated 25,880 residents. Most of it is Willow Grove-area housing built during the postwar growth that took the population from 5,103 in 1940 to 21,032 in 1960. Those years left a stock of mid-century houses, and showings tend to bring questions about the age of the roof and the original systems.

Inspection and certificate rules

The code enforcement department requires no Use and Occupancy Certificate for the sale or resale of a residential or commercial property, and it requires no inspection on resale. Businesses moving into the township do have to file a Zoning Use Registration Permit.

Your own improvements are another story, because a buyer's inspector will look at them. Permit questions go to 117 Park Avenue, Willow Grove, or to 267-607-1032 or 267-607-1033, weekdays from 7:30 in the morning to 4:30 in the afternoon. The rules for open projects are short:

  • A fence needs a permit, with a maximum height of 6 feet in a rear yard and 4 feet in a front yard.
  • Installing a pool requires a building permit.

Did you put up a fence, deck or pool without a permit? Ask the department how to close it out before the house goes on the market.

Schools

The Upper Moreland School District runs by grade band rather than by neighborhood elementary school. Upper Moreland Primary School takes kindergarten through grade 2, the Intermediate School covers grades 3 to 5, the Middle School covers grades 6 to 8, and Upper Moreland High School serves grades 9 to 12. Taxes and paperwork

The state takes 1 percent of the property's value in realty transfer tax and local governments add a share. Together that generally reaches 2 percent, which sellers and buyers usually divide. A completed property disclosure statement, required by 68 Pa.C.S. Section 7303, has to reach the buyer before the agreement of sale is signed. The form asks about roofs, basements, termites, structural problems, plumbing, wiring and storm water facilities. Bring photo ID and your keys, and have your payoff letter confirmed a few days ahead. If a tenant or estate is involved, make sure whoever signs the deed has the authority to do so.

Getting ready to list

A short prep list saves time. Walk the house and note anything that was built or replaced during your ownership, such as a fence, a deck, a pool, a new panel or new plumbing, then check each against the permit rules above. Anything built without a permit is easiest to fix before a buyer's inspector finds it.

Next, gather the paper trail: roof and furnace receipts, recent utility bills, and your deed. Mid-century houses draw questions about original systems, and clear records let you answer them without hesitation. If the house is occupied by a tenant or sits in an estate, settle those details early so the agreement of sale can name a firm closing date.

Is a cash sale a good fit?

Cash makes the most sense if the house needs repairs you would rather not pay for, if you are settling an estate, or if speed beats squeezing out the last dollar. Mid-century houses often have tired roofs and mechanicals, and an as-is buyer ends the cycle of inspection and repair demands. Listing usually brings a higher price, along with showings and a financing window.

No. The township's code enforcement department requires no Use and Occupancy Certificate for the sale or resale of residential or commercial property, and no resale inspection. Contractor-built work still needs the permits the township requires.

Owners report a typical value of $391,600. That is a township-wide midpoint, so use recent sales close to your house to set a price.

Which county records a deed in Upper Moreland?

Montgomery County, through the Recorder of Deeds office. Your title company or attorney handles the filing, so ask them what the recorder needs with the deed, including transfer tax paperwork.

How do I find out who handles trash and sewer for my house?

The township's public works department handles trash and recycling, and the Upper Moreland-Hatboro Joint Sewer Authority provides sewage service. Buyers ask for the latest bills, so gather them before listing.

Can I sell an inherited house in Upper Moreland as-is?

Yes. The seller disclosure chapter does not cover transfers by a fiduciary handling a decedent's estate, but whoever signs still needs proper authority. Ask the estate's attorney who may sign the deed.

Selling in Derry Township and Hershey

Derry Township is the municipality that holds Hershey. It lies in southeastern Dauphin County, east of Harrisburg, and a Hershey address usually carries a Derry Township deed. Palmdale, Swatara, Hockersville, Oakmont, Waltonville and part of Stoverdale are also unincorporated communities inside its lines.

The medical center, the children's hospital, the chocolate business and visitor spending support the local economy, and that tends to keep buyers coming. Who bills property tax, and at what rates

As of January 1, 2023, the Dauphin County Treasurer's Office bills and collects real estate taxes for both the township and the Derry Township School District. The township's Tax Association Office shut that day, and occupation and local services taxes went to Keystone Collections Group.

Tax rates come from the county, the township and the school district after assessments are final, not from this office. If your assessment looks too high, ask for the appeal rules and the filing date that cover your parcel.

Rental owners should know about Act 29 of 2026, which set up a county contact registry for properties without an owner in residence. An owner, or a lender after foreclosure, must supply a name, address, phone number and email for a person who can resolve code violations. The deadline is 30 days after taking ownership and 30 days after any change. A $500 fine applies for noncompliance, and principal residences occupied by their owners are exempt.

Timeline from offer to settlement

After you sign a purchase agreement, a title company starts its file and searches the chain of ownership. It will request tax balances from the treasurer and look for anything else recorded against the property. If a defect turns up, such as an old lien or a misspelled owner name, resolving it can take longer than anything else in the sale, so raise any known title question at the start.

On settlement day you sign the deed and the closing statement. The deed is then recorded in Harrisburg. A buyer using a mortgage needs an appraisal and underwriting first, which adds weeks. A cash buyer skips both, so the schedule follows the title search and your own move-out plans. If you need extra days in the house after closing, negotiate that into the agreement before signing.

Questions to ask each buyer

Whether the buyer is an investor, a family or a company, ask the same short list. Is the offer in writing, and is it contingent on a mortgage, an inspection or the sale of another house? Who pays closing costs and the transfer tax? How long is the buyer willing to wait for you to move? Can the buyer show funds on hand?

The Dauphin County Treasurer's Office, for the township and the school district alike. Call for balances before closing.

Act 29 of 2026 asks owners of non-owner-occupied property for contact details, updated within 30 days of any change. The buyer takes on that duty at purchase.

Selling a house in Springfield Township

Springfield here means Springfield Township in Delaware County, a suburb of single-family homes southwest of Philadelphia with the 19064 ZIP code. Plenty of Pennsylvania townships share the name, so check that your buyer, your title agent and your paperwork all point to the Delaware County one. Any buyer faces the same three stops: a township resale inspection, paid-up tax bills and a deed recorded in Media.

Many Springfield houses date from the postwar building boom, and original layouts and aging mechanicals are common. Expect questions about the roof, furnace and basement at every showing.

The Springfield housing market

Population is 25,039, almost level with the 2020 count of 25,070. Owners live in 93.8 percent of homes, which is very high, and the middle owned home is valued at $414,900. Households average 2.87 people and 24.2 percent of residents are under 18, which points to family buyers who want room near the city.

With so few rentals, investor-owned houses are a small slice of the market. If you rented your house out at any point, landlords file a Business Privilege Rental Tax Return with the township. Ask the tax office which filings you need to close before settlement.

Resale inspection checklist

The township offers a Resale Inspection Appointment Request on its homepage, which tells you a sale brings the code office to your door. Call the Code Department at 610-544-1300, extension 125, and ask what the inspector will check, what it costs and how long a certificate stays valid.

The code office publishes the violations it sees most often. They make a handy walk-through list before you put a sign in the yard:

  • Grass cannot grow higher than 8 inches.
  • Plantings at an intersection can be no taller than 18 inches, and shrubs cannot block signs or signals.
  • House numbers must be 4 inches high and visible from the street.
  • Vehicles may park only on paved surfaces, never on the lawn.
  • Owners maintain the curbs and sidewalks in front of the property, and snow comes off public sidewalks within 24 hours after it stops falling.
  • Trash containers stay behind the front building line and come off the street within 12 hours of pickup.

Repair permits are filed on the township's OpenGov portal. Call the inspector with questions, and keep the paperwork for any large repair, since it is much easier to defend work that has a permit on file.

When are township and school taxes due?

Two bills arrive each year on separate calendars. If your parcel still owes money when you sell, the closing agent pays it from your proceeds.

Springfield Township and Springfield School District billing windows
BillBilling date2% discount throughFace amount10% penalty after
Township tax, sewer, refuseFebruary 1March 31April 1 to May 31June 1
School tax (fiscal year July 1 to June 30)July 1August 31September 1 to October 31November 1

Sewer rent and refuse ride on the township bill, and sewer rent is figured from last year's water use. A sewer or refuse balance left unpaid becomes a lien. Real estate tax that stays unpaid goes to the Tax Claim Bureau in Media by the following January. The township tax office is at 610-544-1300.

Homes with an approved homestead may pay school tax in three installments, and the township's collection books close on December 31. Phone the tax office a few weeks ahead for your parcel's exact figure.

Transfer tax and recording in Delaware County

A transfer here costs 2 percent of the price, with one point going to Harrisburg and one to the township. Four places pay more under county rules: Radnor, Upper Darby, Upper Providence and Chester City. Springfield is not one of them, so the ordinary rate applies to your sale.

Pennsylvania makes both parties answerable for the tax, but your contract picks who actually writes the check. Put that choice on paper in the agreement of sale, and expect the title company to gather the money when you sign.

The Recorder of Deeds sits in Room 108 at Government Center, 201 W. Front Street, Media, and answers at 610-891-4152. The office will not draft your deed or search your title for you, and the only liens in its files are mortgages. Once your loan is paid off the lender files a mortgage satisfaction, which you can confirm later on the county's public access site.

What happens between contract and closing?

Most sales here follow the same order. First comes the agreement of sale, then the buyer's title search, then the inspector's visit. Open tax balances, sewer and refuse charges and any mortgage payoff are then totaled by the closing agent.

  • Request your tax balances from the township tax office a few weeks before the settlement date.
  • Get a payoff letter from your lender and locate your deed.
  • Fix the violations from the checklist above so the inspection does not push back the closing.
  • Confirm the transfer tax split in writing.

On settlement day you sign the deed, the closing agent subtracts liens and unpaid taxes from what you receive, and the paperwork travels to Media. Cash buyers have no lender appraisal to wait on, so their closings can come sooner, yet the township inspection and your tax bills still apply.

What to gather before you list

A short folder saves days later. Buyers, lenders and the title agent all ask for the same few items, and several come from township offices that answer by phone during business hours.

  • Your most recent township and school tax bills, plus a call to the tax office at 610-544-1300 for current balances.
  • Any permit records for decks, finished basements, roofs or other repairs, since the code office may ask for them during the resale inspection.
  • Sewer and refuse account details, because those charges ride on the township bill.
  • If you ever rented the house, proof that your Business Privilege Rental Tax Return filings are closed out.

Inherited the place? Find out from the estate's lawyer who may sign the deed before an offer is accepted.

Choosing how to sell quickly

Listing with an agent works well for a house in good shape. Clearing the violations above before it goes live keeps the resale inspection from delaying your closing date.

If the house needs work or time is short, a sale straight to an investor or cash buyer removes the bank's approval step and most arguments over repairs. Whichever door you pick, ask for price, closing day and transfer tax duty in writing. Then set each offer next to the amount a listing would put in your pocket after commissions and repairs.

Frequently asked questions

Which county records a Springfield, PA deed?

Delaware County. The Recorder of Deeds works from the Government Center in Media. Deeds and mortgages get recorded there, normally by the closing agent on your behalf.

What transfer tax would a Springfield sale carry?

Two percent, split evenly between the state and the municipality. Springfield is not on the county's higher-rate list.

Do I need a resale inspection to sell in Springfield Township?

Plan on one. The township offers a Resale Inspection Appointment Request on its homepage. Call the Code Department at 610-544-1300, extension 125, for the current checklist and fees before you list.

When is the Springfield school tax discount?

School bills go out July 1. Pay by August 31 and you get 2 percent off. Face amount is due September 1 to October 31, and the 10 percent penalty begins November 1.

What happens to unpaid sewer and refuse charges when I sell?

They become liens against the property, so they must be cleared. Phone the township tax office for the balance, and the title company will pay it at settlement.
